nodes.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: Archives, government and religious authority
strands.focus: Ranke’s church/state inquiry and Cam’s medieval local institutions use historical records for different political problems; neither alone founded all source criticism.
strands.works: History of the Popes (1834–1836); Liberties and Communities in Medieval England (1944)

strands.title: Parliamentary connections and collective biography
strands.focus: Reconstruct actors’ social and political connections; the institutional focus raises questions about ideology and people excluded from parliamentary participation.
strands.works: The Structure of Politics at the Accession of George III (1929)

strands.title: Voters and competing group explanations
strands.focus: Benson tests class-centered interpretations against ethnic and religious voting patterns in New York; this is a local historical argument, not a universal electoral rule.
strands.works: The Concept of Jacksonian Democracy (1961)

strands.title: Radical ideas and popular political action
strands.focus: Compare religious radicalism, Chartist participation and colonial peasant insurgency without making one a derivative instance of another.
strands.works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972); The Chartists (1984); Elementary Aspects (1983)

strands.title: Rights movements and political inclusion
strands.focus: Sustained organization for women’s rights is part of political history; it is not merely an appendix to histories of officeholders.
strands.works: Century of Struggle (1959)

strands.title: Collective claims and governing work
strands.focus: Tilly connects performances and repertoires with state/economic change; Cooper asks how colonial labor categories govern social relations. Their regional units and explanations differ.
strands.works: The Contentious French (1986); Decolonization and African Society (1996)

strands.title: Political rhetoric, symbols and social identities
strands.focus: Hunt uses Geertz in an analysis of revolutionary authority and joins symbolic practices with the sociology of political actors.
strands.works: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984)

strands.title: Diplomacy, conflict and expansion
strands.focus: Narrative accounts of political choices differ from Williams’s interpretation of ideology, political economy and American expansion; diplomatic history contains disagreement.
strands.works: The Guns of August (1962); The King’s Peace and The King’s War; The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959)

strands.title: Radical milieus, hostile sources and disputed labels
strands.focus: Davis questions inherited Ranter accounts; Thompson defends a historical milieu; Scott stresses anachronism and Smith disputes both sides’ handling of evidence and theology. These are different positions, not an adjudicated consensus.
strands.works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972); “On the Rant” and correspondence (1987)

strands.title: Local government, record production and representation
strands.focus: Cam’s inquiry connects the making of records, local courts and parliamentary representation. Documentary criticism and inferences about ordinary lives remain distinct tasks.
strands.works: Cam, Studies in the Hundred Rolls (1921), Liberties and Communities (1944), “Stubbs Seventy Years after” (1948)

strands.title: Narrative, motives and contemporary uncertainty
strands.focus: Wedgwood reconstructs decisions without giving actors knowledge of their outcome. Woolrych also asks what this approach leaves unexplained about allegiance and regional differences.
strands.works: The King’s Peace (1955); The King’s War (1958), prefaces discussed by Woolrych (1998)

strands.title: Narrative synthesis and specialist collaboration
strands.focus: Tuchman’s account of producing A Distant Mirror identifies research, medieval advice and editing. These contributions support a synthesis whose event selection and explanatory claims remain open to criticism.
strands.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), acknowledgments and foreword

strands.title: Political ideas in different social situations
strands.focus: Wood questions applying Namier’s skepticism about ideas to revolutionary America. His reading of Bailyn connects changing beliefs with social circumstances and unintended outcomes; it does not make all political action a deliberate pursuit of abstract principles.
strands.works: Namier, “Human Nature in Politics” (1955/2000); Wood, “Rhetoric and Reality” (1966/1968), 69–78

strands.title: Press freedom and institutional dependence
strands.focus: Goldman traces how municipal protection, financing and censorship shaped political printing. Public controversy emerged through conflicts among editors and authorities, rather than automatically following a declaration of press freedom.
strands.works: “Libertad de imprenta” (2000), 10–15

strands.title: Public spaces and competing explanations
strands.focus: Goldman uses a plural account of public spaces. Sábato asks whether the collection’s cultural emphasis loses explanatory specificity and overlooks republican currents or differences among cases, while recognizing its comparative value.
strands.works: Los espacios públicos en Iberoamérica (1998); Goldman and Sábato (2000)

nodes.label: Biography / life writing
nodes.date_label: Ancient roots · Strachey 1918 · Davis 1995 · crosses fields
nodes.description: Uses individual and collective lives to ask historical questions about character, social relations, power and experience. Documentary reconstruction, psychoanalytic interpretation, contextual comparison and relational trajectories pose different problems. Authors, subjects, editors and collaborators shape the surviving account.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Ancient roots; Carlyle’s On Heroes (1841) is one nineteenth-century strand, not its sole foundation. Strachey (1918); Erikson (1958); Davis (1995).

representative_people.context: The opening Heroes lecture gives creative individuals and practical belief a large explanatory role. This is one nineteenth-century strand, not biography’s origin or all Carlyle’s historical writing.
representative_people.works: On Heroes (1841), Lecture I opening (5 May 1840)

representative_people.context: Selects compact portraits using French eloges models and existing biographies. Woolf later praises one royal biography while criticizing another; neither authorial impartiality nor a uniform critical verdict is assumed.
representative_people.works: Eminent Victorians (1918), preface; Queen Victoria and Elizabeth and Essex, evaluated by Woolf (1939)

representative_people.context: His 1970 retrospective connects his Luther interpretation with individual crisis and social transformation. The 1958 book has not been independently read; its original metadata remains separate.
representative_people.works: Young Man Luther (1958); “Autobiographic Notes on the Identity Crisis” (1970), especially p. 750

representative_people.context: Compares Glikl, Marie de l’Incarnation and Merian without making them one universal female trajectory. An explicitly imagined prologue tests her categories; stories, religious difference, colonial power and textual mediation shape interpretation.
representative_people.works: Women on the Margins (1995), prologue, selected Glikl opening, conclusion and acknowledgments

representative_people.context: Revises her assessment of Strafford in light of documents and scholarship; sympathy for subjects remains open to criticism.
representative_people.works: Strafford (1935); William the Silent (1944); Thomas Wentworth, First Earl of Strafford, 1593–1641: A Revaluation (1961)

representative_people.context: Collective lives form an argument against racist historical exclusion.
representative_people.works: The Black Man (1863)

representative_people.context: Uses a female sovereign to examine gender and power in a society restricting women’s political participation; a contemporary reviewer challenges parts of the causal argument.
representative_people.works: Queen Victoria: Gender and Power (1990)

representative_people.context: Questions how convincingly Dorothy Thompson connects a female monarch with changes in women’s rights and republicanism; this is a particular review, not a neutral verdict on the whole book.
representative_people.works: “The Ruling Exception” (1990), review of Queen Victoria: Gender and Power

representative_people.context: Connects Mann’s life with a longer history of labour and radical politics. Collaborative preparation and the unfinished continuation matter; Murphy disputes aspects of her interpretive framing.
representative_people.works: Tom Mann and His Times, vol. 1 (1956); further fragments edited by E. P. Thompson, Our History 26–27 (1962)

representative_people.context: Offers a contemporary criticism of Torr’s framing of Mann, drawing on personal acquaintance and stressing moral/religious development; his alternative remains an attributed interpretation.
representative_people.works: “Tom Mann: ‘Courageous man of vision’” (1956 review)

representative_people.context: Uses reconstructed individual lives to teach social and economic relations, explicitly associating different people with different source genres.
representative_people.works: Medieval People (1924), author’s preface

representative_people.context: Eileen acknowledges her indexing of Medieval People. This particular editorial contribution is distinct from authorship of its historical sketches.
representative_people.works: Index to Medieval People (1924), acknowledged in the author’s preface

representative_people.context: Her memoir of Maitland interprets a historian’s scholarship and methods; this is distinct from her medieval institutional research.
representative_people.works: Memoir prefacing Selected Historical Essays of F. W. Maitland (1957)

representative_people.context: Admires Wedgwood’s mature biography while questioning occasional early eulogy and limits of biographical scale.
representative_people.works: “Cicely Veronica Wedgwood, 1910–1997” (1998), especially pp. 523–525

representative_people.context: Uses Enguerrand de Coucy as a vehicle through fourteenth-century events. The foreword explains the selection; Stone questions how well the shadowy protagonist serves biographical understanding.
representative_people.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), foreword; Stone review (1978)

representative_people.context: Mediates the 1877 commission for Delbrück to complete Pertz’s Gneisenau biography, in his retrospective account.
representative_people.works: Gneisenau biography commission (1877), recalled in Delbrück’s 1900 preface

representative_people.context: His unfinished Gneisenau biography supplies the project Delbrück continues; archival biography becomes a route into wider critical war history.
representative_people.works: Gneisenau biography, completed by Delbrück after the 1877 commission

representative_people.context: Uses minor acts and a portrait analogy to explain a life’s selective treatment of character. One ancient practice, not the origin or entirety of biography.
representative_people.works: Alexander, opening paragraph; archive translation credited to Dryden

representative_people.context: Argues that private particulars can make many lives instructive, while proximity and friendship can both supply and distort information. His moral premise remains situated.
representative_people.works: The Rambler 60 (1750)

representative_people.context: Interweaves letters, recollected conversations and narrative, explicitly adapting Mason’s example. Claims candid portrayal rather than pure praise; actual completeness is not established by that claim.
representative_people.works: Life of Johnson (1791), opening selection in Osgood abridgment (1917)

representative_people.context: Examines verifiable evidence, invention and changing biographical conventions. Differentiates Strachey’s books and asks why failures and humble lives should be excluded; her restricted English canon is not universalized.
representative_people.works: “The Art of Biography” (1939)

representative_people.context: Questions retrospectively unified life stories and examines trajectories across changing social fields. Institutional naming and the interview situation help produce the unity being narrated; this does not rule out every life history.
representative_people.works: “L’illusion biographique” (1986)

representative_people.context: Distinguishes modal, contextual, extreme-case and dialogic uses of lives. Accepts Bourdieu’s warning while emphasizing bounded choices within conflicting norms and questioning assumed group cohesion.
representative_people.works: “Les usages de la biographie” (1989), translated by Olivier Christin

representative_people.context: Levi uses his contextual presentation of the glazier Ménétra to discuss how context makes a life intelligible; Levi also questions treating context as static.
representative_people.works: Editor, Journal de ma vie: Jacques-Louis Ménétra (1982), discussed by Levi

representative_people.context: Levi cites reconstruction of Diderot’s youth to examine contextual comparison where direct documentation is missing. This is mediated methodological reception, not independent verification of the biography.
representative_people.works: Jeunesse de Diderot (1939), p. 16, cited by Levi (1989)

representative_people.context: Publishes Glikl’s Yiddish text, enabling later editions; the editorial history here follows Davis, not a new manuscript collation.
representative_people.works: Yiddish edition of Glikl’s memoirs (1896), discussed by Davis

representative_people.context: Her German translation preserves stories and moral reflection. Davis contrasts it with later abridgment; Pappenheim’s imagined reaction remains conjectural. She appears here as translator, not merely the clinical subject Anna O.
representative_people.works: German translation of Glikl’s memoirs (1910), discussed by Davis

representative_people.context: His translation removes tales and moral commentary and changes divisions, as Davis critically assesses it. The original translation has not been collated.
representative_people.works: German translation of Glikl’s memoirs (1913), discussed by Davis

representative_people.context: Davis identifies their jointly taught 1971 course as the setting in which she first encountered the three subjects. Teaching supplies a concrete research context.
representative_people.works: With Davis, Society and the Sexes in Early Modern Europe and America (1971 course), acknowledged in Women on the Margins

representative_people.context: Davis credits her with suggesting Glikl’s memoirs and dedicates the book to her and Certeau. Source discovery and intellectual companionship have a named role.
representative_people.works: Source suggestion and intellectual contribution acknowledged in Women on the Margins (1995)

representative_people.context: Davis credits Russian translation, research companionship and editorial insistence on clarity. These particular contributions do not imply authorship of the historical interpretations.
representative_people.works: Translation and editorial assistance acknowledged in Women on the Margins (1995)

representative_people.context: Davis explicitly draws on his account of stories and dedicates the book partly to him. This specific resource does not make all comparative biography an application of one theory.
representative_people.works: The Practice of Everyday Life, used in Women on the Margins (1995), Glikl opening

representative_people.context: His Schleiermacher biography and later methodological reflections place an individual in an intellectual and social world. The current claim relies on scholarly discussion, not an independently read biographical chapter.
representative_people.works: Leben Schleiermachers, volume I (1870); later reflections on biography and autobiography through SEP

representative_people.context: Advocates attention to unconscious motives while warning that fragmentary evidence and superficial psychological labels can mislead.
representative_people.works: “Human Nature in Politics” (1955; consulted Spanish translation, 2000), 144

nodes.scope_note: A genre and set of methods with ancient and varied roots, not inherently great-man history, psychohistory or microstoria. The selected roster combines earlier practices, modern historical work and critics. Davis’s comparison preserves religious and colonial differences; her imagined prologue is not historical testimony. Bourdieu questions narrated coherence without banning life histories; Levi emphasizes choices within constraints and investigates group formation. Biography can explain wider relations, but its scale and source gaps remain subjects of criticism. Non-European traditions and original translation witnesses require further research; the current selection is not exhaustive.

strands.title: Labour lives and collective authorship
strands.focus: Torr’s Mann project draws on biographical materials and collaborative preparation. The incomplete continuation, manuscript/publication distinction and Murphy’s criticism make the production of a life history visible.
strands.works: Tom Mann and His Times, vol. 1 (1956); further fragments edited by E. P. Thompson, Our History 26–27 (1962)

strands.title: Individual reconstruction and social explanation
strands.focus: Power pairs lives with estate books, letters, household advice and material remains. Her personal treatment is a teaching method; Postan’s later reconstruction makes editorial mediation visible.
strands.works: Medieval People (1924); Postan preface (1963)

strands.title: Biographical sympathy and revision through evidence
strands.focus: Wedgwood’s two Strafford treatments offer a case of reassessment through new sources and scholarship. Woolrych’s criticism of eulogy remains visible alongside his appreciation.
strands.works: Strafford (1935); Thomas Wentworth ... A Revaluation (1961); Woolrych memoir (1998)

strands.title: A life as narrative vehicle: reach and missing evidence
strands.focus: Tuchman selects Coucy to travel across a turbulent period but acknowledges documentary limits. Stone questions whether that organizing device yields a sufficiently understood person or explains wider institutions.
strands.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), foreword; Stone review (1978)

strands.title: Whose lives and which particulars?
strands.focus: Johnson’s private lives, Brown’s collective recovery and Woolf’s changed criteria show different arguments about biographical significance. They are not a single progression from great men to ordinary people.
strands.works: Rambler 60 (1750); The Black Man (1863); The Art of Biography (1939)

strands.title: Narrated unity and relational trajectories
strands.focus: Bourdieu asks how institutions, interviews and retrospective storytelling produce coherent selves, and proposes trajectories within changing fields. Life history remains possible under relational scrutiny.
strands.works: L’illusion biographique (1986)

strands.title: Scale, norms and bounded agency
strands.focus: Levi distinguishes several uses of lives and locates choices within conflicting norms. Group coherence becomes a question to investigate, not an automatic starting assumption.
strands.works: Les usages de la biographie (1989)

strands.title: Contextual reconstruction and its limits
strands.focus: Roche’s Ménétra and Venturi’s Diderot illustrate different contextual procedures in Levi’s account. Context can illuminate gaps while itself requiring a dynamic explanation.
strands.works: Journal de ma vie (1982); Jeunesse de Diderot (1939), mediated by Levi (1989)

strands.title: Comparative lives, religion and colonial power
strands.focus: Davis holds similarities and differences together, tests her categories through an imagined prologue and rejects a single progressive sequence. Marginality does not prevent participation in colonial domination.
strands.works: Women on the Margins (1995), selected primary passages

strands.title: Publishing, translating and cutting a life record
strands.focus: Davis compares Glikl editions with different treatment of stories and moral commentary. Pappenheim’s role as translator is distinguished from the clinical narrative about her.
strands.works: Glikl editions/translations (1896, 1910, 1913), discussed by Davis (1995)

strands.title: Teaching, source discovery and collaborative work
strands.focus: Davis names course development, source suggestions, translation, archives, libraries and editing as resources. A selective roster does not exhaust the acknowledged labor behind the book.
strands.works: Women on the Margins (1995), acknowledgments

strands.title: Psychoanalytic interpretation and critical limits
strands.focus: Erikson’s 1970 retrospective supplies a primary account of his Luther interpretation, while the original 1958 book remains unread. Levi’s generic psychobiography judgment is not an Erikson-specific rebuttal.
strands.works: Young Man Luther (1958); Levi (1989), methodological discussion; Erikson, Autobiographic Notes (1970), p. 750

strands.title: Individual life and historical surroundings
strands.focus: Dilthey’s biographical work and later reflections join individual initiative to institutions and cultural systems. Biography brings contextual factors into view that recollection alone may not supply.
strands.works: Leben Schleiermachers I (1870), through scholarly discussion

strands.title: Psychological motives and limits of inference
strands.focus: Namier argues that professed reasons may conceal unconscious processes, but insists that psychological origins alone do not refute an argument. His warning about fragmentary evidence limits the use of psychological explanations in historical lives.
strands.works: “Human Nature in Politics” (1955), Spanish translation (2000), 143–146

nodes.label: Annales
nodes.description: A changing journal-centered constellation: comparative inquiry, geography, economic series, belief, social imaginaries, and later experiments with representation and scale. Cultural questions belong to the founders as well as subsequent projects.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Marc Bloch; Lucien Febvre; Fernand Braudel, The Mediterranean (1949).

representative_people.context: Co-founder; comparison, belief and an active interrogation of traces complement social structures.
representative_people.works: The Royal Touch (1924; English 1973); Feudal Society (1939–1940); Apologie pour l’histoire (1949)

representative_people.context: Co-founder; historical conditions of belief and socially organized feelings, with later book-history collaboration.
representative_people.works: The Problem of Unbelief (1942); “La sensibilité et l’histoire” (1941); L’Apparition du livre (1958), with Henri-Jean Martin

representative_people.context: Multiple durations and models tested across changing historical conditions; explicit borrowing from Lévi-Strauss coexists with disagreement over time.
representative_people.works: The Mediterranean (1949); “La longue durée” (1958); Afterthoughts on Material Civilization and Capitalism (1977)

representative_people.context: The 1970 committee member’s medieval religious history connects changing conceptions of the afterlife with social organization; its chronology is a thesis to assess.
representative_people.works: La Naissance du Purgatoire (1981; The Birth of Purgatory, 1984)

representative_people.context: The 1970 committee member works across long agrarian cycles and intensive village reconstruction; these employ different scales and evidence.
representative_people.works: Les Paysans de Languedoc (1966); Montaillou (1975)

representative_people.context: Differential movements of prices, production and income support conjunctural inquiry. His 1956 introduction stresses uneven crises; later debate tests the model’s conditions and distinguishes his experiments from serial routines.
representative_people.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933); La crise de l’économie française à la fin de l’Ancien Régime et au début de la Révolution (1944); “Panoramas de la crise” (1956)

representative_people.context: Methodological interlocutor explicitly reprinted by Annales in 1960 and credited by Bloch for knowledge through traces.
representative_people.works: “Méthode historique et science sociale” (1903; reprinted 1960)

representative_people.context: Comparative/economic historian; Bloch also recalls his attention to contemporary life as a resource for understanding the past.
representative_people.works: “De la méthode comparative en histoire” (1923); Pirenne encounter recounted in Bloch’s Apologie

representative_people.context: Interdisciplinary synthesis and Febvre’s explicitly acknowledged formative reading; his publishing project also precedes L’Apparition du livre.
representative_people.works: Revue de Synthèse Historique; L’Évolution de l’humanité publishing project

representative_people.context: Reading depends on material forms and differentiated practices. Collective representations help explain social divisions; critical fidelity to Annales includes disagreement with Braudel’s hierarchy.
representative_people.works: “Le monde comme représentation” (1989); Lectures et lecteurs dans la France d’Ancien Régime (1987, contextual reference cited in the article)

representative_people.context: Medieval social imaginaries and a later co-directed women’s-history project connect different inquiries; neither represents all Annales.
representative_people.works: Les Trois Ordres (1978; English 1980); Histoire des femmes en Occident (co-directed with Michelle Perrot, 1991–1992)

representative_people.context: Models as explicit constructions and collective rethinking of social categories, within the journal’s critical-turn discussion.
representative_people.works: “L’histoire et les modèles” (1988); Les Formes de l’expérience (editor, 1995)

representative_people.context: Scale experiments provide an interlocutor for Annales’ methodological reconsideration; inclusion does not claim founding Italian microstoria.
representative_people.works: Jeux d’échelles: la micro-analyse à l’expérience (editor, 1996)

representative_people.context: Book historian whose drafting and research developed a project planned and revised with Febvre; preserve his distinct authorship.
representative_people.works: L’Apparition du livre (1958), developed with Lucien Febvre

representative_people.context: A psychologist explicitly used in Febvre’s 1941 account of emotions; a named resource, not an Annales historian or psychoanalytic affiliation.
representative_people.works: “Les émotions,” Encyclopédie française, volume VIII, La Vie mentale (as cited by Febvre)

representative_people.context: Collective psychology is a named resource in Febvre’s sensitivity essay, distinct from a generic Freud lineage.
representative_people.works: Introduction à la psychologie collective (as cited by Febvre)

representative_people.context: A productive reader of Febvre who questions blanket impossibility claims and dated psychological assumptions while acknowledging his intellectual debt.
representative_people.works: “Which Side Was Rabelais On?” (1983)

representative_people.context: Co-direction with Duby connects an independent feminist historical programme with Annales-associated collaboration, without making women’s history its derivative.
representative_people.works: Histoire des femmes en Occident (co-directed with Georges Duby, 1991–1992)

representative_people.context: A British interlocutor who reads Bloch and Duby productively while contesting specific emphases on rebellion and crisis; his inclusion records exchange, not Annales membership.
representative_people.works: Bond Men Made Free (1973); “Warriors and Peasants” (1974; opening consulted)

representative_people.context: Appreciates Hilton’s peasant inquiry but questions period differentiation and treatment of the changing state; a particular review rather than a uniform Annales position.
representative_people.works: Review of Hilton’s Les mouvements paysans du Moyen Âge (1980), p. 1069

strands.title: Founding exchange and historical problems
strands.focus: The 1929 editors invite exchanges across specialties, without claiming to invent economic/social history. Belief and culture are present from the outset.
strands.works: “À nos lecteurs” (1929); The Royal Touch; The Problem of Unbelief

strands.title: Braudel’s multiple historical times
strands.focus: Models must survive comparison with changing evidence; their failure matters. Braudel’s productive Lévi-Strauss borrowing and Chartier’s later objection to an explanatory hierarchy mark disagreements within this conversation.
strands.works: “La longue durée” (1958); “Le monde comme représentation” (1989)

strands.title: Economic series and agrarian cycles
strands.focus: Labrousse’s price/income inquiry and Le Roy Ladurie’s population/resource model differ in objects and scale; quantification does not define every Annales project.
strands.works: Esquisse (1933); Les Paysans de Languedoc (1966)

strands.title: Belief, imagined order and representations
strands.focus: Le Goff’s purgatory, Duby’s social hierarchy and Chartier’s representations offer different historical constructions, not one timeless collective mentality.
strands.works: La Naissance du Purgatoire (1981); Les Trois Ordres (1978); “Le monde comme représentation” (1989)

strands.title: Traces, questions and comparative reasoning
strands.focus: Bloch distinguishes deliberate from unintended testimony and origins from causes. Present observation can inform questions, without making past and present identical.
strands.works: Apologie pour l’histoire (1949)

strands.title: Historical psychology and its criticisms
strands.focus: Febvre historicizes collective feelings with psychological resources and a critical Huizinga reading. Walker later questions universal claims about what people could think.
strands.works: “La sensibilité et l’histoire” (1941); The Problem of Unbelief (1942); Walker review (1983)

strands.title: Village reconstruction and mediated voices
strands.focus: Montaillou uses inquisitorial records for intimate social history. Such records do not provide unfiltered speech, and small scale alone does not establish Italian microstoria affiliation.
strands.works: Montaillou (1975)

strands.title: Models and the critical turn
strands.focus: Lepetit and the editors ask how explicit models and categories can be assessed through historical evidence. Their reconsideration retains comparison and collective inquiry.
strands.works: “L’histoire et les modèles” (1988); Les Formes de l’expérience (1995)

strands.title: Observation, exceptions and generalization
strands.focus: The 1988 editorial explicitly engages microhistory; Revel’s later collective volume explores varying scale. This is an exchange, not a declaration that micro-level explanation replaces all larger patterns.
strands.works: “Un tournant critique?” (1988); Jeux d’échelles (1996)

strands.title: Books as material and social productions
strands.focus: Febvre’s plan/revision and Martin’s drafting form a specific collaboration. Printing is situated among economic, technical and cultural conditions.
strands.works: L’Apparition du livre (1958)

strands.title: Women’s history and collaborative limits
strands.focus: Duby and Perrot co-direct a multi-author project. Its Western scope and Annales’ earlier limited openings matter; feminist history has other origins and commitments.
strands.works: Histoire des femmes en Occident (1991–1992)

nodes.scope_note: Generations overlap and disagree. The founders’ exchange programme differs from Braudel’s duration, serial economic models and the 1988–1989 methodological reconsideration. Roster contexts include named resources, critics and collaborators, not a uniform membership list. Women’s history and Italian microstoria retain independent histories; their specific exchanges do not establish a single Annales origin.

nodes.label: Marxist social history
nodes.description: Class relations, exploitation, conflict, and historical change. British Marxist history emphasizes agency and experience as well as material conditions. Culture and experience were already central to some of its practitioners, notably E. P. Thompson; later feminist and gender historians both developed and contested these resources.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: E. P. Thompson, The Making of the English Working Class (1963); Eric Hobsbawm; Christopher Hill.

representative_people.context: Class formation joins material conditions with culture and agency; later essays examine time discipline and the norms through which crowds judge markets.
representative_people.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); “Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism” (1967); “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

representative_people.context: Labour and popular protest include cultural interpretation. His later Bandits revisions address myth as evidence and political power, retaining a qualified social-protest model. These changes do not make his position identical to Thompson’s.
representative_people.works: Labouring Men (1964); Bandits (1969; fourth revised edition 2000); narrative response (1980)

representative_people.context: Class conflict, religious argument and unrealized radical alternatives are related historical questions. Distinguish the revised bourgeois-revolution pamphlet from the later inquiry into radical ideas and its contested evidence.
representative_people.works: The English Revolution 1640 (1940; 1955 preface); The World Turned Upside Down (1972)

representative_people.context: Chartist research and women’s popular politics inform a critical class analysis; her interview recognizes neglected gender and ethnic conflicts.
representative_people.works: “Women and Nineteenth-Century Radical Politics” (1976); The Chartists (1984); Outsiders (1993)

representative_people.context: Production relations and class conflict shape the effects of trade. The reply to Sweezy preserves interaction, contested historical stages and a concession about insufficient evidence.
representative_people.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167

representative_people.context: Comparative peasant movements join production, conflict, political organization and belief; outcomes and evidence differ across periods. Acknowledges Bloch while criticizing particular Power and Duby emphases.
representative_people.works: Bond Men Made Free (1973); “Warriors and Peasants” (1974; opening consulted)

representative_people.context: Tutoring, translation and collaborative publication coexist with her own biography and political commitments. Accounts differ over whether the group should be understood around a teacher or cooperative practice.
representative_people.works: Tom Mann and His Times, vol. 1 (1956); further fragments edited by E. P. Thompson, Our History 26–27 (1962); Marx–Engels Selected Correspondence (English translation, 1934); Marx on China (introduction and notes, 1951)

representative_people.context: Caribbean revolutionary history with a changing account of leaders and popular action.
representative_people.works: The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963); lectures (1971)

representative_people.context: His popular historical synthesis became a focus for collective revision discussions in Hobsbawm’s account.
representative_people.works: A People’s History of England (1938)

representative_people.context: Crowd history supplies a specific resource for Thompson’s account of protest and market norms.
representative_people.works: The Crowd in History (1964), explicitly credited by Thompson (1971)

representative_people.context: Labour-history collaboration includes an edited collection, discussion of living standards and criticism of Thompson’s Making drafts.
representative_people.works: Democracy and the Labour Movement (editor, 1954); draft criticism acknowledged in Making (1963)

representative_people.context: Imperial diplomacy and international experience broaden the group’s historical questions; Hobsbawm recalls an independent voice in its debates.
representative_people.works: British Diplomacy in China, 1880 to 1885 (1939)

representative_people.context: External interlocutor: Dobb credits his rising-producer interpretation. The exact cited Tawney passage is unresolved; Christian socialism does not imply Marxist membership.
representative_people.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912); Religion and the Rise of Capitalism (1926); reception in Dobb’s 1950 reply

representative_people.context: Recovers plural radical historical traditions and participatory historical practice; the Communist Party group is one institutional formation within a longer history.
representative_people.works: “British Marxist Historians 1880–1980 (Part I)” (1980); “Local History and Oral History” (1976)

representative_people.context: Feminist history develops resources from Thompson while disputing limits in his handling of women; her later recollection also describes his resistance.
representative_people.works: Eve and the New Jerusalem (1983); retrospective Thompson discussion (2024)

representative_people.context: Integrates gender, work, family and radical rhetoric into the making of class; an extension and reworking, not a transition from an originally cultureless field.
representative_people.works: The Struggle for the Breeches: Gender and the Making of the British Working Class (1995)

representative_people.context: Questions how particular political idioms give class meaning. This marks a specific disputed reorientation, not a shared position of all critics or a documented direct attack on Dorothy Thompson.
representative_people.works: Languages of Class (1983)

representative_people.context: Defends a historically grounded class interpretation against different critics; his opening notes limit a Chartist claim to the existence, not typicality, of anti-capitalist ideas. Selected body passages welcome attention to language while disputing its separation from material constraints and highlighting anti-capitalist arguments.
representative_people.works: “In Defence of Class” (1987; opening and notes consulted)

representative_people.context: Questions the definition of feudalism and transfer of evidence between regions; his account permits money and instability while disputing their transformative effects.
representative_people.works: “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), critique; opening pp. 134–137 consulted

representative_people.context: A Japanese intervention develops the social form of labour and questions Dobb’s geographical coverage. The essay explicitly limits this discussion to Western Europe.
representative_people.works: “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism: A Contribution to the Sweezy-Dobb Controversy” (1952 English translation; opening consulted)

representative_people.context: Peasant research is a named resource in Dobb’s reply and Hilton’s later synthesis. The 1956 work is the Hilton context; it is not projected backward as a publication read by Dobb in 1950.
representative_people.works: Studies in the Agrarian History of England in the Thirteenth Century (1956), cited by Hilton (1973); earlier peasant interpretation cited by Dobb (1950)

representative_people.context: Hill values Barg’s differentiation of bourgeois revolutions and disagreement within Soviet Marxism. This is documented reception through Hill, not a full reading of Barg’s Russian books.
representative_people.works: Barg’s scholarship discussed in Hill, “The Bourgeois Revolutions in Soviet Scholarship” (1986)

representative_people.context: Offers a specific Marxist review of Flexner; this selection identifies the argument in the review, not a fully researched career or universal Marxist position.
representative_people.works: “Century of Women’s Struggle” (International Socialist Review, 1960)

representative_people.context: In the 1978 exchange she challenges Stone’s crisis/progress assumptions and defends Tuchman’s narrative interpretation, explicitly without assigning Tuchman to Marxism. This selection concerns that dated intervention.
representative_people.works: Letter in “Tuchman and History” (7 December 1978)

strands.title: Feudalism, labour forms and capitalist development
strands.focus: Dobb gives priority to production relations while allowing trade to interact with conflict. Sweezy questions definition and regional transfer; Takahashi develops labour-form analysis and challenges limited coverage. These are distinct positions.
strands.works: Studies (1946); Sweezy–Dobb exchange (1950); Takahashi contribution (1952)

strands.title: Revolution, religion and radical alternatives
strands.focus: Hill’s 1955 revision call and 1972 radical inquiry have different emphases. Dobb’s resource, Hilton’s draft advice and Barg’s comparative work reveal concrete exchanges; belief and unrealized alternatives belong within social explanation.
strands.works: Hill (1955 preface; 1972; 1986 review)

strands.title: Class formation, labour and popular politics
strands.focus: The Thompsons and Hobsbawm investigate different objects. Experience, organization, families and political language cannot be collapsed into one class model.
strands.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); “Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism” (1967); “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971); Labouring Men (1964); The Chartists (1984)

strands.title: Collective research, tutoring and public history
strands.focus: Morton’s synthesis, Torr’s guidance and Saville’s organizing connect academic and nonacademic inquiry. Tributes and later accounts frame the group differently; drafts, translation, editing and political discipline all belong to its history.
strands.works: A People’s History of England (1938); Democracy and the Labour Movement (1954); Tom Mann and His Times (1956); Hobsbawm (1978); Samuel (1980)

strands.title: Crowds, markets and customary legitimacy
strands.focus: Rudé supplies an explicit resource for Thompson’s inquiry into how people justify and organize market protest. Material deprivation matters, but it does not by itself explain collective action.
strands.works: The Crowd in History (1964); “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

strands.title: Time, labour and industrial discipline
strands.focus: Thompson combines historical and anthropological resources to examine work rhythms, wages, education and coercion. Task and clock time overlap; transformation is uneven.
strands.works: “Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism” (1967)

strands.title: Empire and international exchanges
strands.focus: Kiernan’s diplomacy and James’s Caribbean revolution widen the British focus in different ways. Hobsbawm recalls reading James despite political divisions; James retains an independent intellectual project.
strands.works: British Diplomacy in China, 1880 to 1885 (1939); The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963)

strands.title: Gender, family and the making of class
strands.focus: Dorothy Thompson, Taylor and Clark pursue different combinations of class and gender inquiry. Feminist inheritance and criticism coexist, as do disagreements about cooperation and conflict.
strands.works: “Women and Nineteenth-Century Radical Politics” (1976); Eve and the New Jerusalem (1983); The Struggle for the Breeches (1995)

strands.title: Language, experience and contested class interpretation
strands.focus: Stedman Jones questions political idioms; Kirk defends a class interpretation with limited claims. Dorothy insists language already requires contextual reading. These interventions do not form one debate between two uniform camps.
strands.works: Languages of Class (1983); “In Defence of Class” (1987); Dorothy Thompson interview

strands.title: Peasant movements, belief and political aims
strands.focus: Hilton compares 1381 with continental movements while examining aims, allies and outcomes. Conflict does not mean constant open warfare; economic/social relations require political and religious analysis. Neither quick defeat nor later change settles causation.
strands.works: Bond Men Made Free (1973), selected introduction and conclusion

nodes.scope_note: British Marxist social history is the focus, with selected Caribbean and imperial exchanges and earlier radical traditions. Party-group collaboration, independent journals, adult education and later feminist or linguistic debates are different formations. The rosters include external interlocutors and critics; neither membership nor a single theory of culture, class or historical change is implied.

coverage.basis: Reviewed through 2000 in the original 1920–2000 experiment. Later work is not yet surveyed for this entry; selected later interventions, where present, are dated individually.

nodes.label: Black history
nodes.description: Challenges racist historical narratives and recovers Black agency, institutions, and political struggle. Abolitionism, community scholarship, and Black institutions provide independent roots, not merely applications of European theory.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: William Wells Brown; George Washington Williams (1882–83); Carter G. Woodson; W. E. B. Du Bois, Black Reconstruction (1935). Carter G. Woodson and colleagues founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History (now ASALH) in 1915. Postwar and later examples include John Hope Franklin, From Slavery to Freedom (1947), and Darlene Clark Hine, Black Women in White (1989).

representative_people.works: The Black Man: His Antecedents, His Genius, and His Achievements (1863)

nodes.scope_note: Independent scholarship, community education, publishing and collecting precede later academic recognition. Biography, national synthesis and Black women’s history pursue different questions. This selection remains weighted toward African American scholarship; diaspora links do not make all Black histories one national tradition.

nodes.label: Anti-colonial histories
nodes.description: Recasts empire through slavery, resistance, liberation, and colonized peoples’ historical agency. Caribbean, African, and other projects develop through different political struggles and intellectual traditions; historical scholarship and theories of decolonization overlap without forming one school.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: C. L. R. James, The Black Jacobins (1938); Eric Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944); Frantz Fanon, The Wretched of the Earth (1961); Walter Rodney, How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972). Individual entries distinguish their contributions.

representative_people.context: Recasts revolutionary history through enslaved people’s action; successive versions reflect changing political and dramatic concerns.
representative_people.works: The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963)

representative_people.context: Makes distinct, disputed arguments about slavery, capitalist development and abolition.
representative_people.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944)

representative_people.context: Psychiatrist and political theorist of domination and liberation; not the same kind of historical inquiry as Williams or James.
representative_people.works: The Wretched of the Earth (1961)

representative_people.context: Connects African economic history, unequal power and popular political education; underdevelopment is a historical relationship.
representative_people.works: How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972); The Groundings with My Brothers (1969)

representative_people.context: Challenges imperial claims to civilization and examines colonialism’s effects on the colonizer.
representative_people.works: Discourse on Colonialism (1950; revised 1955; English 1972)

representative_people.context: Relates culture and liberation to production, class differences and political organization.
representative_people.works: “National Liberation and Culture” (1970), in Return to the Source (1973)

representative_people.context: An Indian precursor who redeploys political economy against colonial assurances; drain analysis does not require rejecting every European theoretical resource.
representative_people.works: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901),55–56

nodes.scope_note: James, Williams, Fanon, and Rodney make different arguments. Colonial subjects and liberation politics do not establish one school or Marxist identity. Césaire’s polemic and Cabral’s political theory add distinct questions; cultural struggle and economic explanation can interact. The present Caribbean/African selection does not exhaust anti-colonial historical writing in Asia or elsewhere. Naoroji adds one Indian precursor through a specific1901argument; his use of Mill distinguishes theoretical borrowing from acceptance of colonial policy.

strands.title: Colonial domination and liberation

nodes.label: Women’s history
nodes.date_label: Nineteenth-century and interwar work; renewed expansion from the 1960s
nodes.description: Studies women as historical actors and examines work, family, politics, and structures of power. Earlier scholarship, activism, teaching, and documentary collecting precede the field’s expansion alongside later feminist movements. Recovery, institutional growth, rediscovery, and methodological disagreement overlap; this is not a field created from nothing in the 1960s or one account of a shared female experience.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Lucy Maynard Salmon, Domestic Service (1897); Alice Clark (1919); Ivy Pinchbeck (1930); Julia Cherry Spruill (1938); Mary Ritter Beard (1946); Eleanor Flexner (1959); Eileen Power; Dorothy Thompson; later work by Gerda Lerner and Sheila Rowbotham. Individual entries distinguish contributions and approaches. Leonore Davidoff and Catherine Hall: Family Fortunes (1987); Elizabeth Fox-Genovese: Within the Plantation Household (1988).

representative_people.context: Investigates domestic employment through both employers and workers, historical change and statistical comparison; she distinguishes inquiry from a cure for household difficulties.
representative_people.works: Domestic Service (1897; expanded second edition 1901); Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

representative_people.context: Explains changes in women’s work and wages through training, household organization and industrial/agrarian change. Her qualified optimistic interpretation differs from Clark’s longer decline account.

representative_people.works: Ehefrau und Mutter in der Rechtsentwicklung (1907), scholarly account in Graf (2020)

representative_people.context: Her comparison of men’s and women’s inventories is an explicit starting point for Vickery’s inquiry into meanings.
representative_people.works: “A Possession of One’s Own” (1986), through Vickery (1998); Consumer Behaviour (1996), preface

representative_people.context: Examines routine purchasing authority alongside unequal access to property and uncertain ultimate financial control.
representative_people.works: The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), selected “Elegance” passages

representative_people.context: With Catherine Hall, analyses gender, family and class in the English middle class; a standard work of women’s and gender history. Hall’s coauthor credit is retained.
representative_people.works: With Catherine Hall, Family Fortunes (1987)

representative_people.context: Coauthor with Leonore Davidoff of Family Fortunes; both credits are retained. Her imperial-history contexts remain distinct.
representative_people.works: With Leonore Davidoff, Family Fortunes (1987)

representative_people.context: Within the Plantation Household examines Black and white women of the Old South; a standard work of Southern women’s history. Her exchange with Stone on narrative is recorded elsewhere.
representative_people.works: Within the Plantation Household (1988)

nodes.scope_note: Earlier documentary, economic and institutional projects overlap with later feminist reconstruction and theory. Periodization, class, race, caste and regional contexts create disagreements within women’s history. Gender history develops some of these questions without superseding the field; this roster remains selective and uneven geographically.

strands.title: Earlier histories of work and their disagreements
strands.focus: Clark’s overlapping household forms and Pinchbeck’s industrial transition ask different period questions. Paid and unpaid production, training, marital status and class complicate a single progress/decline story; maternalist commitments remain visible.
strands.works: Clark (1919); Pinchbeck (1930)

strands.title: Documents, rights and historical agency
strands.focus: Beard’s documentary project, Spruill’s colonial study and Flexner’s rights history offer different forms of recovery.
strands.works: Woman as Force in History (1946); Women’s Life and Work (1938); Century of Struggle (1959)

strands.title: Socialist and feminist historical work
strands.focus: Class, community and women’s organizing are connected questions, with differences among practitioners.
strands.works: Outsiders (1993); Hidden from History (1973); Eve and the New Jerusalem (1983)

strands.title: Work and family change
strands.focus: Tilly and Scott question assumptions that women at home were unproductive and that wage work automatically meant emancipation.
strands.works: 1975 joint article; Women, Work, and Family (1978)

strands.title: Period boundaries and historical explanation
strands.focus: Kelly’s Renaissance question and Lerner’s historical account of patriarchy challenge supposedly timeless or universally progressive narratives.
strands.works: “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” (1977); The Creation of Patriarchy (1986)

strands.title: Black women’s historical questions
strands.focus: Slavery, professional institutions, religion and racial analysis are distinct subjects and methods.
strands.works: Black Women in White (1989); Ar’n’t I a Woman? (1985); Righteous Discontent (1993)

strands.title: National and regional syntheses
strands.focus: French collaborative synthesis, German social history and Nigerian women’s history have different scopes and documentary bases.
strands.works: Histoire des femmes, vol. 4 (1991); Women in German History (1989 English); Nigerian Women (1992)

strands.title: Life histories and written lives
strands.focus: Davis, Bozzoli/Nkotsoe and Kaplan use different personal evidence; no single life stands for all women.
strands.works: Women on the Margins (1995); Women of Phokeng (1991); Between Dignity and Despair (1998)

strands.title: Caste and historical patriarchy
strands.focus: Chakravarti examines upper-caste sexual control and social hierarchy through early Indian texts. Prescriptions must be distinguished from lived practices.
strands.works: “Conceptualising Brahmanical Patriarchy” (1993)

strands.title: Medieval women, rules and recorded practice
strands.focus: Power examines the production and survival of visitation evidence and warns against equating a catalogue of faults with the whole life of a community. Her confidence in truthful findings remains an argument to test.
strands.works: Medieval English Nunneries (1922), pp. 493–498

strands.title: Collecting records, access and unequal authority
strands.focus: Preserving documents, making them discoverable and bringing them into teaching involve collective labor. WCWA’s broadened mission and Black women’s limited authority/funding complicate an uncomplicated recovery narrative.
strands.works: WCWA and Smith collecting; Voss-Hubbard (1995); Cott, ed., A Woman Making History (1991)

strands.title: Southern women: documentary scope and later reissues
strands.focus: Spruill distinguishes domestic institutions, public activity and status. Scott’s reissues renew access; Richter values the book while questioning its limited inquiry into Black and Native women.
strands.works: Women’s Life and Work (1938; reissues 1972, 1998); Richter review (1999)

strands.title: Rights movements, archival reach and historical boundaries
strands.focus: Flexner’s labor and Black women’s coverage broadens a suffrage narrative. Rupp distinguishes participants’ self-definition from historians’ expanded categories; James asks a different question about structural explanation.
strands.works: Century of Struggle (1959); James (1960) and Rupp (1992) reception

nodes.label: Modernization theory
nodes.description: Explains change through transitions from traditional to modern societies. Often takes Western development as the model; social-scientific variants differ. Growth stages, democratic legitimacy and political institutionalization answer different questions. Eisenstadt’s later multiple-modernities program disputes convergence on one Western pattern while retaining comparative inquiry.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: W. W. Rostow, The Stages of Economic Growth (1960); Daniel Lerner, The Passing of Traditional Society (1958); Talcott Parsons, “Evolutionary Universals in Society” (1964); Seymour Martin Lipset, “Some Social Requisites of Democracy” (1959).

representative_people.context: Proposes five growth stages with qualified timing and some change within the traditional category. His dynamic-production discussion combines sectoral change and political choices; the staged hierarchy remains contestable.
representative_people.works: The Stages of Economic Growth (1960), chapter 2, pp. 4–16

representative_people.context: Communication researcher linking media, changing dispositions, and modernization; his Cold War model is historically situated.
representative_people.works: The Passing of Traditional Society (1958)

representative_people.context: Compares institutional arrangements through proposed evolutionary universals and adaptive capacity. Explicitly uses Durkheim and Weber while acknowledging variation; his hierarchical and political predictions remain authorial claims.
representative_people.works: Evolutionary Universals in Society (1964), selected pp. 339–341, 348–350, 355–357

representative_people.context: Tests proposed associations among development, legitimacy and democracy. He distinguishes legitimacy from effectiveness and explicitly rejects guaranteed democratization, noting provisional comparisons and multivariate causes.
representative_people.works: Some Social Requisites of Democracy (1959), selected pp. 69–71, 84–87, 102–104

representative_people.context: Uses action theory and differentiation to frame changes in British cotton production and family life. The checked description identifies the project; Thompson’s separate primary criticism should not replace reading Smelser.
representative_people.works: Social Change in the Industrial Revolution (1959), description and contents

representative_people.context: Participates in the early comparative conversation acknowledged by Parsons. In 2000 he argues that modern cultural and institutional programs remain multiple, contested and capable of destruction as well as revision.
representative_people.works: The Political Systems of Empires (1963), cited by Parsons; Multiple Modernities (2000), selected pages

representative_people.context: Distinguishes political institutionalization from growth or electoral form and argues that mobilization can outpace institutional capacity. His priority of order and regional generalizations are situated, contested claims.
representative_people.works: Political Order in Changing Societies (1968), pp. 1–7, 12–13

representative_people.context: Coauthors an inquiry into individual modernity, research design and possible school/media/workplace settings. The checked contents identify the project; Eisenstadt later invokes awareness of wider roles and communities.
representative_people.works: With David H. Smith, Becoming Modern (1974), metadata/contents; cited in Eisenstadt (2000), p. 4 and note 6

representative_people.context: Coauthor of Becoming Modern. Authorship and the individual-change project are documented; the unread body’s sampling and causal findings are not certified.
representative_people.works: With Alex Inkeles, Becoming Modern: Individual Change in Six Developing Countries (1974)

representative_people.context: Lipset explicitly identifies multivariate analysis as a methodological resource alongside, rather than replacing, useful ideal-type comparison. This is a named reception, not adherence to a complete development model.
representative_people.works: Interpretation of Statistical Relations as a Research Operation (1955), cited in Lipset (1959), p. 104

representative_people.context: Lipset cites his definition of democracy as an electoral arrangement. This particular borrowing does not make Schumpeter a founder of every modernization program.
representative_people.works: Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1947 edition), cited in Lipset (1959), p. 71

representative_people.context: Parsons acknowledges discussion of evolutionary universals with Bellah and Eisenstadt at a 1963 Harvard seminar. The acknowledgment supports collaboration, without assigning sole authorship of Parsons’s proposals.
representative_people.works: Harvard seminar discussion (1963), acknowledged in Evolutionary Universals in Society (1964), p. 339

nodes.scope_note: Economic stages, communication and social dispositions, institutional differentiation, and democratization are distinct explanations. These contributors are not all historians, and the models do not form one inevitable path. Lipset explicitly denies automatic democratization, Huntington prioritizes institutional capacity, and Eisenstadt’s 2000 argument revises convergence assumptions. These differences do not erase hierarchical categories, Cold War purposes or disputed empirical claims in earlier models; a later program is not projected into every 1950s text.

strands.title: Economic stages
strands.focus: Rostow proposes five growth stages, qualified timing and a dynamic production theory attentive to sectors and policy choices. Permitting variation does not establish the staged hierarchy as a universal history.
strands.works: The Stages of Economic Growth (1960), chapter 2, pp. 4–16

strands.title: Communication and social dispositions
strands.focus: Mass media and changing orientations within a Cold War account of modernization.
strands.works: The Passing of Traditional Society

strands.title: Social differentiation and institutions
strands.focus: Parsons proposes adaptive institutional universals with variable historical development; Smelser applies differentiation/action theory to cotton industry and family change. Their specific claims and Thompson’s criticism must be distinguished.
strands.works: Parsons (1964), selected pages; Smelser (1959), description/contents

strands.title: Development and democratic legitimacy
strands.focus: Lipset separates economic development, legitimacy and effectiveness, investigates probabilistic associations and explicitly denies that greater prosperity guarantees democracy. His comparative coding and statistics remain open to testing.
strands.works: Some Social Requisites of Democracy (1959), selected pages

strands.title: Political institutionalization and order
strands.focus: Huntington asks whether organizations and procedures acquire stability and value as social mobilization increases. Adaptability, complexity, autonomy and coherence are proposed criteria; order-first priorities and empirical comparisons remain contestable.
strands.works: Political Order in Changing Societies (1968), pp. 1–7, 12–13

strands.title: Individual change and measured dispositions
strands.focus: Inkeles and Smith’s project distinguishes individual orientations and their possible settings from national growth stages. Available contents identify a scale and comparative research design; those headings alone do not establish its validity or causal findings.
strands.works: Becoming Modern (1974), metadata/contents; Eisenstadt (2000), p. 4

strands.title: Multiple modernities and contested cultural programs
strands.focus: Eisenstadt’s 2000 account separates modernity from Westernization and recognizes changing programs within and across societies. It includes destructive forces and challenges to the nation-state, without making every difference a timeless civilizational essence.
strands.works: Multiple Modernities (2000), pp. 1–4, 24–26

strands.title: Comparative methods, translations and collaboration
strands.focus: Lipset specifies Schumpeter/Weber definitions and Lazarsfeld’s multivariate resource; Parsons cites Durkheim/Weber and acknowledges seminar discussion with Bellah/Eisenstadt. Shared resources do not erase distinct explanatory aims.
strands.works: Lipset (1959), pp. 71, 103–104; Parsons (1964), selected pages

nodes.label: New social history
nodes.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm; Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society in Industrializing America (1976); Natalie Zemon Davis, Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); Charles Tilly; E. A. Wrigley and historical demography. Earlier social inquiry provides comparisons, not membership in a later school. Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996). Geoff Eley and Keith Nield: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980).

representative_people.context: Class is a historical relationship formed through material experience and culture; the Making preface explicitly restricts its study to English developments.
representative_people.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); “Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism” (1967); “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

representative_people.context: Chartist aims and organization connect political action with communities and class relations; her interview resists separating political leaders from their constituencies.
representative_people.works: “Women and Nineteenth-Century Radical Politics” (1976); The Chartists (1984); Outsiders (1993)

representative_people.context: Social and cultural inquiry into ordinary people’s lives.
representative_people.works: Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975)

representative_people.works: Domestic Service (1897), preface and chapters I–II

representative_people.context: Relates everyday claim-making and changing collective performances to wider political/economic processes; his chiefly British/French examples do not establish a universal path.
representative_people.works: The Contentious French (1986); “Social Movements as Historically Specific Clusters of Political Performances” (1993–1994)

representative_people.context: Historical demography and population reconstruction; a different evidential practice from cultural accounts of class formation.
representative_people.works: The Population History of England (1981), with Schofield

representative_people.works: Decolonization and African Society: The Labor Question in French and British Africa (1996)

nodes.scope_note: Class formation, demographic reconstruction, communities, and everyday life have different methods; Marxist history is one substantial component. The 1950s–1970s label marks expansion, not termination: later mapped works extend and dispute these programmes. Earlier women’s social inquiry remains visible as comparison. Neither one European class trajectory nor transparent experience supplies a universal model; critical interventions do not erase productive inheritances.

strands.title: Class formation and working lives
strands.focus: Culture and experience are part of class explanation, not a later replacement for it.
strands.works: The Making of the English Working Class; The Chartists; Work, Culture, and Society

strands.title: Community, culture, and collective action
strands.focus: Davis’s social/cultural inquiry and Tilly’s repertoires connect collective processes with meanings through different scales and methods.
strands.works: Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); The Contentious French (1986)

strands.title: Population and household reconstruction
strands.focus: Demographic reconstruction is one important component of the wider field.
strands.works: Cambridge Group population and household studies

strands.title: Mobility, property and linked lives
strands.focus: Separate occupational mobility from savings and property using linked local evidence; representativeness is a historical problem.
strands.works: Poverty and Progress (1964)

strands.title: Gender, family and middle-class formation
strands.focus: Study religious commitments, family arrangements, gender and economic opportunities together in selected English settings.
strands.works: Family Fortunes (1987)

strands.title: Colonial labor and contested categories
strands.focus: Chakrabarty questions universal class narratives through Bengal jute workers; Cooper examines colonial labor classifications and African social relations. Neither supplies one model for all colonized workers.
strands.works: Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Decolonization and African Society (1996)

strands.title: Experience, identities and historical explanation
strands.focus: Read Scott’s critique of foundational experience alongside Thompson’s historical class formation. Scott’s proposed historicization is not a consensus or a demand to abandon experience.
strands.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

strands.title: Peasant movements, belief and political aims
strands.focus: Hilton compares 1381 with continental movements while examining aims, allies and outcomes. Conflict does not mean constant open warfare; economic/social relations require political and religious analysis. Neither quick defeat nor later change settles causation.
strands.works: Bond Men Made Free (1973), selected introduction and conclusion

strands.title: Bandit narratives, political power and local research
strands.focus: Hobsbawm’s revised model responds to myth and patronage objections and draws on Colombian scholarship. Songs are mediated evidence; political actors and social settings cannot be inferred directly from heroic stories.
strands.works: Bandits (1969; revised edition 2000); Sánchez/Meertens (1987)

strands.title: Migration and the timing of observation
strands.focus: Ferrie’s response to Thernstrom asks who disappears from a local sample and what happens before its first observation. His male immigrant sample does not represent every worker or family.
strands.works: Ferrie (1996 manuscript),1–8,21

strands.title: Culture under capitalism: continuity or reworking?
strands.focus: Chakrabarty rejects deriving workers’ culture from economic function alone. Nair asks whether describing traditions as survivals makes them too fixed, and how their reworking within capitalism should enter the explanation.
strands.works: Rethinking Working-Class History (1989/2000), preface xi–xv; Nair review (1990), 98

strands.title: Separate spheres: categories, chronology and regional evidence
strands.focus: Davidoff and Hall connect class formation to gender and familial support. Vickery values their detailed research but questions its chronology and generalization: her Lancashire comparison crosses land and trade, while prescriptive language does not straightforwardly establish women’s confinement.
strands.works: Family Fortunes (1987), prologue opening; Vickery (1993), 393–401

strands.title: Experience, agency and changing discourse
strands.focus: Canning accepts the need to historicize experience but questions treating identity recovery and analysis of difference as alternatives. She asks how subjects reinterpret or transform discourse; this is a sympathetic criticism of Scott, not a return to self-evident experience.
strands.works: Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Canning (1994), 374–378

strands.title: Politics within social-history debate
strands.focus: Eley and Nield participate in debate about politics within social history. The verified article metadata establishes this intervention; no detailed account of its unread argument is supplied.
strands.works: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980), coauthored

nodes.label: Identity histories
nodes.description: Teaching shorthand for Hunt’s “identity politics” grouping: historical recovery linked to struggles over exclusion and recognition. Its constituent fields have much older and distinct roots.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Women’s, Black, ethnic, and other histories; this umbrella is itself open to criticism.

representative_people.context: Earlier women’s historical agency tests the limits of the later umbrella.
representative_people.works: Woman as Force in History (1946)

representative_people.works: “Priorities and Challenges in Women’s History Research” (1988)

representative_people.context: Caribbean and diasporic identities have histories and differences; recovery and representation do not disclose an unchanged collective essence.

representative_people.context: Questions treating experience as transparent evidence while retaining historical inquiry into how subjects are formed.
representative_people.works: “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

Recovery, multicultural synthesis, category criticism and self-determination have different stakes. Earlier Black and women’s historiography retains independent roots; named critics do not reject every collective claim.

strands.title: Recovery and historical agency
strands.focus: Compare independently rooted histories rather than treating a later umbrella as their origin.

strands.title: Multicultural historical synthesis
strands.focus: How do differently situated histories alter the account of a shared polity?

strands.title: Experience and exclusions
strands.focus: Scott’s historical question and Crenshaw’s legal intervention challenge different ways of treating groups as homogeneous.

strands.title: Diaspora and changing identifications
strands.focus: Historical recovery can coexist with attention to transformation, positionality and internal difference.

strands.title: Sexual categories and collective action
strands.focus: Distinguish historical explanations of identity from the claim that collective politics requires timeless categories.

strands.title: Self-determination and research authority
strands.focus: Who sets questions and controls knowledge? A generic recognition frame cannot contain all these claims.

nodes.label: Oral history
nodes.description: Oral history creates and interprets testimony through interviews, archives and collaborative projects. Recorded accounts illuminate events, memory and narrative, while the interviewer, editing and social relations shape the evidence.

nodes.label: Quantitative history
nodes.description: Uses serial evidence, linked records, statistics and explicit models to ask different historical questions. Labrousse’s prices, Henry’s reconstructed families, Benson’s voting groups, Thernstrom’s mobility and Curtin’s slave-trade estimates extend beyond cliometrics. Fogel’s counterfactuals and North’s institutions represent distinct economic programmes; Gutman’s criticism shows that evidence and interpretation remain contested within quantitative debate.

nodes.scope_note: Serial history, demographic reconstruction, and cliometrics use numbers differently. A quantitative method does not establish a common theory. Counting, source linkage and formal modeling require different assumptions. Recorded categories, missing people and units of comparison shape conclusions; neither criticism nor narrative history ended quantitative research.
