nodes.label: Postcolonial history / critique
nodes.description: Questions imperial knowledge, Eurocentric universals, and the assumption that all societies follow Europe’s historical path.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Edward Said, Orientalism (1978); Gayatri Spivak (1988); Dipesh Chakrabarty, Provincializing Europe (2000). Gyan Prakash: “Writing Post-Orientalist Histories of the Third World” (1990); Stuart Hall: “When Was ‘the Post-colonial’?” (1996); Paul Gilroy: The Black Atlantic (1993).

representative_people.context: Studies imperial authority through texts and institutions, combining discourse analysis with hegemony and attention to particular writers.
representative_people.works: Orientalism (1978)

representative_people.context: Questions intellectual representation through colonialism, labor and gender; uses deconstruction critically.
representative_people.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988)

representative_people.context: Tests European social-science categories against South Asian political histories while retaining their critical uses.
representative_people.works: Provincializing Europe (2000)

representative_people.context: Develops colonial historical difference through an explicit disagreement with Anderson.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

representative_people.context: Examines ambivalence, mimicry and hybrid cultural production; these concepts are debated interpretations.
representative_people.works: The Location of Culture (1994)

representative_people.context: Criticizes homogenizing accounts of women and develops historically situated feminist solidarity.
representative_people.works: “Under Western Eyes” (1984; revised 1991)

representative_people.context: Reworks Foucault through colonial archives, race and sexuality.
representative_people.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995)

representative_people.context: Historical anthropology examines the colonial production of authoritative knowledge in British India.
representative_people.works: Colonialism and Its Forms of Knowledge (1996)

representative_people.context: His criticism of idealized and denigrating images of India supplies a specific resource for Guha’s environmental argument. Original article remains to be distinguished from its documented reception.
representative_people.works: “Orientalist Constructions of India” (1986), especially442, through Guha (1989)

representative_people.context: Historian whose essays set out postcolonial historiography from Indian historiography and read Subaltern Studies as postcolonial criticism. His Subaltern Studies context remains distinct.
representative_people.works: “Writing Post-Orientalist Histories of the Third World” (1990); “Subaltern Studies as Postcolonial Criticism” (1994)

representative_people.context: Cultural theorist whose essays on diasporic identity and on the category of the “post-colonial” are standard resources in postcolonial critique. His cultural-studies context remains separate.
representative_people.works: “Cultural Identity and Diaspora” (1990); “When Was ‘the Post-colonial’? Thinking at the Limit” (1996)

representative_people.context: The Black Atlantic criticizes national and racial closure and reads modernity through the Black Atlantic; a standard postcolonial and diaspora text for historians. His Atlantic and diaspora contexts remain.
representative_people.works: The Black Atlantic (1993)

representative_people.context: Coedited Tensions of Empire with Ann Laura Stoler (1997) and coauthored its opening research-agenda chapter. The publisher describes a historical and anthropological inquiry into relations between metropole and colony and changing categories of colonial rule. This contextual inclusion does not identify Cooper as an adherent of every postcolonial theory; his later criticisms require a separate dated claim.
representative_people.works: Tensions of Empire (1997), coedited with Ann Laura Stoler; opening chapter, “Between Metropole and Colony: Rethinking a Research Agenda”

nodes.scope_note: Said, Spivak, and Chakrabarty address different problems; literary critique and historical scholarship interact without becoming the same discipline. Feminist critiques, colonial archival research and theories of ambivalence introduce further disagreements. These selections do not make postcolonial thought synonymous with South Asian history, literary theory or all anti-colonial politics.

strands.title: Imperial knowledge and cultural authority
strands.focus: Texts acquire authority through institutions and citation; individual writers remain consequential.
strands.works: Orientalism (1978)

strands.title: Representation and intellectual responsibility
strands.focus: Speaking for others and depicting them pose connected political problems.
strands.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988)

strands.title: Provincializing historical categories
strands.focus: Critique works through inherited concepts without treating Europe as every society’s model.
strands.works: Provincializing Europe (2000)

strands.title: Colonial nationalism and difference
strands.focus: Bengal supplies the setting for a disputed account of cultural autonomy and political modernity.
strands.works: The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

strands.title: Mimicry, ambivalence and hybridity
strands.focus: Colonial authority and identification are examined through unstable cultural meanings.
strands.works: The Location of Culture (1994)

strands.title: Feminist difference and coalition
strands.focus: Neither women’s situations nor feminist scholarship form a single homogeneous subject.
strands.works: “Under Western Eyes” (1984/1991)

strands.title: Race, sexuality and colonial archives
strands.focus: Empire becomes part of the history of European bourgeois sexuality.
strands.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995)

strands.title: Critiquing the romanticized East
strands.focus: Guha applies Inden’s critique of hostile and admiring Orientalist images to environmental appropriations of Asian traditions. This documents a particular reception, without making those traditions homogeneous or certifying Inden’s whole argument.
strands.works: Inden (1986), quoted and discussed by Guha (1989),77–78/note9

strands.title: Metropole and colony in a shared research agenda
strands.focus: Cooper and Stoler’s 1997 edited collection supplies a contextual reading on connections between imperial centres and colonial settings and the historical formation of categories of rule. This is the publisher’s description and contents, not a passage-level check or a claim that one programme defines postcolonial history.
strands.works: Tensions of Empire (1997), especially the opening chapter credited to Stoler and Cooper

nodes.label: Memory studies
nodes.description: Studies remembering, commemoration and forgetting through social relations, narratives, bodies and cultural forms. Recollection is evidence requiring interpretation; memory and history are connected in different, contested ways.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Maurice Halbwachs (1925) as a precursor; Pierre Nora, Les Lieux de mémoire (1984–92). Aby Warburg: Bilderatlas Mnemosyne (1924–29), as precursor.

representative_people.context: Social frameworks make remembering a relational process; later English selections are distinct from the original French works. The original French conclusion also addresses changes in traditions through relations between groups.
representative_people.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); On Collective Memory, ed. and trans. Lewis Coser (1992 selections)

representative_people.context: Studies sites where remembrance and historical reconstruction interact; his memory/history distinction is a situated argument.
representative_people.works: Les Lieux de mémoire (1984–92); “Between Memory and History” (English 1989)

representative_people.context: Brings habitual bodily practices into the study of social remembering.
representative_people.works: How Societies Remember (1989)

representative_people.context: Distinguishes everyday communication from institutionally maintained cultural memory while acknowledging collaboration with Aleida Assmann.
representative_people.works: “Collective Memory and Cultural Identity” (German 1988; English 1995)

representative_people.context: Studies the media and uses of cultural remembering; her contribution is visible beside their collaborative work.
representative_people.works: Erinnerungsräume (1999)

representative_people.context: Examines mourning after the Great War and questions a clean break between older and modern cultural forms.
representative_people.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995)

representative_people.context: Examines Holocaust memorials and museums as historically situated forms of remembrance. A 1994 adapted extract examines memorial production, political disagreement and public participation.
representative_people.works: The Texture of Memory (1993)

representative_people.context: Treats popular historical practices as part of the production of historical knowledge.
representative_people.works: Theatres of Memory, vol. 1 (1994)

representative_people.context: Interprets recollections of daily life under fascism without equating memory with either transparent evidence or resistance.
representative_people.works: Fascism in Popular Memory (English 1987)

representative_people.context: Brings feminist questions of subjectivity and the unconscious into historical work.
representative_people.works: Becoming a Woman (UK 1994; US 1995)

representative_people.context: Mnemonic techniques and their historical transformations provide a comparison with social frameworks and commemoration, without a founding claim.
representative_people.works: The Art of Memory (1966), preface and concluding chapter

representative_people.context: Studies archival access and historical authority; Derrida explicitly credits her investigation. Included as an archival-history interlocutor, without identifying archives with all collective memory.
representative_people.works: Archives interdites: les peurs françaises face à l’histoire contemporaine (1994), as cited in Archive Fever, p. 4 note 1

representative_people.context: Examines institutions, inscription and preservation/destruction while distinguishing an archive from spontaneous recollection. A conceptual contribution, not proof that all memory historians adopted it.
representative_people.works: Archive Fever (lecture 1994; English book 1996), opening and selected exergue

representative_people.context: Connects public memory with urban landscapes through collaborative historical work.
representative_people.works: The Power of Place (1995)

representative_people.context: Studies contested remembrance and human-rights politics in Argentina through a CEDES research project.
representative_people.works: The Politics of Memory (1994)

representative_people.context: Credited with active participation in preparing Jelin’s article; the credit does not identify him as its coauthor.
representative_people.works: Research contribution to The Politics of Memory (1994)

representative_people.context: Investigates Vichy’s changing political and cultural remembrance and historians’ position within that history of representations.
representative_people.works: Le Syndrome de Vichy (1987; revised 1990); Pour une histoire de la mémoire collective (1991), opening

representative_people.context: Distinguishes Jewish remembering from professional historiography; his separate essay on forgetting is explicitly used by Jelin.
representative_people.works: Zakhor (1982); Reflexiones sobre el olvido (Spanish 1989), as cited by Jelin

representative_people.context: Jelin explicitly uses her analysis of amnesty and mourning as a comparative resource; that essay has not been independently read here.
representative_people.works: De la amnistía y su contrario, in Usos del olvido (Spanish 1989), as cited by Jelin

representative_people.context: Jan Assmann discusses Warburg with Halbwachs as an early theorist of social and cultural memory, alongside the Warburg Institute’s own account of his library. A precursor in Assmann’s account, not a founder of memory studies as a field.
representative_people.works: Bilderatlas Mnemosyne (1924–29, unfinished)

nodes.scope_note: Halbwachs’s social frameworks, Nora’s commemorative sites, and Samuel’s popular uses of the past are distinct projects. Communicative and cultural memory are the Assmann project’s distinctions, not a universal taxonomy. War mourning, Holocaust memorials and feminist subjectivity require different historical explanations; this selection remains weighted toward European debates. Jelin’s Argentina project adds a pre-2000 case beyond Europe; it does not represent all Latin American memory work.

strands.title: Social frameworks of remembering
strands.focus: Family, religious and class contexts organize recollection; a collective framework is not proof of one identical group memory.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); English selections (1992)

strands.title: Sites of memory and historical reconstruction
strands.focus: Sites combine material, symbolic and functional dimensions, extending beyond monuments alone.
strands.works: “Between Memory and History” (1989)

strands.title: Habit, bodies and ceremony
strands.focus: Remembering includes bodily competence, not only recalled propositions or pictures.
strands.works: How Societies Remember (1989), “Bodily practices”

strands.title: Communication and cultural objectivation
strands.focus: Everyday recollection and durable cultural forms operate differently; Assmann revises rather than merely repeats Halbwachs.
strands.works: Jan Assmann (1988/1995); Aleida Assmann (1999)

strands.title: Media and uses of cultural memory
strands.focus: Writing, images and monuments organize what can be stored and recalled.
strands.works: Erinnerungsräume (1999)

strands.title: Mourning and cultural continuities after war
strands.focus: Traditional and modern forms overlap in Great War mourning; this is not a template for every subsequent catastrophe.
strands.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995)

strands.title: Holocaust memorials and their contexts
strands.focus: Memorial forms and meanings vary across places and institutions.
strands.works: The Texture of Memory (1993)

strands.title: Popular practices of historical knowledge
strands.focus: Family research, images and reenactment make historical work visible outside professional writing.
strands.works: Theatres of Memory (1994)

strands.title: Life histories, gender and subjectivity
strands.focus: Fascist everyday life and feminist psychoanalytic inquiry are distinct routes into interpreted recollection.
strands.works: Passerini (1987); Alexander (1994)

strands.title: Archival authority, access and inscription
strands.focus: Combe’s inquiry into access supplies a named resource to Derrida. His account differentiates archives from spontaneous memory and examines institutional authority and technical inscription.
strands.works: Archives interdites (1994); Archive Fever (1994/1996)

strands.title: Urban landscapes and public memory
strands.focus: Hayden’s collaborative practice links historical interpretation to lived places.
strands.works: The Power of Place (1995)

strands.title: Traditions in contact and conflict
strands.focus: Halbwachs explains revisions of collective remembering through contact with other groups and their traditions; social frameworks are not an assurance of a unanimous or unchanging past.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925), final concluding subsection

strands.title: Memorial production and public disagreement
strands.focus: Young’s Saarbrücken account follows a covert art project into public controversy and political recognition. His interpretation makes the memorial’s production and reception part of its meaning.
strands.works: Germany’s vanishing Holocaust monuments (1994), adapted extract

strands.title: Argentina: rights, remembrance and generations
strands.focus: Jelin examines competing public memories and tensions within human-rights activism. Her conclusion questions both political forgetting and repetition that prevents younger generations from reinterpreting the past.
strands.works: The Politics of Memory (1994), selected sections

strands.title: Vichy’s afterlife and historical inquiry
strands.focus: Rousso distinguishes memory as an object of research, as a preliminary examination of inherited representations, and as a way to extend an event’s historical study into its aftermath.
strands.works: Pour une histoire de la mémoire collective (1991), 163–166

strands.title: Jewish remembrance and historiography
strands.focus: Yerushalmi’s prologue asks why concern with historical meaning and remembrance need not give professional historical writing the central role. This is a situated historical question, not a timeless definition of Jewish people.
strands.works: Zakhor (1982), selected prologue passages

strands.title: Resources for studying forgetting
strands.focus: Jelin’s 1994 analysis explicitly draws on Yerushalmi’s transmission argument and Loraux’s treatment of amnesty and mourning. Their Spanish 1989 essays are distinct from Zakhor.
strands.works: Usos del olvido essays (1989), as used by Jelin (1994)

nodes.label: World / global / connected history
nodes.description: Moves across national containers through comparison, interaction, circulation, and connections. These approaches differ; global scale need not imply one theory of globalization.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: William McNeill (1963); Eric Wolf (1982); Sanjay Subrahmanyam (1997); Kenneth Pomeranz (2000).

representative_people.context: World synthesis and an explicit account of historical interpretation; source criticism and better-fitting accounts remain valuable within his ecumenical program.
representative_people.works: The Rise of the West (1963); “Mythistory, or Truth, Myth, History, and Historians” (1986)

representative_people.context: Historical anthropology connects peoples usually separated from accounts of European expansion; the recorded source remains a publisher/retrospective check.
representative_people.works: Europe and the People Without History (1982)

representative_people.context: Reconstructs circulation of people, ideas and goods across local and supraregional settings, criticizing national/area boxes without erasing differences.
representative_people.works: “Connected Histories: Notes towards a Reconfiguration of Early Modern Eurasia” (1997), selected primary pages

representative_people.context: Combines regional comparisons with coal location, overseas resources and colonial coercion; no single factor or uniform Eurasian path suffices.
representative_people.works: The Great Divergence (2000)

representative_people.context: Questions Eurocentric geographical and historical categories within an interregional history. His vocabulary and civilizational rankings remain open to criticism.
representative_people.works: “The interrelations of societies in history” (1963); Rethinking World History (posthumous collection1993)

representative_people.context: Edits and contextualizes Hodgson’s writings, acknowledging changes to spelling/transliteration and the institutional work enabling publication.
representative_people.works: Rethinking World History (1993), editor’s preface

representative_people.context: Reconstructs earlier intercity networks and argues against a predetermined European ascendancy; integration is explicitly partial and institutionally diverse.
representative_people.works: Before European Hegemony (1989); “The World System in the Thirteenth Century” (AHA copyright1993), selected later reprint

representative_people.context: Examines conditions of cross-cultural conversion, conflict and compromise before1492.
representative_people.works: Old World Encounters (1993)

representative_people.context: Compares economic change, state formation and protest without treating European development as the universal path.
representative_people.works: China Transformed (1997), selected chapter openings

representative_people.context: Studies competing national, local and transnational histories rather than making the nation a singular subject of linear progress.
representative_people.works: Rescuing History from the Nation (1995)

representative_people.context: Subrahmanyam identifies his multilateral imperial explanation as an inspiration while recording differences.
representative_people.works: Imperial Meridian (1989), discussed and acknowledged in Connected Histories (1997),741–742n16

representative_people.context: Indian Ocean comparison and trade research provide resources and contested structural models; Subrahmanyam’s criticism is not a neutral verdict.
representative_people.works: Trade and Civilisation in the Indian Ocean (1985); Asia Before Europe (1990), discussed by Abu-Lughod and Subrahmanyam

representative_people.context: Work on indigenous power and colonial imagination enters Subrahmanyam’s discussion of imperial symbolism.
representative_people.works: Les Hommes-dieux du Mexique (1985); La colonisation de l’imaginaire (1988), cited in Connected Histories739n11

representative_people.context: A comparative interlocutor whose regional-state framework is both credited and criticized by Subrahmanyam.
representative_people.works: 1997 comparative theme essay on six Eurasian polities, discussed in Connected Histories735–736

representative_people.context: An Ottoman self-writing study mediates a Davis resource in Subrahmanyam’s questions about individualism.
representative_people.works: “Self and Others: The Diary of a Dervish in Seventeenth Century Istanbul and First-person Narratives in Ottoman Literature” (1989), cited in Connected Histories740n13

representative_people.context: Ecological histories provide explicitly cited resources in Subrahmanyam’s account of connected changes.
representative_people.works: Ecological Imperialism (1986); cited in Connected Histories738n10

representative_people.context: Cross-cultural trade supplies a world-historical subject distinct from his quantitative reconstruction of the slave trade.
representative_people.works: Cross-Cultural Trade in World History (1984), bibliography in Rethinking World History (1993); The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census (1969)

representative_people.context: His household involution argument is disputed by Pomeranz; later criticism distinguishes rising output from returns to labor.

representative_people.context: Pomeranz explicitly uses his method of comparing positions within a larger connected system.
representative_people.works: Big Structures, Large Processes, Huge Comparisons (1984), through Pomeranz (2000),4/note3 and10

representative_people.works: Industrialization in the Low Countries,1795–1850 (1976),132–164, through Pomeranz (2000),21–22

strands.title: World-historical synthesis
strands.focus: Large-scale synthesis differs from tracing specific connections.
strands.works: The Rise of the West (1963)

strands.title: Capitalism and connected societies
strands.focus: Anthropological and historical inquiry questions isolated societies.
strands.works: Europe and the People Without History (1982)

strands.title: Connected histories
strands.focus: Circulating merchants, diplomats, religious specialists and ideas join local/regional with supraregional processes; connection preserves historical difference.
strands.works: Connected Histories (1997)

strands.title: Comparative development
strands.focus: Comparisons test explanations of divergent development; not simply a world-system model.
strands.works: The Great Divergence (2000); China Transformed (1997)

strands.title: Interregional history and historical categories
strands.focus: Hodgson contests maps and a single Western mainstream; the later edited collection transmits earlier essays.
strands.works: Interrelations (1963); Rethinking World History (1993)

strands.title: Earlier world systems and partial integration
strands.focus: Abu-Lughod’s intercity networks connect diverse subsystems without making all production globally dependent.
strands.works: Before European Hegemony (1989); Trade and Civilisation (1985)

strands.title: Cross-cultural encounters and religious change
strands.focus: Conversion, conflict and compromise are historical processes requiring conditions of contact.
strands.works: Old World Encounters (1993)

strands.title: Eurasian states, economies and popular action
strands.focus: Economic similarities and political differences require distinct comparisons; European categories need historical testing.
strands.works: China Transformed (1997); The Great Divergence (2000)

strands.title: Imperial networks and political imagination
strands.focus: Bayly’s imperial explanations and Gruzinski’s colonial symbolism are different named resources in Subrahmanyam.
strands.works: Imperial Meridian (1989); La colonisation de l’imaginaire (1988); Connected Histories (1997)

strands.title: Competing narratives beyond national unity
strands.focus: Duara frames national, local and transnational histories as potentially conflicting rather than one evolutionary story.

nodes.label: Indigenous history & decolonizing methods
nodes.description: Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and scholarly research meet in varied academic practices. Oral histories, family relationships, archival inquiry and collaborations contribute different resources; authority and methods remain situated.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier selected writing includes Guaman Poma (c. 1615/1616), Cusick (checked 1828 edition), Apess (1836), Te Rangikāheke (manuscripts before 1854), and Cree/Tainui interwar work. Twentieth-century examples include McNickle (1949), Deloria (1969), Adams and LaRocque (1975), Dickason (1984, 1992), Sioui (1989), Walker (1990), Kameʻeleihiwa (1992), O’Brien (1997), Wilson (1996), and Smith (1999). See the distinct approaches for works, collaborators and evidence limits. Related scholarship includes Miller, White, Harris and Lutz; Stó:lō field-school practice credits community and university participants. Leddy’s 2010 reflection supplies a separately dated later case.

nodes.scope_note: A selective grouping of independently rooted Indigenous historical practices and decolonizing research, with Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Māori, Osage, Native Hawaiian, Yukon and Australian examples. Earlier writing, community knowledge, academic historical scholarship and decolonizing methodology have different histories. Community historians, academic historians and outside collaborators have different positions. Neither anthropology nor European theory is their common origin; no selection stands for every nation or protocol. Membership is a contextual intellectual contribution, not a binary Indigenous-identity classification. Journal counts are venue-based publication proxies and cannot date the origins of these practices or identify Indigenous authorship. Academic Indigenous history includes documented collaborations with scholars working across historical, anthropological and geographical inquiries. Shared research subjects do not establish intellectual descent. Later source dates are separate from earlier events; only Leddy’s 2010 article is accepted here as a selected post-2000 intervention.

strands.works: Vikings of the Sunrise (1938); The Coming of the Maori (1949)

strands.works: “American Indian History or Non-Indian Perceptions…” (1996)

strands.title: Collaborative Yukon life narratives
strands.focus: Three elders and an anthropologist collaborate; life interviewing and transmitted traditions remain distinct practices.
strands.works: Life Lived Like a Story (1990)

strands.focus: Rivera describes THOA’s collective work and community review; research priorities do not belong solely to outside intellectuals.

strands.title: Early Andean manuscript history
strands.focus: An early colonial-period historical manuscript, situated in a Christian and royal political framework. It demonstrates earlier Indigenous-authored historical writing without making a modern field or THOA descend directly from it.
strands.works: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno (manuscript c. 1615/1616)

strands.title: Haudenosaunee histories in print
strands.focus: Cusick’s preface presents gathering materials and translation as historical work. The 1828 second edition is a verified witness; printed publication is not the origin of the traditions it recounts.
strands.works: Sketches of Ancient History of the Six Nations (checked second edition, 1828)

strands.title: Historical argument and colonial commemoration
strands.focus: Apess challenges colonial historical judgments and Pilgrim celebration. His Christian moral argument is an earlier intervention; no borrowing by later theorists is asserted.
strands.works: Eulogy on King Philip (1836), selected paragraphs

strands.title: Ojibwe oral knowledge and written history
strands.focus: Warren’s history draws on relatives and tribal leaders while addressing white readers. The publisher’s discussion retains the author’s nineteenth-century assumptions and limitations.
strands.works: History of the Ojibway People (first publication, 1885)

strands.title: Māori manuscript authorship and colonial publication
strands.focus: Te Rangikāheke’s genealogy and historical narration survive within manuscripts and Grey’s altered publications. Attribution reveals an Indigenous author behind texts circulated under a governor’s name.
strands.works: Historical and genealogical manuscripts before 1854; material reused in Grey’s publications, 1853–55

strands.title: Cree narration and interwar writing
strands.focus: Thunderchild’s narration, Ahenakew’s 1923 recording and literary writing, his 1929 publication, and the 1973 edited book carry different dates and authorial roles. Cuthand’s 1995 criticism makes editorial selection visible.
strands.works: 1923 narration/recording; Cree Trickster Tales (1929); Voices of the Plains Cree (1973; 1995 introduction)

strands.title: Tainui genealogies and historical writing
strands.focus: Jones’s Māori-language historical work and the history of its publication distinguish interwar research from the 1995 posthumous volume. The institutional biography describes disputed reuse of an earlier English manuscript.
strands.works: Māhinārangi (1929); English historical manuscript by c. 1936; Ngā iwi o Tainui (1995, posthumous)

strands.title: Canadian historical synthesis and regional inquiry
strands.focus: Dickason’s studies of representations and historical synthesis sit alongside Stonechild and Waiser’s Saskatchewan study. These are different scales and collaborations, not one doctrinal programme.
strands.works: The Myth of the Savage (1984); Canada’s First Nations (1992); Stonechild and Waiser, Loyal Till Death (1997)

strands.title: Métis scholarship and criticism of representation
strands.focus: Adams’s colonial and class interpretation and LaRocque’s criticism of representation broaden the 1970s bibliography. Her 1999 dissertation p. 34 explicitly connects the earlier book to curriculum research and resistance. These are distinct intellectual positions.
strands.works: Prison of Grass (1975); Defeathering the Indian (1975)

strands.title: Wendat autohistory and historical interpretation
strands.focus: Sioui’s author interview supplies an explicit historiographical proposal about self-interpretation and oral transmission. His moral account remains attributed and situated; French and English publication dates are distinct.
strands.works: Pour une autohistoire amérindienne (1989); author interview (1991); English translation by Sheila Fischman (1992)

strands.title: Historical synthesis and Native history institutions
strands.focus: McNickle’s 1949 work and role in creating the Newberry centre in 1972 establish an earlier bibliography and institutional contribution. Neither the centre nor a university is treated as the origin of Indigenous historical knowledge.
strands.works: They Came Here First: The Epic of the American Indian (1949); Newberry history centre (1972)

strands.title: Osage historical writing across the century
strands.focus: Mathews’s 1932 work and 1961 history supply earlier and mid-century examples. The publisher describes oral and documentary historical resources; detailed methodological claims await the works.
strands.works: Wah’Kon-Tah (1932); The Osages: Children of the Middle Waters (1961)

strands.title: Hawaiian land history and sovereignty
strands.focus: Kameʻeleihiwa’s land history and Trask’s political essays provide distinct Hawaiian contributions. Hawaiian-language historiography has earlier authors; neither regional programme is a subset of the Māori examples.
strands.works: Native Land and Foreign Desires (1992); From a Native Daughter (1993; revised 1999)

strands.title: Aboriginal interviews and life writing
strands.focus: Gilbert’s interviews and Ginibi’s autobiography broaden the historical bibliography beyond university monographs. Their forms and authorial positions differ from each other and from community-transmitted oral histories.
strands.works: Living Black (1977); Don’t Take Your Love to Town (1988)

strands.title: Aymara political and local history
strands.focus: Mamani’s catalogued 1991 study complements the existing collective-history strand. The period 1866–1935 belongs to the subject, not its publication or the foundation of THOA.
strands.works: Taraqu, 1866–1935 (published 1991)

strands.title: Stó:lō community–university historical practice
strands.focus: Community priorities, cultural teaching, archives and university instruction contribute different resources. Planning in 1997 preceded the first class in 1998; elders, hosts and students also participated.
strands.works: Field-school planning (1997); first class (1998); later accounts (2009, 2011, 2016)

strands.title: Indigenous labour and exchange

strands.works: After the Fur Trade (1992)

strands.focus: Family knowledge, scholarly dialogue and mentorship shape historical practice; the roles remain distinct.

Selected nineteenth-century and interwar practices precede the 1970s–90s academic/methodological growth. The baseline selection is through 2000; a separately marked 2010 article supplies one selected later intervention. Open from revision 1.133: the former 2000 end was the atlas boundary, not an ending.

nodes.label: Freudian psychoanalysis
nodes.description: A clinical practice and family of theories concerning unconscious conflict, development, sexuality, interpretation and relationships. Freud’s changing methods, later child-analysis disputes, psychosocial history, linguistic rereading and feminist adaptations require distinct accounts.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Sigmund Freud; later adaptations include Erik Erikson’s historical psychobiography and Jacques Lacan’s rereading through language. Historical interpretation must address evidence and context rather than assume access to an unrecorded inner life.

representative_people.context: Develops an account of repression, association, dreams, sexuality and transference, then investigates group bonds. These are historically situated theoretical arguments; his clinical claims are not a substitute for evidence about people in the past.
representative_people.works: The Origin and Development of Psychoanalysis (1910; lectures 1909); Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego (1921; English 1922)

representative_people.context: Connects individual development with historical social orders, and asks that the identity-crisis concept itself face historical scrutiny. His later Luther formulation remains his interpretation.
representative_people.works: Young Man Luther (1958), existing metadata; “Autobiographic Notes on the Identity Crisis” (1970), selected primary passages

representative_people.context: Rereads Freud through identification, signifying relations and symbolic exchange; his return is a contested intervention in psychoanalysis.
representative_people.works: “Le stade du miroir” (1949); “Fonction et champ” (report 1953; publication 1956); “L’instance de la lettre” (1957); collected Écrits (1966)

representative_people.context: Freud credits an earlier cathartic practice while distinguishing it from his later account of repression. Breuer treated the patient later known as Anna O.; Freud did not.
representative_people.works: Studies on Hysteria (1895), with Freud, as discussed in the Clark lectures

representative_people.context: Freud recalls his Paris training as a resource while distinguishing later psychological explanations. This is Freud’s account, not a complete review of Charcot.
representative_people.works: Clinical work recalled in Freud’s Clark Lecture II (1910)

representative_people.context: Hypnotic recall supplies an experimental prompt in Freud’s account; he later questions treating suggestion as a final explanation.
representative_people.works: Nancy observations recalled in Clark Lecture II (1910); Group Psychology IV (1921)

representative_people.context: Freud explicitly credits association experiments and the Zurich complex vocabulary in 1909. This dated collaboration does not imply agreement throughout their later careers.
representative_people.works: Diagnostische Assoziationsstudien (1906), cited in Clark Lecture III

representative_people.context: Freud uses his catalytic analogy for the analyst’s role in transference. The cited article remains mediated through the lecture.
representative_people.works: “Introjektion und Übertragung” (1909), cited in Clark Lecture V

representative_people.context: Her defense concepts are a named resource for Gay’s proposed historical research; her work also belongs to contested developments in child analysis. Lacan’s 1949 mirror-stage paper explicitly invokes her defense concepts; this is another specific reception, without implying agreement across child-analysis schools.
representative_people.works: Defense concepts discussed by Gay (1997); child-analysis practice discussed by Amos (2015)

representative_people.context: Uses children’s play to interpret an inner world and develops accounts of anxiety and defense. The institutional overview describes disagreements; original clinical writings remain unread.
representative_people.works: The Psycho-Analysis of Children (1932); “Notes on Some Schizoid Mechanisms” (1946)

representative_people.context: The publisher presents her feminist use of psychoanalysis as an explanation of patriarchy rather than its endorsement; this is one contested feminist position.
representative_people.works: Psychoanalysis and Feminism (1974; reissue 2000)

representative_people.context: Challenges Freud’s Leonardo interpretation through translation, source context and alternative explanations. Faulty application is distinguished from disproof of all psychoanalysis.
representative_people.works: “Leonardo and Freud: An Art-Historical Study” (1956), selected passages

representative_people.context: Linguistic resource explicitly credited by Lacan for his discussion of metonymy; this is a psychoanalytic appropriation, not a clinical affiliation.
representative_people.works: Fundamentals of Language, with Morris Halle, cited in Lacan’s “L’instance de la lettre” (1957), notes 3 and 10

representative_people.context: Defends Lacan’s return to Freud while later qualifying culturalist overtones of his own reading. A philosophical intervention in Communist debates, not a clinical case study.
representative_people.works: “Freud and Lacan” (written 1964; NLR 1969), public opening and editorial qualification

representative_people.context: Reworks Freud’s destruction drive and recording models in a philosophical account of archives; raises questions about technical supplements to memory without independently validating psychoanalytic mechanisms.
representative_people.works: Archive Fever (1994/1996), pp. 7–15; references there to Civilization and Its Discontents and the Mystic Pad

nodes.scope_note: This is a tradition entry, not an individual Freud node. Clinical claims and normative sexual classifications are historically situated. Breuer treated Anna O.; Freud’s account is not an independent outcome audit. Klein, Anna Freud, Erikson, Lacan and feminist interpreters pursue divergent questions. Historical motive inference requires documentary criticism; neither clinical access nor a uniform Freudian school can be assumed. Primary readings here cover the Clark lectures and selected Group Psychology chapters, not Freud’s entire career.

nodes.label: History of science
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots · History of Science Society founded 1924 · later approaches
nodes.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: George Sarton; Alexandre Koyré, Études galiléennes (1939); Robert K. Merton; Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962); Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985). Yates and Foucault provide additional, distinct contributions; they do not substitute for these historians and programmes. Further approaches include Metzger’s history of chemistry (1923), Maier’s medieval natural philosophy (1949), Fleck’s scientific fact (1935), Needham’s collaborative Chinese science project (from 1954), Rossiter’s Women Scientists in America (1982), and Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980).

nodes.scope_note: Kuhn is a central reorientation, not the field’s sole founder. Sarton, Koyré, Merton, and historians of experimental practice distinguish important approaches; Yates and Foucault are additional contributions. Chinese science and women’s scientific work expand this selection; it still needs fuller coverage of other regions and material practices. Named Chinese-series contributors and Daston/Galison’s image and instrument studies deepen the selection. Publication credits do not replace primary argument checks; wider regional coverage remains selective. Arabic mathematics, colonial Indian science, African healing and a Beninese knowledge programme are separate selected projects, not regional proxies or exhaustive coverage.

nodes.label: Hayden White / narrative theory
nodes.description: Examines how emplotment, argument, and tropes organize historical accounts. Narrative form helps constitute an interpretation rather than merely decorating established facts. His work raises disputes about historical explanation and representation; it should not be reduced to the claim that evidence is irrelevant.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Metahistory: The Historical Imagination in Nineteenth-Century Europe (1973). White’s analysis of historical narrative is a distinct contribution within debates grouped here as the linguistic turn.
nodes.scope_note: Metahistory’s formalist reading of selected nineteenth-century European works is one project; the1999 afterword also affirms a Marxian commitment. Narrative construction does not erase the distinction between historical and invented events. The1992 Holocaust essay is represented only by a short course extract, not its full argument.

nodes.label: Thomas Kuhn
nodes.description: Explains scientific development through normal science, disciplinary commitments, crises, and revolutions. Paradigms organize problems and standards of inquiry. Later sociologists adapt these arguments, sometimes in ways Kuhn disputes; this is not a universal law that all intellectual history moves through discrete paradigms. His preface acknowledges Koyré, Metzger, Maier and Fleck as distinct resources. The later distinction between shared disciplinary commitments and exemplary solutions makes “paradigm” more precise. In his 1970 exchange, Kuhn stresses substantial agreement with Popper while distinguishing tests of puzzle solutions from challenges to basic theory. Popper accepts that normal research exists but disputes its educational desirability; Lakatos later proposes appraisal of research programmes through novel predictions. Their accusations of irrationalism are criticisms of Kuhn, not his own stated position. Skinner, Dunn and deMause use Kuhn for different historical purposes.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962; expanded second edition 1970). Distinguish his analysis of scientific communities from loose uses of paradigm to mean any school of historical writing. Read the 1962 preface alongside the 1969 postscript included in the second edition: sources of the argument and later clarification are different evidence.

nodes.label: Bruno Latour / laboratory studies
nodes.description: Studies the practical work through which scientific claims become established facts, including experiments, inscriptions, instruments, and relations among researchers. Laboratory ethnography offers a route into science studies that should not be collapsed into textual interpretation or into Bloor’s programme. The Pasteur study extends his inquiry into historical scientific change and distinguishes that analysis from an explanation by social forces alone. Bloor’s1999response contests the treatment of sociological explanation in the Pasteur case. Law’s1986edited volume provides a particular publication context shared with Callon; collaboration does not establish agreement.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: With Steve Woolgar, Laboratory Life: The Social Construction of Scientific Facts (1979). The revised 1986 edition drops Social from the subtitle. Latour is one contributor within a wider field. Les Microbes: guerre et paix, suivi de Irréductions (1984; translated as The Pasteurization of France, 1988) joins historical investigation to a separate theoretical argument.

nodes.label: Sociology of scientific knowledge / SSK
nodes.description: Investigates how scientific beliefs become accepted within social practices and institutions. The Edinburgh Strong Programme seeks causal explanations of both accepted and rejected knowledge using the same kinds of explanation. SSK includes different programmes; it is neither all sociology of science nor all STS. Collins’s replication studies and Pinch’s work on controversies expose additional empirical programmes; these differ from treating SSK as only Bloor’s principles. Bloor explicitly includes material causes and rejects equating symmetry with equal credibility. His disagreement with Latour concerns the analytical roles of objects and society.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: David Bloor, Knowledge and Social Imagery (1976; second edition 1991); Barry Barnes. The symmetry principle is a rule for explanation, not a claim that all scientific assertions have equal evidential merit. Barnes, Bloor and Henry, Scientific Knowledge (1996); Collins, Changing Order (1985); Pinch and Bijker, “The Social Construction of Facts and Artefacts” (1984).

nodes.label: Science and technology studies / STS
nodes.description: An interdisciplinary field examining how knowledge, technologies, institutions, and social arrangements develop together. Historical, sociological, ethnographic, and policy-oriented inquiries coexist. SSK and laboratory studies contribute to STS but do not define its entire scope. Knorr Cetina’s comparative laboratory cultures, Harding’s feminist epistemology, and Sussex/Cornell institution building add distinct approaches and histories.

nodes.label: Conceptual history / Begriffsgeschichte
nodes.description: Traces changing political and social concepts in relation to historical experience, conflict, and expectations. Koselleck links conceptual change to different temporalities and to the emergence of modern historical consciousness. This overlaps with contextual intellectual history while asking different questions about semantic change across time. Collective German lexicon work, French studies of polemical usages and Richter’s comparisons represent distinct programs. Concepts can register and help shape social processes without exhausting those processes.

nodes.scope_note: Koselleck’s conceptual change and historical time differ from reconstructing a particular author’s intervention. Brunner, Conze and Koselleck’s editorial association does not imply identical methods or political commitments. Experience and expectation are formal research categories with variable contents; the proposed modern temporal transformation is neither a universal timetable nor a prediction of particular events.

strands.title: Words, concepts and overlapping semantic layers
strands.focus: The same word can persist while conceptual content changes; a concept can carry multiple historical layers. Koselleck combines synchronic usage with diachronic comparison without treating every word as a key historical concept.
strands.works: Futures Past, chapter 5, pp. 75–92

strands.title: Concepts as indicators and factors
strands.focus: Concepts register social relations and can help act upon them, but social events are not identical with their linguistic conceptualization. Historians must also distinguish actors’ terms from their own justified analytical categories.
strands.works: Futures Past, chapter 5, pp. 75–92

strands.title: Experience, expectation and unequal temporalities
strands.focus: These formal categories direct questions about remembered pasts and anticipated futures. Their asymmetry does not independently predict contents; Koselleck’s modernity thesis recognizes simplification, unequal social temporalities and recurring structures.
strands.works: Futures Past, preface and selected chapter 14 pp. 255–264, 271–275

strands.title: Collective lexicon, distinct programs and political criticism
strands.focus: Brunner, Conze and Koselleck participate in one editorial project with different research emphases. Criticism of Brunner’s political framing and textual revisions must be attributed and assessed through evidence, without assigning a uniform position to all editors and contributors.
strands.works: Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe; Koselleck’s preface and Tribe’s selected introduction

strands.title: French social roles and opposing uses
strands.focus: Gumbrecht and Reichardt investigate philosophe as a social role. Opponents can use similar semantic contents with opposed force; dictionaries participate in polemics instead of neutrally settling every usage. Their court discussion explicitly draws on Elias.
strands.works: Philosophe, Philosophie, Handbuch Heft 3 (1985), pp. 7–14

strands.title: Comparing conceptual history and political languages
strands.focus: Richter’s 1995 comparison makes differences among the German lexicon, French Handbuch and Skinner/Pocock programs explicit. Shared historical vocabulary questions do not establish one method or an origin of one school in another.
strands.works: The History of Political and Social Concepts (1995), chapters 4 and 6, abstracts

strands.title: Public opinion and contested sovereignty
strands.focus: Goldman distinguishes appeals to an enlightened general will from the divergent opinions of provinces. The meaning of public opinion changes within struggles over who can speak for a sovereign people.
strands.works: “Libertad de imprenta” (2000), 15–20; earlier joint presentation acknowledged in note 26

nodes.label: Psychohistory / psychoanalytic history
nodes.description: A contested range of historical uses of psychological interpretation: psychosocial life studies, psychoanalytically informed contextual history and theories of childrearing and collective fantasy. Disagreements concern sources, explanatory scale, historical variability and retrospective inference.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Erik H. Erikson, Young Man Luther: A Study in Psychoanalysis and History (1958); Peter Gay, Freud for Historians (1985). These projects should not be treated as straightforward applications of Lacan.

representative_people.context: Connects individual development with historical social orders, and asks that the identity-crisis concept itself face historical scrutiny. His later Luther formulation remains his interpretation.
representative_people.works: Young Man Luther (1958), existing metadata; “Autobiographic Notes on the Identity Crisis” (1970), selected primary passages

representative_people.context: Argues for psychoanalytic interpretation alongside external historical circumstances and distances his work from reductionist versions of psychohistory.
representative_people.works: Freud for Historians (1985); The Bourgeois Experience; methodological interview (1997)

representative_people.context: Challenges Freud’s Leonardo interpretation through translation, source context and alternative explanations. Faulty application is distinguished from disproof of all psychoanalysis.
representative_people.works: “Leonardo and Freud: An Art-Historical Study” (1956), selected passages

representative_people.context: Proposes an autonomous science linking childrearing with group fantasies. His causal theory and progressive narrative are contested, including by Pollock.
representative_people.works: Foundations of Psychohistory (1982), preface; “On Writing Childhood History” (1988), selected passages

representative_people.context: Questions deMause’s source selection and broad narrative of improvement. His later criticism of her 1983 book concerns inferences from diary silence; the exchange remains unresolved here.
representative_people.works: The Forgotten Children (1981 thesis), pp. 93–94; Forgotten Children (1983), discussed by deMause (1988)

representative_people.context: Gay values the integration of psychological and contextual explanation in his witchcraft study while disputing their relative weight. This is reception evidence.
representative_people.works: Entertaining Satan, discussed in Gay’s 1997 interview

representative_people.context: Gay recalls the 1950/1951 Freud reading circle as an impetus to his interests. Neumann’s wife also participated; the account does not name her.
representative_people.works: Freud reading circle recalled by Gay (1997)

representative_people.context: Gay recalls the 1950/1951 Freud reading circle as an impetus to his interests. Neumann’s wife also participated; the account does not name her.
representative_people.works: Freud reading circle recalled by Gay (1997)

nodes.scope_note: Erikson, Gay and deMause have different explanatory ambitions; they are not interchangeable applications of Lacan. Schapiro’s art-historical criticism supplies a methodological interlocutor, not blanket rejection of psychoanalysis. Pollock’s thesis and deMause’s later response address distinct texts and disputed evidential procedures. Original case books and wider political, religious and regional applications remain selective research limits; theoretical or clinical assertions are not established diagnoses of past people.

strands.title: Psychosocial lives and historical orders
strands.focus: Erikson places identity within somatic, ego and social orders; his later discussion relates Luther’s personal crisis to transformation. This is an attributed interpretation.
strands.works: Young Man Luther (1958); retrospective account (1970), p. 750

strands.title: Psychoanalytic resources within contextual history
strands.focus: Gay insists on external circumstances and inner life together; his qualified judgment of Demos shows disagreement about explanatory weight.
strands.works: Gay interview (1997)

strands.title: Childrearing, group fantasy and causal ambition
strands.focus: deMause proposes an independent explanatory science. His progressive model and reductionist commitment differ from other approaches represented in this umbrella.
strands.works: Foundations of Psychohistory (1982), preface

strands.title: Childhood sources, selection and silence
strands.focus: Pollock questions selected evidence and sweeping change; deMause disputes inferences from unrecorded punishment. The thesis, later book and reply are distinct texts, without independent diary collation here.
strands.works: Pollock thesis (1981), pp. 93–94; deMause (1988), selected reply

strands.title: Psychobiography and historical knowledge
strands.focus: Schapiro examines translation and contextual evidence in Freud’s Leonardo interpretation. His particular criticism neither dismisses every psychobiography nor directly rebuts Erikson.
strands.works: Schapiro (1956), selected passages

strands.title: Historicizing psychological concepts
strands.focus: Erikson asks for historical scrutiny of identity crises and the categories used to describe them. Retrospective self-interpretation itself becomes evidence requiring criticism.
strands.works: Autobiographic Notes (1970), selected passages

nodes.label: Frantz Fanon
nodes.description: Analyzes colonial domination through racialized experience, psychic injury, and struggles for liberation. A psychiatrist and political theorist whose work supplies historians with questions about subject formation, violence, and the limits of national liberation; his arguments are not confined to individual psychology.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Black Skin, White Masks (French original 1952); The Wretched of the Earth (French original 1961). Later English editions have different publication dates.
nodes.scope_note: Black Skin, White Masks (1952) treats racialized experience through psychological and social explanation; its introduction names Freud while insisting on sociogeny. The Wretched of the Earth (1961) combines liberation strategy, criticism of elite nationalism and psychiatric cases. These are connected inquiries, not one invariant doctrine or membership in psychohistory. Gendered and regional generalizations require critical reading.

nodes.label: Walter Rodney
nodes.description: Explains underdevelopment through historically unequal relations of slavery, colonial extraction and capitalism. Regional African research, Guyanese labor history and popular education give his work distinct scales and audiences. His account of systemic constraints also investigates changing societies; dependency analysis captures only part of his scholarship and politics.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Groundings with My Brothers (1969); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972).
nodes.scope_note: A History of the Upper Guinea Coast, 1545–1800 (1970, from a 1966 thesis) reconstructs regional change; The Groundings with My Brothers (1969) concerns political education; How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972) offers a didactic synthesis. A History of the Guyanese Working People, 1881–1905 (posthumous, 1981) examines labor and racial divisions. His 1975 Marxism lecture distinguishes method from fixed European conclusions. James’s later strategic criticism coexists with formative intellectual exchange.

nodes.label: C. L. R. James
nodes.description: Places enslaved people’s revolutionary action at the center of the Haitian Revolution and reworks Marxist historical explanation through the Caribbean. His writing also investigates colonial society, race, and cultural life through cricket and autobiography.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963); Beyond a Boundary (1963). The two editions of The Black Jacobins should not be treated as an unchanged argument.
nodes.scope_note: The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963) and the 1971 lectures distinguish successive historical perspectives. James later sought closer study of rank-and-file leaders and praised Du Bois’s attention to political imagination. His recollections identify Trotsky, Lenin and Marx among resources, alongside Caribbean projects. Beyond a Boundary (1963) examines social divisions through clubs and treats cricket as an art. These connections do not make him a disciple of postwar British social history.

nodes.label: Eric Williams
nodes.description: Argues that slavery and slave-trade wealth contributed to British capitalist development, and that changing economic interests helped explain abolition. These are related but distinguishable theses whose mechanisms, timing, and weight remain debated. His work challenges accounts centered on European benevolence.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944). Distinguish the original book from later editions and from subsequent arguments about capitalism and slavery.
nodes.scope_note: The 1944 preface separates slavery’s contribution to industrial finance from industrial capitalism’s role in abolition; the conclusion gives economic forces explanatory priority. Williams names Ragatz, Pitman, Herskovits, Burch and Harlow among scholarly helpers. Drescher’s 1977 challenge concerns decline and the 1807 slave-trade abolition, not a refutation of every slavery/capitalism claim. From Columbus to Castro (1970) is a later Caribbean synthesis, here checked only bibliographically.

nodes.label: Antonio Gramsci
nodes.description: Hegemony, common sense, subaltern groups, and intellectuals help explain domination through consent as well as coercion. Later historians and cultural theorists adapt these concepts differently. Anglophone reception predates the widely used 1971 Selections and does not follow a single timetable.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Antonio Gramsci (1891–1937); Selections from the Prison Notebooks (1971). Guha’s Subaltern Studies and Hall’s cultural studies are distinct adaptations.
nodes.scope_note: Unfinished and revised prison writings reach readers through editorial selections and translations. Intellectuals are defined by social functions, common sense is historically layered, and subaltern inquiry includes organization and autonomous activity. Gramsci’s broad geographical and linguistic hierarchies are open to criticism; later adaptations are distinct projects.

nodes.label: Historicism & idealist philosophies of history
nodes.description: Groups related arguments for historical specificity and interpretive understanding. German Historismus and British and Italian idealism are not one doctrine: Collingwood’s re-enactment is a particular account of historical thought, not a method shared by everyone here. This usage differs from Popper’s criticism of predictive laws of historical development. Approaches separate documentary interpretation, the human sciences, living historical questions, developmental individuality and rethinking past arguments; their disagreements concern evidence, values, political power and historical context.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Wilhelm Dilthey; Benedetto Croce, Theory and History of Historiography (1917); Friedrich Meinecke, Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936); R. G. Collingwood, The Idea of History (1946, posthumous).

representative_people.context: Develops a foundation for human sciences encompassing history, theory and practical judgments. Later attention to expression and shared historical worlds qualifies an account based only on individual psychology; the later primary text remains separately scoped.
representative_people.works: Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883), chapters 1, 2, 6; The Formation of the Historical World in the Human Sciences (1910), through editors’ introduction and SEP

representative_people.context: Historical thought responds to present questions while drawing on preserved documents. His distinction between living history and chronicle is idealist, not a distinction between important and trivial subjects or an instruction to disregard evidence.
representative_people.works: Theory and History of Historiography (Italian 1917; consulted 1921 Ainslie translation from 1919 edition), I.1

representative_people.context: Studies individuality and development in a selected genealogy of historicism. His account of national statehood and power receives a specific, attributed criticism from Paddock; neither the definition nor the criticism represents every historicism.
representative_people.works: Weltbürgertum und Nationalstaat (1907); Die Ideen der Staatsräson (1924); Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), through publisher and scholarly selections

representative_people.context: Re-enactment reconstructs an intelligible act of thought through evidence, not its original sensations or total immediacy. Skinner later credits changing questions and question/answer logic while emphasizing other philosophical resources.
representative_people.works: An Autobiography (1939), reception through Skinner; The Idea of History (1946, posthumous), Epilegomena §4, selected paragraphs

representative_people.context: Combines interpretive understanding with a critical method and a conception of the moral historical world. His approach bridges documentary scholarship and philosophical reflection without becoming identical to Dilthey or Croce.
representative_people.works: Grundriss der Historik (public edition 1867; consulted 1893 English translation)

representative_people.context: Provides an earlier comparison for historical individuality and the value of epochs. His theology and documentary practice differ from later philosophies; no backward influence is implied.
representative_people.works: 1824 preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

representative_people.context: Dilthey expands the critical project toward historical reason and embodied human experience. This identifies a named philosophical resource, not agreement with every Kantian premise.
representative_people.works: Critique of Pure Reason; Dilthey’s Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883) as a documented reworking

representative_people.context: Dilthey contests speculative system-building while adapting objective spirit to shared historical forms. A productive appropriation with disagreement; the original Hegel corpus is not independently collated here.
representative_people.works: Objective spirit; Dilthey’s Die Jugendgeschichte Hegels (1906) and later Formation project as documented reception

representative_people.context: Hermeneutics and religious life become objects of Dilthey’s editorial, biographical and philosophical work; the intellectual setting extends beyond a private psychological portrait.
representative_people.works: Hermeneutical writings and letters; Dilthey’s 1860 hermeneutical study and Leben Schleiermachers, volume I (1870) as reception

representative_people.context: A resource in Dilthey’s expanded critical perspective and an author central to Meinecke’s selective genealogy. These distinct receptions do not establish one unbroken school.
representative_people.works: Historical philosophy; Meinecke’s Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), through Paddock’s account

representative_people.context: An explicitly documented recipient of Collingwood’s question/answer logic, with substantial analytical-philosophical commitments. Placement records selective reception and does not label the Cambridge approach idealist.
representative_people.works: “Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas” (1969), reception discussed in the 2002 interview

nodes.scope_note: German historicism, Italian idealism, and Collingwood’s re-enactment are not one doctrine; neither is this Popper’s usage of historicism.

strands.title: Understanding through historical investigation
strands.focus: Droysen makes interpretable traces, interdependent critical operations and wider conditions central; neither bare testimony nor complete psychological access suffices.
strands.works: Outline of the Principles of History (1893), selected sections

strands.title: Human sciences, theory and practical judgment
strands.focus: The 1883 program distinguishes historical assertions, theoretical uniformities and evaluations/rules. Its broad remit includes humanities and social sciences, rather than forbidding every explanatory generalization.
strands.works: Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883), chapters 1, 2 and 6

strands.title: Expressions and shared historical worlds
strands.focus: Later Dilthey situates understanding in meaningful expressions, institutions and common historical life. Hegel’s objective spirit is appropriated with different commitments; individual introspection is insufficient.
strands.works: Formation of the Historical World (1910) and related drafts, through editors and SEP

strands.title: Present questions and preserved records
strands.focus: Croce distinguishes historical thinking from preserved chronicle without rejecting preservation. His explicit engagement with Droysen joins appreciation to criticism of abstract source categories.
strands.works: Theory & History of Historiography, I.1

strands.title: Individuality, development and state power
strands.focus: Meinecke’s genealogy privileges historical development and particularity. Paddock challenges its treatment of national statehood and supposed breaks in the author’s outlook; that is an attributed interpretation based on selected passages.
strands.works: Weltbürgertum und Nationalstaat (1907); Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), mediated readings

strands.title: Re-enactment, context and changing questions
strands.focus: Rethinking an argument differs from reliving its sensations. Skinner’s particular reception stresses questions and answers while drawing heavily on analytical philosophy; this is not the shared method of everyone in the umbrella.
strands.works: The Idea of History, Epilegomena §4; An Autobiography through Skinner’s interview

nodes.label: Explanation & objectivity debates
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots · Becker address 1931 · Hempel 1942 · Carr 1961 · Elton 1967
nodes.description: Disputes concern general laws, understanding actions, historical facts, and the possibility of objectivity. Analytic philosophy’s covering-law debate overlaps with historians’ arguments about evidence and interpretation without being identical to them. Narrative theory enters a discussion already under way.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Becker’s 1931 address (published 1932); Hempel, “The Function of General Laws in History” (1942); Dray, Laws and Explanation in History (1957); Carr, What Is History? (1961); Elton, The Practice of History (1967).

representative_people.context: Connects everyday inquiry, social memory and changing interpretation while retaining critical checks.
representative_people.works: Everyman His Own Historian (address 1931; publication 1932)

representative_people.context: Proposes testable laws and initial conditions, allowing probability and incomplete explanation sketches.
representative_people.works: The Function of General Laws in History (1942)

representative_people.context: Challenges reducing all historical explanations to a covering-law model; rational action and pragmatic questions are distinct concerns.
representative_people.works: Laws and Explanation in History (1957)

representative_people.context: Treats selection, interpretation and research as reciprocal while rejecting equal validity for every account.
representative_people.works: What Is History? (1961)

representative_people.context: Addresses research, imagination, writing and teaching; Mink cites his insistence on immersion in a period.
representative_people.works: The Practice of History (1967)

representative_people.context: Historian of evidence who distinguishes origins from explanation and treats traces as answers to questions under evidential constraints.
representative_people.works: Apologie pour l’histoire ou Métier d’historien (1949)

representative_people.context: Earlier philosophical questions about history’s uses, the explanation of moral values and the conditions of objectivity. This is not membership in the later covering-law debate.
representative_people.works: On the Use and Abuse of History for Life (1874); On the Genealogy of Morals (1887), preface, II.12–13 and III.12

representative_people.context: A specific interlocutor in Nietzsche’s account of genealogical explanation: Nietzsche names his book as a stimulus and disputes its hypotheses. Included at this mediated scope, not as a founder of later historical philosophy.
representative_people.works: The Origin of the Moral Feelings (1877), as discussed in Nietzsche’s Genealogy preface §§4–7

representative_people.context: Nietzsche calls him a teacher while challenging the value assigned to pity. This explains one background to a critique of values, not agreement or an independent reading of Schopenhauer.
representative_people.works: Schopenhauer’s account of pity as discussed in Nietzsche, Genealogy preface §5 (1887)

representative_people.context: Combines rhetorical analysis of historiography with attention to source-based construction; adopts Barthes while questioning a uniform disappearance of concern with reality.
representative_people.works: “Analysing the discourse of history” (1983); The Inventions of History (1990)

representative_people.context: Examines how historical discourse constructs signification and claims reference. Historians’ engagement includes productive use and criticism, not one settled verdict on evidence.
representative_people.works: “The Discourse of History” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968)

representative_people.context: Michelet explicitly appropriates humanity’s self-making as a historical principle; original Vico is not read here.
representative_people.works: Scienza nuova as recalled in Michelet (1869)

representative_people.context: A named resource against fixed innate explanations in Michelet’s account of historical formation.
representative_people.works: Passage quoted by Michelet (1869), p. 142

representative_people.context: Lamprecht credits a conception of collective historical life; this is a mediated resource, not a universal origin claim.
representative_people.works: Ideas concerning the History of Mankind, as cited by Lamprecht (1905)

representative_people.context: Reflects on the reciprocal formation of historian and history through research and historical imagination.
representative_people.works: Preface to History of France (1869), pp. 143–144

representative_people.context: Asks how source survival and artistic forms shape historical perception.
representative_people.works: The Waning of the Middle Ages (1924), preface and chapter XIX opening

representative_people.context: Combines close documentary work with relations among events, peoples and epochs. Historical individuality and religious commitments coexist; his selected European scope and civilizational judgments are contestable, and he is not the sole origin of criticism.
representative_people.works: History of the Popes (1834–1836; Austin translation 1840); 1824 historical preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

representative_people.context: Source search, criticism and interpretation cooperate. Material remains, accounts and monuments are not interchangeable; neither authentic documents nor individual intentions alone yield a complete historical explanation.
representative_people.works: Grundriss der Historik (public edition 1867; consulted Andrews English 1893), §§1–11, 20–24, 28–41

representative_people.context: Develops a foundation for human sciences encompassing history, theory and practical judgments. Later attention to expression and shared historical worlds qualifies an account based only on individual psychology; the later primary text remains separately scoped.
representative_people.works: Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883), chapters 1, 2, 6; The Formation of the Historical World in the Human Sciences (1910), through editors’ introduction and SEP
