nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the argument of The Great Divergence as its introduction states it (pp. 3–27 read, with the contents, in a preview of the later Princeton edition; page numbers are that edition's). The Making of a Hinterland is checked at contents level and through Bianco's 1996 review, read in full; its text is unread. He is not presented as the originator of reciprocal comparison: he writes that the approach was 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong', takes the 'encompassing comparison' from Charles Tilly, and notes parallels with Sugihara Kaoru. Arguments from colonial extraction (Williams, Frank, Amin) precede his. His estimates are contested: Cooper (2000) notes 'plausible guesstimates', and Bianco (1996) judges that the 1993 book 'postule plus qu'il ne prouve' a deliberate strategy of selective development. Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for the 2000 argument.

nodes.label: William Cronon
nodes.date_label: Changes in the Land 1983 · Nature’s Metropolis 1991 · “The Trouble with Wilderness” 1995
nodes.description: A historian of North American environments who treats ecological change as a two-way relation between people and the rest of nature, worked out through property, markets and ideas of nature. Changes in the Land (1983) assumes that 'the interactions of the two are dialectical' and finds in colonial New England not a choice between landscapes with and without people but 'two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'. Nature’s Metropolis (1991) follows grain, lumber and meat between Chicago and its hinterland on the premise that 'city and country have a common history, so their stories are best told together'. 'A Place for Stories' (1992) asks environmental historians for 'stories about stories about nature', and 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995) calls wilderness 'quite profoundly a human creation'. Reviewers found the Chicago book distant from farmers and townspeople, or moralising; he replied that he saw 'no pure heroes or pure villains'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: William Cronon (b. 1954); Changes in the Land: Indians, Colonists, and the Ecology of New England (1983); “Modes of Prophecy and Production: Placing Nature in History” (JAH 1990); Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991); “Kennecott Journey: The Paths out of Town” (1992); “A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative” (JAH 1992); “The Uses of Environmental History” (1993); “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995). Readings: the Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response (1992); Sessions’s reply on wilderness (1996); his own afterword to Changes in the Land (2003).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-13: chapter 1 of Changes in the Land in an unpaginated web transcription; 'A Place for Stories' (JAH 1992; pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read) and 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993; OCR of the author’s scan, journal pagination); 'Kennecott Journey' (1992); passages of 'The Trouble with Wilderness' in the author’s reflow; and the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response read in full. Nature’s Metropolis itself is unread: its words appear here only as forum contributors quote them with page numbers. 'Modes of Prophecy and Production', his 1990 response to Worster in the JAH round table, is paywalled and unread. He is not presented as a founder. He places environmental history among the 'new' histories 'born or reenergized in the wake of the 1960s' (1993, p. 2), names Nash, Hays, Worster, Merchant, Tarr and Pyne as practitioners (pp. 2–3), footnotes lessons to Crosby, Richard White, McEvoy and others (pp. 8–10), and echoes Leopold (n. 11). On Mahoney’s reading (1992, p. 492), Nature’s Metropolis demonstrates 'this fundamental urban historical premise' rather than inventing it. His approaches were contested in period: Danbom (1992, p. 503) finds 'environmental moralism'; Mahoney (p. 491) that urban and economic history 'seem only to serve the interests of environmental history'; Sessions (1996) that the wilderness essay underweights wild habitat. His 2003 afterword, McNeill (2003) and Canadian uses after 2000 are later readings.

nodes.label: Donald Worster
nodes.date_label: Nature's Economy 1977 · Dust Bowl 1979 · Rivers of Empire 1985 · 'Transformations of the Earth' 1990
nodes.description: A historian of the American Great Plains and arid West who set out a three-level model of environmental history. In 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) he wrote that 'there are three levels on which the new history proceeds': 'understanding nature itself', 'the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment', and 'the purely mental or intellectual', which together 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. His 1990 Journal of American History essay turned to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena', chiefly the capitalist transformation of agriculture, which Dust Bowl (1979) had called 'the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature'; Rivers of Empire (1985) described the West as 'a modern hydraulic society'. Merchant's 1990 response called the levels 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field' but found that the essay 'lacks a gender analysis'. Cronon (1992) read Dust Bowl as a story whose 'chief agent' is capitalism and whose plot 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Donald Worster (b. 1941); Nature's Economy: The Roots of Ecology (1977); Dust Bowl: The Southern Plains in the 1930s (1979); Rivers of Empire: Water, Aridity, and the Growth of the American West (1985); 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', in The Ends of the Earth (1988); 'Transformations of the Earth: Toward an Agroecological Perspective in History', Journal of American History (1990), reprinted in The Wealth of Nature (1993). Readings: Merchant's round-table response (1990); Cronon, 'A Place for Stories' (1992); Hennessey's review of Rivers of Empire (1987); McDean (1986).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the three-level model in Worster's 1988 wording, checked in an abridged reprint and by full-text search of the 1988 edition, and the 1990 essay in his own 1993 reprint; the Journal of American History pages of 1990 were not reachable and are given only where another writer cites them (Isenberg 2013). Dust Bowl and Rivers of Empire are quoted at the pages given by Cronon (1992) and Hennessey (1987), with the wording confirmed by search of the original editions. He is not presented as the founder of the field or the sole author of the scheme: he grounds the idea in Aldo Leopold's call for 'an ecological interpretation of history', and Arthur McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. The scheme was contested at once: Merchant (1990) added gender and 'a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction', Cronon (1992) treated Dust Bowl as a declensionist narrative, and McDean (1986) criticised its generalisation across the Plains. The 1990 objections of White and Cronon in the round table are known here only through Isenberg (2013), a later reading.

nodes.label: Alfred W. Crosby
nodes.date_label: The Columbian Exchange 1972 · Virgin Soil Epidemics 1976 · Ecological Imperialism 1986
nodes.description: A historian of the biological consequences of European expansion. The Columbian Exchange (1972) followed pathogens, plants and animals between the Americas and the Old World after 1492, and 'Virgin Soil Epidemics' (1976) defined epidemics among peoples who, as Jones (2003, pp. 703–704) quotes the definition, 'have had no previous contact with the diseases that strike them' (the 1976 article itself is unread). Ecological Imperialism (1986) starts from the fact that 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation', asks why 'the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion', and suggests that 'the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component': crops, livestock, weeds and diseases helped Europeans make temperate 'Neo-Europes'. Later critics charge the model with ecological determinism and argue that the virgin-soil idea was flattened into a claim that Indigenous Americans had 'no immunity'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred W. Crosby (1931–2018); The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492 (1972); 'Virgin Soil Epidemics as a Factor in the Aboriginal Depopulation in America' (William and Mary Quarterly, 1976); Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986); 'The Past and Present of Environmental History' (American Historical Review, 1995). Readings: Miller's review (1987); Cook (1990); Cronon (1993); Subrahmanyam (1997); later, Jones (2003), McNeill (2003) and Isenberg (2013).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents Ecological Imperialism as its prologue states the argument (pp. 1–7 read, with the contents and acknowledgments, in the publisher's sample of the 2004 second edition; page numbers are that edition's). The Columbian Exchange (1972), 'Virgin Soil Epidemics' (1976) and the 1995 AHR essay are unread: the 1972 book is characterised from Cook (1990) and McNeill (2003), and the 1976 wording is quoted as Jones (2003) quotes it. His 1978 American Heritage essay on New England, read in full, states the disease argument in his own words: 'Innocent of immunity or experience, the Indians were helpless.' He is not presented as the founder of environmental history: the ASEH's own history lists him among several 'founding members' with Worster, Flader and Opie, and in 1982 among 'the already widely known historians'; he thanks William McNeill, who 'read the whole thing in first draft'. Contested readings: in period, Subrahmanyam (1997) calls the books 'oft-cited (and oft-criticized)', while Miller (1987) finds Crosby 'careful not to overestimate the significance of any single component'. Later, McNeill (2003) records that 'Some readers felt that Crosby had relocated historical agency (and responsibility for genocide and colonialism) from humans to wheat and whooping cough'; Isenberg (2013) judges that his analysis 'devolved into little more than ecological determinism'; Jones (2003) argues that the virgin-soil model 'has been misunderstood and misrepresented', that the 1976 article itself stressed malnutrition and 'the social chaos generated by European colonization', and that Crosby's other writings stressed lack of immunity. These are later readings, not evidence for the edges. The 2004 preface, in which he calls Pomeranz's Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario', is a later self-reading and is not used.

nodes.label: Carolyn Merchant
nodes.date_label: The Death of Nature 1980 · Ecological Revolutions 1989 · Radical Ecology 1992
nodes.description: A historian of science and environmental historian who argued in The Death of Nature (1980) that a science 'reconceptualizing reality as a machine rather than a living organism, sanctioned the domination of both nature and women'. In Ecological Revolutions (1989), a study of New England from 1600 to 1860, she treated major changes in human relations with nature as arising from tensions 'between a society’s mode of production and its ecology, and between its modes of production and reproduction', which in turn reshape consciousness. Answering Worster's three levels of ecology, production and cognition in 1990, she wrote that environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' and a gender analysis of each level. Her reading of Bacon's metaphors was disputed in the 1990s (Soble 1995; Pesic 1999, whom she answered in 2006), and a 1991 reviewer, praising her integration of gender, found 'painfully few people making history' in the New England book.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Carolyn Merchant (b. 1936); The Death of Nature: Women, Ecology, and the Scientific Revolution (1980); “The Theoretical Structure of Ecological Revolutions” (1987); Ecological Revolutions: Nature, Gender, and Science in New England (1989); “Gender and Environmental History” (JAH round table, 1990); Radical Ecology: The Search for a Livable World (1992). Readings: Cronon (1993); Steinberg's review (1991); Soble (1995); Leach and Green (1997); Pesic (1999); Merchant's own retrospectives (1998, 2006).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents Merchant's framework as her own in-period texts state it: the 1987 Environmental Review article and the 1990 JAH response (both read in full, original pagination); The Death of Nature (1980) and Ecological Revolutions (1989) through author-hosted reprinted excerpts (pages are the reprints'); and the 1992 conclusion to Radical Ecology (facsimile, original pages). She is not presented as the founder of environmental history or of ecofeminism. She builds on Kuhn and on Marx and Engels, on Meillassoux, Peterson and Bridenthal for reproduction, and on Worster's levels; in 1998 she credits Hessen, Zilsel, Leiss and Kubrin ('It was Kubrin’s idea that the key concept of early modern science was that matter was dead'). She separates her socialist ecofeminism from a radical feminism that 'runs the risk of perpetuating the very value hierarchies it seeks to overthrow' (1989). The Bacon reading is contested (Soble 1995 and Pesic 1999, abstracts only), Leach and Green (1997) place The Death of Nature among the ecofeminist histories they criticise, and Steinberg (1991) faults the New England book's narrative. McNeill (2003) and Merchant's 2006 Isis response are later readings, not evidence for the 1980–1992 framework.

nodes.label: Richard White
nodes.date_label: Land Use, Environment, and Social Change 1980 · The Roots of Dependency 1983 · field survey 1985 · The Middle Ground 1991 · The Organic Machine 1995
nodes.description: A historian of the American West, of Native American history and of environmental history. The Middle Ground (1991; quoted from Cambridge Core first-page excerpts of the introduction and chapters) rejects accounts of Indian–white contact with 'but two outcomes', conquest or persistence, because contact 'creates as well as destroys': in the Great Lakes pays d'en haut, French and Algonquian allies 'had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting', a middle ground which White describes as a process of creative and often expedient misunderstanding, sustained because whites could not simply command Indians or disregard them, until in the nineteenth century its compromises 'yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness'. His environmental books trace Salish and settler land use and environmental change in Island County, Washington (1980), subsistence, environment and dependency among the Choctaws, Pawnees and Navajos (1983), and the Columbia River as an organic machine, an energy system remade by human labour that keeps natural qualities, in which human work is energy as much as the river's flow (1995). His 1985 Pacific Historical Review essay surveyed environmental history as a new field, and he responded to Worster's agroecological essay in the 1990 Journal of American History round table.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Richard White (b. 1947); Land Use, Environment, and Social Change: The Shaping of Island County, Washington (1980; 1992 paperback with Cronon's foreword and a new preface); The Roots of Dependency: Subsistence, Environment, and Social Change among the Choctaws, Pawnees, and Navajos (1983); “American Environmental History: The Development of a New Historical Field” (1985); “Environmental History, Ecology, and Meaning” (1990); The Middle Ground: Indians, Empires, and Republics in the Great Lakes Region, 1650–1815 (1991); The Organic Machine: The Remaking of the Columbia River (1995); “‘Are You an Environmentalist or Do You Work for a Living?’” (1995). Readings: Savard (1992), Edmunds (1993) and D. R. Miller (1994) on The Middle Ground; Cronon's foreword (1992) to Land Use.
nodes.scope_note: Not Hayden White (node white). Witnesses for The Middle Ground: Cambridge Core first-page excerpts (full pages, folios observed) of the introduction (1991 p. ix) and of the chapters opening at pp. 50, 94 and 518; the next page of the introduction (1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi) and pp. 52–53 and 93 only in Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 twentieth-anniversary edition, whose body pagination matches 1991 at the pages checked (the equation 1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi is inferred from the introduction's opening at 1991 p. ix and 2011 p. xxv). The rest of the book is unread, and wording witnessed only by snippets is paraphrased in node text. Land Use (1980; 1992 paperback) and The Organic Machine (1995) are known from Google Books search-within snippets of their framing pages, not from page images; The Organic Machine's preface folios were not visible, so its framing is paraphrased. The Roots of Dependency (1983), the 1985 survey, the 1990 round-table response and the 1995 Uncommon Ground essay are unread (paywalled or not previewed) and are known through Cronon (1993, 1994), Worster (1990, Portuguese translation), Cook (1990), Isenberg (2013) and the publisher's records. He is not presented as a founder of environmental history: Land Use credits James Malin's neglected Great Plains studies as a trail to follow (snippet, p. 7), and Isenberg (2013) names him in a group of synthesisers. The middle ground was contested in period: Savard (1992) doubts its premise of Iroquois devastation, Edmunds (1993) finds the post-1770 chapters 'less convincing', and D. R. Miller (1994) notes the neglect of peoples neither Iroquoian nor Algonquian; Merrell's in-period critique (Into the American Woods, 1999) is known here only through White's later 2011 response. Havard (2003) and Deloria (2006) are later critiques, also known here only through that 2011 preface, a later reading. Canadian environmental historians cite him chiefly for the 1985 survey; Canadian use of The Middle Ground before 2000 is checked only in reviews and one legal article.

nodes.label: Aldo Leopold
nodes.date_label: Land ethic and ecological interpretation of history · A Sand County Almanac 1949
nodes.description: A forester, wildlife ecologist and conservationist, not a historian, whose posthumous A Sand County Almanac (1949) set out a 'land ethic' that 'changes the role of Homo sapiens from conqueror of the land-community to plain member and citizen of it'. In the same essay he wrote that an 'ecological interpretation of history' shows that 'many historical events, hitherto explained solely in terms of human enterprise, were actually biotic interactions between people and land', and took as his example the Kentucky canelands that became bluegrass under 'the cow, plow, fire, and axe of the pioneer'. He asked: 'Is history taught in this spirit? It will be, once the concept of land as a community really penetrates our intellectual life.' Environmental historians later cited the call: Worster (1988) wrote that Leopold 'projected such an alliance' between history and ecology, and Cronon (1993) described the field's subject as 'the history recorded in Aldo Leopold’s tree rings'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Aldo Leopold (1887–1948); A Sand County Almanac, and Sketches Here and There (1949), especially 'Good Oak' and 'The Land Ethic'. Readings: Nash, Wilderness and the American Mind (1967), chapter 'Aldo Leopold: Prophet'; Worster, 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) and 'Transformations of the Earth' (1990); Cronon, 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993) and History 901 syllabus (1994). Later readings: Wynn (2001); MacEachern (2002); Cronon's afterword to Changes in the Land (2003).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents Leopold as a precursor whose writing environmental historians cited, not as a historian and not as the founder of environmental history. 'The Land Ethic' and 'Good Oak' are read in two unpaginated transcriptions (the 1966 enlarged Oxford text and an excerpt of the 1949 essay); the 1949 page of the history passage (p. 205) is the one Worster (1990, n. 1) and Wynn (2001, n. 55) both cite. Worster's 1988 essay dates 'the idea of environmental history' to the 1970s, the global-predicament conferences and the environmental movement, not to Leopold. His 1990 essay, read only in Portuguese translation, cautions that the Kentucky case is more complicated than Leopold's example and needs more than a simple environmental determinism, and adds that bluegrass was a European import, which Leopold had said was not known. Cronon's 1993 uses are echoes of a moral and literary voice, not a borrowed method. Canadian writing differs: MacEachern (2002, p. 219) faults a history of Ontario conservation for assuming, without evidence, that Leopold 'was being read by Canadians, let alone influencing them' (a remark about naturalists of the 1950s, not about historians), and Wynn (2001, p. 145), a historical geographer, urges geographers to 'respond to Leopold’s call' and observes: 'Few have done so'.

nodes.label: Rachel Carson
nodes.description: A marine biologist and science writer whose Silent Spring (1962) was a catalyst for environmental concern and became a shared text for US environmental historians; it is not a work of history. The book argued that 'the central problem of our age has therefore become the contamination of man’s total environment' by persistent chemicals, followed pesticides through 'the web of life — or death — that scientists know as ecology', and called the 'control of nature' 'a phrase conceived in arrogance'. It did not reject all control: 'control must be geared to realities, not to mythical situations'. Historians who shaped the field took the book up as a starting point: John Opie's 1971 reader opens 'The Contemporary Controversy Begins' with her, and Donald Worster's history of ecological ideas (1977) places Silent Spring near the opening of 'The Age of Ecology'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Rachel Carson (1907–1964); Silent Spring (1962). Readings: Opie's reader, with Graham's account of the outcry (1971); Worster, Nature's Economy (1977); Dunlap, DDT (1981); Hays, in collaboration with Barbara D. Hays, Beauty, Health, and Permanence (1987); Nash, The Rights of Nature (1989); Cronon's graduate seminar (1994). Later readings: Lear's introduction (2002); Carruthers (2004).
nodes.scope_note: A precursor entry for a catalyst of environmental concern, not a historian. Silent Spring is quoted from the 2002 Mariner edition (a partial scan was read: pp. 1–9, 172–198, 278–279 and 296–297, with Lear's introduction); Worster's 1977 notes cite pp. 8 and 297 for the same sentences, so the pagination matches the 1962 edition at those points. She is not presented as a founder or as the catalyst of environmental history as a discipline. Worster (1977; Internet Archive full-text search, page located by the index) credits her with launching the recent ecology movement, which is the movement, not the field. The disciplinary claim is a later, geographically qualified reading: Carruthers (2004) reports that Grove conceded Silent Spring's importance to the discipline only for the United States. The Canadian self-accounts read for this batch name her as 1960s context, not as a model. The book was contested from the start. Velsicol's general counsel attributed attacks on the chemical industry to sinister influences (his letter as quoted by Graham, 1970, in Opie's reader, p. 93 from a running head). Dunlap (1981, pp. 3–4 and 7 from running heads) records that defenders of DDT condemned her as a crank, and judges that she had done no original research. Nash (1989, p. 80 from a running head) finds much traditional anthropocentrism in her ethics. These three are known only through Internet Archive full-text search of borrow-only scans (page images not seen), so they are paraphrased. Lear (2002), a later reading, writes that the cancer evidence still fuels an 'acrimonious' debate. The 1962 reviews in Science (Baldwin) and Time were not read.

nodes.label: Dipesh Chakrabarty
nodes.date_label: Rethinking Working-Class History 1989 · “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History” 1992 · Provincializing Europe 2000 · “The Climate of History” 2009
nodes.description: A historian of modern South Asia in the Subaltern Studies collective. He argues that, within university-based historical discourse, an imagined 'Europe' remains its dominant theoretical reference: 'the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call “Indian,” “Chinese,” “Kenyan”', where 'Europe' and 'India' are 'hyperreal terms', figures of the imaginary 'subject to contestation' (1992). Rethinking Working-Class History (1989) reads Bengal’s jute-mill workers against an assumption of 'a hegemonic bourgeois culture' in Marx’s category of capital. 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (1992) calls Europe 'a silent referent in historical knowledge', and Provincializing Europe (2000) criticises the historicist 'first in Europe, then elsewhere' that placed colonized peoples in 'an imaginary waiting room of history', while holding European thought 'both indispensable and inadequate'; a 2000 essay separates History 1, the past 'posited by capital', from History 2, pasts that are 'not pasts separate from capital' but 'inhere in capital and yet interrupt and punctuate' its logic. In period, Sumit Sarkar called the trajectory he described 'debilitating', and the labour historian Rajnarayan Chandavarkar found a 'static, timeless, indeed Orientalist' culture in his Bengal book. After 2000, 'The Climate of History' (2009) argued that climate change spells 'the collapse of the age-old humanist distinction between natural history and human history'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Dipesh Chakrabarty (b. 1948); Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (1989); “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History: Who Speaks for ‘Indian’ Pasts?” (Representations, 1992); “Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts” (Perspectives, 1997); Provincializing Europe: Postcolonial Thought and Historical Difference (2000); “Universalism and Belonging in the Logic of Capital” (Public Culture, 2000). After 2000: “The Climate of History: Four Theses” (Critical Inquiry, 2009). Readings: Nair’s review (1990); Dirlik (1994); Chandavarkar (1997); Sarkar (1997); Whose Anthropocene? (2016), with his response.
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the 1989 preface (pp. xi–xv) and introduction (pp. 3–6) in the publisher preview; 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (Representations 37, 1992, pp. 1–26) in full; the 1997 AHA essay in full (web text, no page numbers); the Provincializing Europe introduction (pp. 3–23, in the publisher’s excerpt); 'Universalism and Belonging in the Logic of Capital' (Public Culture, 2000), which he describes as a slightly different version of the book’s chapter 2; and 'The Climate of History' (2009) in full. The rest of the 1989 and 2000 books is unread, including chapter 2 itself. He is not presented as a founder. He calls Ranajit Guha 'the founder of the group' (1997) and writes that his 'argument for provincializing Europe follows directly from my involvement in this project' (2000, p. 15). The book’s critique of historicism builds on Guha’s rejection of Hobsbawm’s 'prepolitical' and cites Fabian’s 'denial of coevalness' (pp. 8, 11–15). Contested in period: by Sarkar (1997), by Chandavarkar (1997) and, in a critique aimed mainly at Prakash, by Dirlik (1994). O'Hanlon and Washbrook (1992) criticised the wider post-Orientalist programme, principally Prakash's, without naming him; only their opening page and notes were read. The 2009 essay and its reception (2014–16) are after 2000 and support only the separate environment edge, which is dated 2009 in its label and text; they are not evidence for any claim about his work before 2000.

nodes.label: Bryan D. Palmer
nodes.date_label: ‘Most Uncommon Common Men’ 1976 · A Culture in Conflict 1979 · ‘Response to Joan Scott’ 1987 · Descent into Discourse 1990 · E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions 1994 · ‘Radical Reasoning’ 2009
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of labour and the left who took up E. P. Thompson's account of class and culture and later defended historical materialism against the linguistic turn. His first essay in Labour/Le Travailleur (1976) traced artisan culture and restated what he called 'a standard axiom of an emerging social history': 'As a class for itself, the working class was born, not in the factory, but in the workshop'; the critic David Bercuson read his study of Hamilton's skilled workers (1979) as 'echoing E.P. Thompson' (1981). In the International Labor and Working-Class History forum of 1987 he answered Joan Scott's case for reconceiving labour history through language and gender, which on his reading reduced class and its material relations to discourse, while granting, as Ted McCoy (2021) quotes him, that 'to say that language matters is not to say it is all that matters'; and Descent into Discourse (1990) held, as the Marxist reviewer Alex Callinicos quoted it, that 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected', while granting that discourse theory 'contains insights and guides'. Scott replied that 'class struggle is produced in discourse', a discourse she took to include 'ways of organizing lives, institutions, societies', not words alone, and that there is no choice, 'as Bryan Palmer insists there is, between a focus on class or gender'; Callinicos, broadly sympathetic, suggested that his treatment of class might underestimate 'the objective determinants of subjective action' and noted that he took Thompson and Raymond Williams 'to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure'. In 2009 he criticised Ian McKay's liberal order as, in his reading, 'a seemingly trans-historical analytic framework' that 'sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism's changing historical structures'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Bryan D. Palmer (b. 1951); “Most Uncommon Common Men: Craft and Culture in Historical Perspective” (Labour/Le Travailleur, 1976); A Culture in Conflict: Skilled Workers and Industrial Capitalism in Hamilton, Ontario, 1860–1914 (1979); The Making of E. P. Thompson: Marxism, Humanism, and History (1981); with Gregory S. Kealey, Dreaming of What Might Be: The Knights of Labor in Ontario, 1880–1900 (1982); Working-Class Experience (1983; 2nd ed. 1992); “Response to Joan Scott” (International Labor and Working-Class History, 1987); Descent into Discourse: The Reification of Language and the Writing of Social History (1990); “Homage to Edward Thompson” (Labour/Le Travail, 1993–94); E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions (1994). After 2000: Canada’s 1960s (2009); “Radical Reasoning” (Underhill Review, 2009). Readings: Bercuson (1981); Scott’s reply (1987); Callinicos (1992); Dissenting Traditions (2021), with essays by Rogers, McCoy and Pearson.
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: his 1976 Labour/Le Travailleur essay in full; the first page of his 1987 'Response to Joan Scott' (publisher's preview image) and its notes as listed by the publisher; Scott's 1987 essay (first page) and her 'A Reply to Criticism' (1987) in full; Bercuson (1981, pp. 95–97); Callinicos's 1992 review of Descent into Discourse in full; 'Homage to Edward Thompson' (1993–94), searched in full and read at pp. 67–68 (Part I) and 16–18 (Part II); and 'Radical Reasoning' (2009) in full. Unread here: the monographs (A Culture in Conflict, Dreaming of What Might Be, Working-Class Experience), Descent into Discourse itself (borrow-only; its words are quoted as Callinicos quotes them, with his page references), pp. 15–23 of the 1987 response (quoted only through Scott's reply and through McCoy, 2021), The Making of E. P. Thompson (1981), Objections and Oppositions (1994) and Canada's 1960s (2009). He is not presented as a founder: Freeman (2002) names him with Kealey and Sangster in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail, and the 1976 essay presents its thesis as 'a standard axiom of an emerging social history'. Contested in period by Bercuson (1981) on working-class culture, by Scott (1987) on language and gender, and, from a sympathetic Marxist position, by Callinicos (1992). The 2009 critique of the liberal order is dated in its label and text. The essays in Dissenting Traditions (2021) are later readings and are labelled as such wherever they are cited.

edges.relationship: Later Wittgenstein supplies a resource for Geertz’s public meaning
edges.evidence_note: “Thick Description,” pp. 12–13, explicitly invokes Wittgenstein in explaining why meaning cannot be reduced to private mental contents. This is a bounded borrowing. Selected Investigations sections now supply primary context for varied use and shared practices; they do not make all meaning a single formula.

edges.relationship: Geertz explicitly borrows Ryle’s thick-description distinction
edges.evidence_note: Primary pp. 5–7 use the twitch/wink example to distinguish acts that outwardly resemble one another. More detail alone does not supply the relevant interpretation. The complete reproduced 1968 lecture now supplies the original distinction’s philosophical context, including purpose, competence and exploration; original-edition wording remains uncollated.

edges.relationship: Geertz invokes Weber for an interpretive account of culture
edges.evidence_note: Primary p. 5 explicitly invokes Weber while presenting meaning as the object of interpretation. This does not make every part of Geertz’s work Weberian.

edges.relationship: provides the disciplinary setting for interpretive anthropology
edges.evidence_note: Disciplinary location is not an upstream intellectual event. Interpretive anthropology is a project within anthropology.

edges.relationship: Geertz’s interpretation of symbolic practices becomes a resource for cultural history
edges.evidence_note: Hunt’s primary 1984 p. 87 supplies a named reception example; the existing political-history edge specifies that use. Davis remains an earlier proposed example whose direct reception is not established by the passages checked here. Darnton’s original acknowledgments now add a specific Princeton co-teaching mechanism with Geertz; his introduction names Lévi-Strauss and acknowledges archival mediation. This does not certify Davis’s direct reception or all anthropological routes.

edges.relationship: Geertzian interpretation and microhistory invite comparison as well as methodological disagreement
edges.evidence_note: Compare contextual interpretation; do not assume Ginzburg or Italian microstoria simply adopted Geertz’s method. Ginzburg 1993 note 69 cites Levi’s “I pericoli del geertzismo”; that essay was not read, so its detailed critique is a follow-up, not an asserted directed influence.

edges.relationship: Lévi-Strauss adapts Jakobson’s and Trubetzkoy’s phonological resources
edges.evidence_note: Structural Anthropology pp. 31–36 and notes 8–14 identify the resources and warn against literal transfer of phonemic analysis to kinship. Saussure’s node is a broader linguistic tradition, not a claim of direct collaboration.

edges.relationship: Barthes adapts linguistic distinctions and proposes reversing the semiology hierarchy
edges.evidence_note: Elements of Semiology introduction explicitly invokes the Course but proposes making semiology part of linguistics. The categories are a provisional research programme, not an unchanged transfer or a summary of Barthes’s later work. Myth Today adapts the sign as a second-level signifier; the history essay also explicitly uses Jakobson’s shifters. These passages extend rather than erase the earlier scoped 1964 reading.

edges.relationship: Lacan transforms Saussurean signification and explicitly uses Jakobson’s linguistic resources
edges.evidence_note: Primary 1957 PDF pp. 3–4 visually checked: Lacan acknowledges S/s is not exactly a Cours diagram and substitutes matching doors for the tree illustration. Notes 3/10 credit Jakobson; appropriation does not establish identity between linguistic and psychoanalytic theories.
edges.map_label: The sign diagram, metaphor and metonymy

edges.relationship: Lacan explicitly uses Lévi-Strauss on symbolic efficacy and language/social laws
edges.evidence_note: Mirror-stage note 1 cites “L’efficacité symbolique” (1949); Function and Field PDF p. 27/note 18 cites “Language and the Analysis of Social Laws” (1951), alongside symbolic exchange on p. 24. These primary receptions replace the earlier generic evidence; original printings and Lévi-Strauss articles are not newly collated.

edges.relationship: provides a distinct structuralist project within the discipline
edges.evidence_note: Structural anthropology is situated within the discipline. A containing field is not itself a dated transmitter.

edges.relationship: Durkheimian scholarship and Mauss provide acknowledged resources
edges.evidence_note: The dedication acknowledges Durkheim and the Année sociologique; chapter 2 opens with Mauss’s call to learn from linguistics. These passages strengthen named antecedents without independently verifying every proposed exchange/classification mechanism.

edges.relationship: Derrida questions the speech/writing hierarchy while working through differential relations
edges.evidence_note: Corrected 1997 English pp. 27–35 and 44–50 distinguish nonnatural signification from private caprice and question the exclusion of writing. This is neither rejection of every linguistic insight nor a claim that Saussure assigns fixed meanings to isolated words. This edition is identified; the separate MIA excerpt’s exact witness remains unresolved.

edges.relationship: Derrida questions nature/culture and the grounds of structural analysis
edges.evidence_note: The consulted English transcription engages the incest-prohibition problem and bricolage. Derrida recognizes Lévi-Strauss’s own questioning while disputing its conceptual limits; criticism does not imply that Lévi-Strauss naively ignored them.

edges.relationship: helps form an intellectual context that decenters the subject
edges.evidence_note: Shared intellectual setting is not evidence of a direct Saussure-to-Foucault borrowing. Preserve Foucault’s separate epistemological and genealogical routes.

edges.relationship: Foucault explicitly situates Canguilhem and conceptual histories among his resources
edges.evidence_note: The available 1985 opening names Canguilhem, Bachelard, Cavaillès and Koyré and explains the significance of medicine and biology. This is Foucault’s selective retrospective account, distinct from structural linguistics; the original Canguilhem works and full revised preface are not newly read.
edges.map_label: Canguilhem and histories of scientific concepts

edges.relationship: Foucault reworks Nietzsche’s descent and emergence as genealogical questions
edges.evidence_note: The 1971 essay, English pp. 139–152, explicitly examines changing Nietzschean terms, documentary detail and struggles over rules. It opposes teleological recovery of a pure origin; Foucault’s historical and biological interpretations remain attributed, with cited originals uncollated. Nietzsche’s own preface and II.12–13 are now separately read, including the distinction between genesis and later utility; this does not establish identity with Foucault’s whole interpretation.
edges.map_label: Descent, emergence and struggles over rules

edges.relationship: Barthes contributes distinct analyses of myth, historical discourse and authorial authority
edges.evidence_note: Primary selections differentiate naturalized meanings, uttering/utterance, narrative detail and the theoretical reader. Bann supplies a particular historical adaptation and qualification; these do not define every linguistic approach or prove that past events are imaginary.
edges.map_label: Myth, historical discourse and authorial authority

edges.relationship: Lacan contributes a linguistically constituted, divided subject as a contested conceptual resource
edges.evidence_note: The 1949 and 1957 primary selections distinguish identification and signifying mechanisms. Scott’s 1986 response supplies a particular historical reception and limitation; the linguistic turn is not uniformly Lacanian.

edges.relationship: Foucault contributes historical inquiries into discourse, practices and subjects
edges.evidence_note: The three archaeology chapters relate actual statements and objects to institutional practices; the genealogy essay and 1982 subject account distinguish further questions about contingent formation and action. Goldstein’s profile documents one empirical reception. These do not define all language-centered history or reduce material relations to text.

edges.relationship: Derrida contributes critical readings of hierarchies and conditions of signification
edges.evidence_note: Selected Grammatology passages and the complete 1983 letter distinguish differential relations and contextual translation from arbitrary interpretation or a mechanical method. Scott supplies a specific historical use of deconstruction; historians do not all adopt one program.

edges.relationship: informs analysis of power and subject formation
edges.evidence_note: Power and historical categories are resources for some gender analyses, not a sole origin of gender or racial-formation scholarship. Scott explicitly proposes Foucault’s dispersed conception of power on p. 1067; this is a named use, not an origin claim.

edges.relationship: Foucault supplies a named resource that sexuality historians adapt and question
edges.evidence_note: D’Emilio’s 1983 note 1 explicitly acknowledges Foucault, McIntosh and Weeks while arguing that a wage-labor explanation remains necessary. Stoler’s 1995 project critically extends Foucault into colonial history. This supports specific reception, not a sole origin of the field.

edges.relationship: Said adopts Foucault’s discourse analysis while retaining individual authors’ effects
edges.evidence_note: This compressed link concerns Said’s use and revision of discourse analysis, not every postcolonial historian. The checked introduction explicitly states both debt and disagreement.

edges.relationship: Spivak uses and tests Derridean deconstruction in a critique of representation
edges.evidence_note: This route concerns Spivak’s critical use of deconstruction; it does not define every postcolonial approach. The checked conclusion explicitly distinguishes this use from treating deconstruction as feminism in itself.

edges.relationship: Althusser rereads Marx through problematics, epistemological break and structural effectivity
edges.evidence_note: The For Marx introduction and Reading Capital opening distinguish a philosophical question about scientific objects from a simple summary of economic results. The break and structural causality remain contested interpretations; the revised foreword qualifies theoreticism.
edges.map_label: Marx’s questions, objects and structural explanation

edges.relationship: Thompson challenges theoretical abstraction and loss of agency
edges.evidence_note: Thompson’s 1978 attack is a particular intervention, not a common position of every Marxist social historian.

edges.relationship: Althusser’s material ideology and subject formation become resources for cultural theory
edges.evidence_note: Selected 1970 passages tie interpellation to practices and distinguish mixed apparatus functions, resistance and class struggle beyond institutions. Hall supplies a specific adoption and criticism; this is not a claim that all historical language analysis follows Althusser.
edges.map_label: Material practices, ideology and subject formation

edges.relationship: Cunningham’s textbook and teaching, and Ashley’s institutional work, help establish economic history
edges.evidence_note: Ashley and related historical economists helped institutionalize economic history. Institutional formation and intellectual agreement are different claims.
edges.map_label: Cunningham and Ashley: establishing the subject

edges.relationship: Rogers challenges formulaic laws; Schmoller disputes Menger’s abstractions without rejecting abstraction itself
edges.evidence_note: The issue is the historical scope of economic generalization; historical economists themselves differ. Rogers’s preface and Schmoller’s 1883 review supply specific criticisms. Toynbee explicitly values deduction; Mill and Marshall also qualify economic propositions. This is not a unanimous opposition between two camps.
edges.map_label: Rogers and Schmoller: scope of economic laws

edges.relationship: Toynbee uses political economy to frame historical questions; North later revises neoclassical assumptions through institutions and change
edges.evidence_note: Economic historians use changing theoretical resources: Tawney’s religious-economic questions differ from North’s institutional explanation. Toynbee’s opening lecture explicitly explains this reciprocal use. North’s existing scoped lecture check supports the later distinction; no direct Smith-to-North lineage is claimed. Furtado explicitly invokes Keynes in chapter XXXI while retrospectively interpreting coffee-surplus destruction as support for income and employment. Novais’s1961review welcomes the income-flow analysis but requests structural explanation. No claim that1931policymakers followed Keynes’s1936book is made.

edges.relationship: neoclassical theory informs the cliometric branch
edges.evidence_note: The claim concerns economic modelling within cliometrics, not all statistical or serial history.

edges.relationship: Marx critically reworks Smith and Ricardo while treating capitalism as historically specific
edges.evidence_note: Marx critically engages classical political economy; nineteenth-century neoclassicism is not treated as the same source. His 1873 afterword discusses Ricardo’s class distribution and Sieber’s account of his debt to Smith and Ricardo; it does not endorse classical political economy without qualification.

edges.relationship: Human geography provides distinct resources for Bloch and Febvre
edges.evidence_note: Bloch’s existing Vidal acknowledgment is mediated by Friedman’s indexed introduction. Febvre’s own Combats preface names Reclus as formative reading. These different examples strengthen the geographical connection without proving the identical transmission to both founders. The Febvre-specific Vidal connection is now directly supported: selected La Terre passages discuss Vidal’s regional method and limits of geographical explanation, while Combats printed 378 recalls Sion enlisting Vidal to encourage this book. This supplements, without replacing, the separate Reclus testimony and mediated Bloch evidence.

edges.relationship: Marsh, Leopold and Sauer supply distinct resources for environmental historical inquiry and teaching
edges.evidence_note: Marsh is an environmental precursor; do not derive every environmental-history tradition from Vidal or Annales. Lowenthal documents Marsh’s environmental-history relevance; Cronon recalls workshops modeled on Leopold’s course. These are distinct historical resources, not one direct genealogy. A further named teaching use is Cronon’s Fall 1994 History 901 assignment of Sauer’s 1941 Foreword to Historical Geography. This is separate from the 1925 Morphology essay and establishes a syllabus use, not universal reception. Hewes’s The Suitcase-Farming Frontier (1973) supplies another specific resource: Worster’s 1986 note14 explicitly uses it, and McDean124/note37 identifies Hurt’s use. This shared historical geography does not establish identical causal interpretations. Original Hewes book unread.
edges.map_label: Inquiry, landscape training and Sauer reading

edges.relationship: provides an earlier cultural tradition that later work transforms
edges.evidence_note: Burckhardt and Huizinga are earlier resources; later cultural histories change subject matter, social reach, and method. Burke’s selective account explicitly rejects a simple succession of superior methods and describes the continuing German cultural-history tradition alongside alternatives; it is not a complete transmission chain for every later historian.

edges.relationship: shares interest in historical meanings; methods differ
edges.evidence_note: Shared attention to meaning does not establish a Burckhardt-to-Skinner genealogy.

edges.relationship: Compare inherited life-writing practices with modern historical uses of biography
edges.evidence_note: Plutarch, Johnson, Carlyle, Strachey and Woolf pose distinct questions about character, selection and evidence. The teaching overlap remains undirected; neither Carlyle nor Strachey founded or exhausted biography.

edges.relationship: supplies distinct strategic, critical and maritime resources for historical inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Clausewitz’s selected text examines judgment and friction; Delbrück’s preface explains mutually checking criticism, and Keegan explicitly uses his work. Mahan and Corbett state maritime purposes. These are named resources, not one uniform origin of military history.
edges.map_label: Strategic questions, criticism and maritime scope

edges.relationship: Interpretive anthropology supplies specific resources for cultural history
edges.evidence_note: Geertz’s essay supplies the methodological account and Hunt’s 1984 p. 87 supplies a named historical adaptation. Tylor, Boas and all other anthropological programmes are not implied by this route. Darnton’s original acknowledgments now add a specific Princeton co-teaching mechanism with Geertz; his introduction names Lévi-Strauss and acknowledges archival mediation. This does not certify Davis’s direct reception or all anthropological routes.

edges.relationship: Anthropological and microhistorical inquiry can be compared while their methods and exchanges remain distinct
edges.evidence_note: Compare ethnographic attention and close historical reconstruction without asserting one origin for microstoria and Alltagsgeschichte. Medick’s documented working exchange now has a separate contribution edge; this broader comparison still does not establish the origins of Italian microstoria.

edges.relationship: Anthropological scholarship and Indigenous histories intersect through distinct collaborations and disputes
edges.evidence_note: The comparison preserves independent Indigenous authority. Buck’s Māori scholarship and the Yukon collaboration are named examples; Wilson’s critique is separately directed toward interpretation practices. Neither collaboration establishes anthropology as an origin.

edges.relationship: helps organize national narratives and institutional agendas
edges.evidence_note: National frames organize some historical writing; the relationship is contextual rather than one school’s intellectual descent.

edges.relationship: James, Williams and Césaire challenge different imperial historical narratives
edges.evidence_note: James, Williams, and Rodney challenge different imperial narratives; national liberation is not a single explanatory position. Césaire’s checked opening attacks civilizing claims; Williams’s economic propositions remain disputed.

edges.relationship: Chatterjee questions derivative national models and the exclusions of nationalist history
edges.evidence_note: Targets imperial knowledge and nationalist universalism; not every national history makes the same claims. The checked 1993 chapter supplies a specific argument alongside the broader inherited claim.

edges.relationship: Nell recovers Black military service from patriotic exclusion
edges.evidence_note: His 1855 preface states this recovery project and credits Whittier’s compilation. This is a substantive contribution, not demonstrated reception by every later military historian.

edges.relationship: investigates paid and unpaid labour and household economies
edges.evidence_note: Clark and Pinchbeck investigate women’s work; Power links institutions and social life. Paid employment is not all economic activity.

edges.relationship: Ranke’s source-centered church/state history exemplifies one earlier political-historical practice
edges.evidence_note: Ranke exemplifies professional archival practice; source criticism predates him and extends beyond political history. The checked work and Austin translation now specify a contextual example. This does not establish Ranke as the sole inventor of archival method. The selected 1824 preface now independently supports political/religious interconnections and the stated source base; the Popes volumes themselves remain uncollated.
edges.map_label: Ranke: church, state and historical sources

edges.relationship: source criticism persists despite a change in questions
edges.evidence_note: A methodological continuity, not a demonstrated direct Ranke-to-Annales lineage. On p. 729 Braudel recognizes advances in documentary methods while rejecting documentary authenticity as sufficient explanation, and distinguishes Ranke from a blanket caricature of short-term history.

edges.relationship: provides materialist concepts debated by later historians
edges.evidence_note: Thompson’s explicit discussion of his debt to Marx provides a concrete British Marxist example of this conceptual inheritance. Later practitioners debate and revise the concepts; the tradition is not uniform.

edges.relationship: provides one influential account of capitalism
edges.evidence_note: Marx’s analysis of capitalism informs approaches such as Dobb’s; it does not define the entire field of economic history.

edges.relationship: Bloch’s selective reception and Simiand’s methodological intervention connect sociology with Annales
edges.evidence_note: The existing Bloch acknowledgment supports a qualified intellectual debt. Annales’ 1960 editors explicitly reprint Simiand’s 1903 essay to sustain their dialogue with social science. These are distinct reception examples, not evidence that every Annales historian follows Durkheim. Bloch’s Apologie explicitly credits Simiand for knowledge by traces; the checked primary passage supports this named methodological resource.

edges.relationship: Parsons explicitly draws on Durkheim in his evolutionary comparison
edges.evidence_note: Durkheim’s book III discussion of failed solidarity still qualifies a simple differentiation story. Parsons’s 1964 p. 341 now supplies actual named reception of a different work, The Elementary Forms of Religious Life, concerning social orientation and religion. This resolves the formerly unsupported generic transmission only in this narrower form; it does not establish that Parsons accepts all Durkheim’s claims.

edges.relationship: Halbwachs’s sociological account makes social relations central to remembering
edges.evidence_note: Halbwachs develops collective-memory analysis within a sociological tradition; Nora’s later project is not identical to it. The 1925 original is now distinguished from the 1992 English collection. Assmann’s critical reuse supplies later reception, not proof of every step in Halbwachs’s Durkheimian formation.

edges.relationship: is selectively read through later sociology, including Parsons
edges.evidence_note: Parsons’s selective reception mediates some modernization readings; Weber’s own account is not a simple celebratory stage model. Parsons’s 1930 preface documents translation of the revised 1920 essay; his 1964 pp. 348–349 explicitly use Weber’s bureaucracy analysis. Lipset’s 1959 definitions and conclusion make a different use, including Weber via Pipes to reject guaranteed democratization. These are specified receptions, not one shared stage model.

edges.relationship: connects capitalism, institutions, and religious meanings
edges.evidence_note: Tawney explicitly acknowledges Weber while reserving disagreement, providing a named example of reception within economic history.

edges.relationship: informs histories of domination, bureaucracy, and states
edges.evidence_note: Domination and bureaucracy supply conceptual tools; this broad link does not establish borrowing by every political historian.

edges.relationship: Pirenne’s comparative economic history and Labrousse’s study of economic conjunctures contribute to different parts of Annales
edges.evidence_note: The original journal title and Gurevich’s methodological account support economic history as a constituent of the project. This is a field-level contribution, not the claim that one later economic-history school founded Annales.
edges.map_label: Pirenne and Labrousse: distinct economic histories

edges.relationship: Dobb’s account of capitalist development and engagements with Tawney help shape British Marxist historical debates
edges.evidence_note: Dobb’s historical synthesis and engagements with Tawney identify concrete intersections. Economic history as a whole is not a single precursor school.

edges.relationship: Compare Rostow’s stages with Gerschenkron’s different industrial paths and North’s institutional explanation
edges.evidence_note: Compare Rostow’s stages with other explanations of growth; North’s institutional account is not simply another name for modernization theory. Gerschenkron’s title essay supports distinct instruments and sequences in European cases. This remains a comparison; the reviewed passage does not directly address Rostow. Rostow’s chapter 2 allows timing variation and change within his traditional category while retaining five stages. Comparing these qualifications with Gerschenkron’s instruments/sequences still does not establish direct exchange between them.

edges.relationship: Fogel and North develop distinct quantitative and institutional approaches within new economic history
edges.evidence_note: Fogel’s quantitative research and North’s institutional work show different developments within new economic history. Earlier Fogel research is now distinguished from his later population programme: McClelland’s railroad criticism and the Fogel–Engerman/David–Temin productivity exchange identify specific methodological disputes. The 1980 reply is located bibliographically; its argument and disputed numerical results remain unchecked. Kumar’s1965 southern Indian labour study supplies an additional quantitative economic-history example, with explicitly stated caste/occupation assumptions and changing census categories. This expands the examples, without claiming she belonged to Fogel’s or North’s programme.

edges.relationship: extends analysis to unequal international relations
edges.evidence_note: Williams and Rodney make empire, slavery, and unequal development historical problems. This does not derive all dependency theory from a generic field. Frank’s notes add particular Latin American histories, including Furtado and Góngora, used selectively rather than as a generic economics origin.

edges.relationship: Comparative development and the resources of empire: economic-history questions taken into global history
edges.evidence_note: Comparative development and transregional exchange are resources, not a claim that all global history adopts economic modelling. Williams's argument on slavery and capitalism and the comparison of Eurasian economies are among the economic-history questions global history takes up. Pomeranz's own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.130). Huang’s 2002 criticism and Pomeranz’s reply document a later disagreement over the 2000 comparison; neither is a settled verdict or an extension of mapped coverage.

edges.relationship: intersects through strategy, diplomacy, and state power
edges.evidence_note: Strategy and state power create overlapping subjects; no causal direction follows from that overlap.

edges.relationship: joins military inquiry to social context, institutional change and the lives of soldiers
edges.evidence_note: Howard’s war-studies setting and social scope provide a named case; Roberts and the military-revolution debate ask how military organization relates to wider change. This specifies an exchange of questions rather than claiming social history invented contextual war study; Rogers’s account mediates most individual debate essays. Lucassen and Zürcher (1998) add a named recruitment study: their comparative framework joins military labor to household strategies and state resources, with specific European and Middle Eastern examples. Its broad claims remain attributed to the authors.
edges.map_label: Howard: social context and war studies

edges.relationship: makes combat representation and culturally situated understandings of war objects of inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Keegan’s Face of Battle excerpt criticizes narrative conventions and unexamined testimony. The distinct 1993 book is represented through Bassford’s criticism, preserving disagreement about culture and politics; neither work is treated as the voice of all cultural history.
edges.map_label: Keegan: combat narratives and cultural argument

edges.relationship: Bourke makes men’s bodies and wartime masculinity historical questions
edges.evidence_note: The 1996 publisher description specifies personal/public evidence and distinctions among injury, disease and masculine ideals. This supports a contribution, not demonstrated uptake by all military historians or every chapter argument.

edges.relationship: Winter’s study of Great War mourning connects memory research to war’s cultural aftermath
edges.evidence_note: Remembrance becomes an object of historical inquiry; not all military history is memory studies. The checked introduction questions a clean modernist rupture and explicitly limits transfer to later catastrophes. This specifies a contribution to military/war history without identifying it with operational history.
edges.map_label: Winter: mourning after the Great War

edges.relationship: Compare individual political lives with Namier’s collective biographical study of parliamentary connections
edges.evidence_note: Political biography is an intersection of genre and field; it is not a one-way origin claim. The link remains an undirected comparison of genre and method; no new universal origin claim is inferred.

edges.relationship: Compare intensive life-based inquiry with microhistorical questions about scale and social relations
edges.evidence_note: A close study of a life is not automatically Italian microstoria. Levi’s 1989 distinctions clarify differences between modal, contextual, extreme-case and dialogic uses, and make group formation and bounded agency questions for inquiry. This comparison remains undirected alongside his separately evidenced methodological contribution.
edges.map_label: Life inquiry, scale and bounded agency

edges.relationship: Davis’s comparative biographies develop through women’s-history teaching, source discovery and revised questions of significance
edges.evidence_note: Davis names the 1971 course with Conway and Colie’s Glikl suggestion in her acknowledgments. Her prologue and conclusion compare three lives while retaining religious difference and colonial power. This primary selection supplements the existing catalogue description; it is not a full source audit or a claim that women’s history originated biography.
edges.map_label: Davis, Conway and Colie: teaching into research

edges.relationship: Brown uses collective biography to contest racist exclusion
edges.evidence_note: The 1863 preface explains this biographical project. Individual biographies and later reception remain unreviewed; the edge does not assert that Black history invented life writing.

edges.relationship: Davis examines stories, self-representation and culturally situated differences within comparative life history
edges.evidence_note: The Glikl opening uses Certeau’s account of stories; prologue and conclusion test categories, religious commitments and power. This named case specifies a cultural resource without making every biography a cultural-history application or treating an imagined dialogue as testimony.

edges.relationship: challenges event- and elite-centered explanation
edges.evidence_note: Braudel, p. 729, criticizes concentration on great events and short durations. The target is that mode of political explanation, not all political history or the elimination of events.

edges.relationship: Hill’s radical religious politics and Dorothy Thompson’s popular politics broaden the explanation of political conflict
edges.evidence_note: Hill’s radical religious politics and Dorothy Thompson’s popular politics explain the exchange more precisely than a generic class arrow.

edges.relationship: Interdisciplinary exchange, structures and reconsidered social categories contribute different methods
edges.evidence_note: The 1929 programme, Braudel’s temporal analysis and Lepetit’s collective reconsideration of actors/practices represent different resources. These contributions do not make every national social-history movement an Annales descendant.

edges.relationship: Labrousse’s serial prices and incomes connect economic conjunctures with social structures
edges.evidence_note: Braudel, p. 729, discusses price, wage, and demographic series; Gurevich identifies quantitative inquiry among Annales approaches. This does not derive econometric cliometrics or all historical demography from Annales. The 1933 title is now checked; this remains a specific French serial contribution, not the source of every form of quantitative history.
edges.map_label: Labrousse: serial prices, incomes and social structure

edges.relationship: from Bloch and Febvre’s inquiry into belief to Chartier’s representations, cultural questions are developed and reworked
edges.evidence_note: Febvre’s sensitivity essay and Le Goff’s religious-history project add specified arguments to this contribution. Chartier’s representation approach reworks cultural explanation; this is not a uniform mentalités lineage or a single origin of new cultural history.

edges.relationship: Braudel influences Wallerstein’s long-duration analysis
edges.evidence_note: Steiner, p. 66, records Wallerstein’s debt to Braudel’s long-duration questions alongside theoretical differences. The arrow concerns Wallerstein, not a common Annales origin for all dependency theory. Wallerstein 1974 p. 388 explicitly uses Braudel’s criticism of rigid historical models. This named primary reception complements the prior retrospective evidence.

edges.relationship: Thompson’s class formation and Hobsbawm’s labour history contribute distinct accounts of collective agency
edges.evidence_note: Thompson’s class formation and Hobsbawm’s labour histories supply distinct resources; neither exhausts new social history.

edges.relationship: Thompson’s experience and culture provide a bridge
edges.evidence_note: Experience and culture already participate in Thompson’s class explanation; later cultural inquiry both inherits and changes these resources.

edges.relationship: shares Marxist questions about capitalism and class; explanatory scales and traditions differ
edges.evidence_note: Comparative editorial link. Direct conceptual resources from historical materialism are separately represented by karl → dependency. Shared Marxist questions do not establish British social history as the origin of dependency theory or world-systems analysis.

edges.relationship: British Marxist social history becomes a resource and disputed interlocutor for Subaltern Studies
edges.evidence_note: Thompson is a named interlocutor in Indian historical debate. Subaltern Studies also critiques European models and has distinct colonial problems. Sarkar’s participant account, p. 83, names Hill, Hobsbawm and Thompson and points to Guha’s Thompson citations. This strengthens reception evidence without making the collective a derivative British school; cited Guha passages remain to be inspected.

edges.relationship: Black historiography’s independent roots test the limits of a later recovery umbrella
edges.evidence_note: Black history’s institutions and intellectual roots precede Hunt’s grouping; Gilroy also questions closed racial categories. This is a comparison of distinct projects, not an assertion of a single identity position or an influence event.

edges.relationship: shares diasporic and emancipatory arguments
edges.evidence_note: Diasporic and emancipatory concerns intersect, without making all Black and anti-colonial histories one school.

edges.relationship: Black women’s histories reshape analysis of race and gender
edges.evidence_note: White contributes a history of enslaved women; Higginbotham’s 1992 opening challenges thin racial analysis while developing feminist accounts of power. Distinct interventions, not a claim that one theorist founded intersectional inquiry.
edges.map_label: White and Higginbotham: race and gender

edges.relationship: James’s changing historical and dramatic work recasts Marxist questions through enslaved revolution
edges.evidence_note: The earlier wording grouped James and Williams too closely under Marxist social history. Individual entries now distinguish their arguments. James is a specified participant who recasts Marxist historical questions through slavery and revolution. Not all anti-colonial thinkers share that position. Douglas’s publisher description supplies edition-specific support, not a single Marxist identity for the umbrella.
edges.map_label: James: revolution and changing Marxist questions

edges.relationship: Fanon supplies an earlier resource for later debates about colonial domination and humanism
edges.evidence_note: Fanon supplies one earlier resource; later postcolonial critiques are not identical to all liberation histories. Chakrabarty’s 2000 introduction explicitly takes up Fanon in discussing Enlightenment inheritances.
edges.map_label: Fanon in Chakrabarty’s account of humanism

edges.relationship: Rodney and Williams connect empire with distinct explanations of unequal economic change
edges.evidence_note: Rodney and Williams provide distinct arguments concerning empire and economic change; neither stands for every dependency theorist. Rodney’s primary excerpt emphasizes power and control; its broad loss-of-agency rhetoric remains his argument.
edges.map_label: Rodney’s power relations; Williams’s slavery debate

edges.relationship: Older women’s histories combine recovery with disagreement about subjects and priorities
edges.evidence_note: Lerner’s 1988 primary priorities discuss biography and differences among women. The comparison retains earlier women historians and independent roots; it is not the founding of identity politics or evidence of one feminist position.

edges.relationship: opens questions about gender as a relation of power
edges.evidence_note: Research on women creates questions and evidence that gender historians develop and contest; gender history does not simply supersede women’s history. Chakravarti’s 1993 opening explicitly takes up Lerner’s historical approach while developing a separate caste argument.

edges.relationship: overlaps in histories of work, family, and everyday life
edges.evidence_note: Work, households, and everyday life are overlapping subjects; women’s history is not a subset originating in postwar social history.

edges.relationship: offers a rival account of historical development
edges.evidence_note: Compare explanatory premises and historical agency. Rivalry between broad approaches is not evidence of influence in either direction. The comparison is now grounded in Rostow’s staged growth/dynamic-production summary and Thompson’s class/agency preface. Distinct Marxist and modernization approaches must not be collapsed into two uniform opposing schools; Thompson’s explicit criticism has its own directed edge_471.

edges.relationship: shares some social-scientific methods
edges.evidence_note: Shared social-scientific tools do not establish common politics or a single account of development. Lipset’s multivariate comparison and Smelser’s differentiation inquiry specify some social-scientific methods. Neither establishes that all new social historians adopted modernization assumptions; the link remains an undirected teaching comparison.

edges.relationship: Frank and Wallerstein challenge national-stage explanations of underdevelopment
edges.evidence_note: Relational underdevelopment contests a picture of independent national stages; dependency arguments themselves differ. Frank’s sections I–IX reject a prior-stage/dual-society explanation; Wallerstein p. 389 directly names Rostow, but retains stages of systems. This target does not describe every modernization theorist or abolish all historical sequencing.

edges.relationship: Chakrabarty questions Europe as a universal path while retaining critical historical concepts
edges.evidence_note: Chakrabarty questions universalizing European historical categories while continuing to use them critically. Primary introduction pp. 3–6 supports this qualified engagement.

edges.relationship: Social recovery and identity questions overlap without identical assumptions
edges.evidence_note: D’Emilio’s organizational history and Chauncey’s urban research exemplify social inquiry that also historicizes sexual categories. This teaching comparison does not equate all social history with recognition or derive all identity histories from it.

edges.relationship: Portelli and the Phokeng project make testimony an interpreted source for everyday lives
edges.evidence_note: Testimony changes the evidence available for everyday lives; interpretation must include narration and the interview relationship. The Phokeng introduction places material relations alongside narratives rather than treating experience as transparent.

edges.relationship: Life-history inquiry expands access to experiences while questioning homogeneous group identities
edges.evidence_note: Interview projects may expand participation, but interviewees are not transparent representatives of homogeneous groups. Bozzoli’s introduction connects women’s narratives to differentiated social positions; representation is an analytical question.

edges.relationship: Oral-history inquiry makes recollection’s meanings and social organization research questions
edges.evidence_note: Portelli treats the meanings of recollection and narrative difference as evidence, not merely as errors to correct. Passerini’s retrospective account qualifies collective memory and discusses everyday negotiation; Frisch’s contents add public mediation as a reading route. Assmann’s 1995 discussion explicitly draws on oral-history research and Niethammer when describing communicative memory. This is an additional named reception alongside Portelli and Passerini, not a common founding doctrine.

edges.relationship: Cambridge population studies and Thernstrom’s linked mobility research contribute distinct methods to social history
edges.evidence_note: The Cambridge Group’s population reconstruction supplies a concrete example of aggregate evidence within social history. Thernstrom’s primary openings distinguish occupation/property and pose representativeness as a question. This is not proof that all social history is quantitative. Ferrie’s1996 manuscript explicitly revisits Thernstrom: local stayers and delayed observation after arrival can affect measured mobility. His linked male immigrant sample and occupational categories have their own stated limitations; the earlier findings are not simply replaced by a universal law.
edges.map_label: Population reconstruction and linked mobility evidence

edges.relationship: renews study of political argument and action
edges.evidence_note: Skinner’s interventions and Pocock’s political languages renew political-intellectual questions; their approaches are not identical. Skinner’s selected 1969 pages distinguish causal conditions from intended interventions. Pocock’s methodological excerpt asks about actual levels of thinking, while the 1975 introduction selects republican fragility and a proposed Atlantic continuation; the latter’s full transmission argument is not independently verified here.

edges.relationship: shares attention to language; theoretical premises differ
edges.evidence_note: Attention to language does not make contextual intellectual history equivalent to deconstruction or discourse analysis.

edges.relationship: informs analysis of representation and discourse
edges.evidence_note: Representation and discourse provide resources, not a shared doctrine of all cultural historians. Hunt’s introduction distinguishes Kramer’s White/LaCapra comparison from Chartier’s material reading practices and Starn’s visual inquiry; these are differentiated uses, not a single textualist model.

edges.relationship: Scott questions experience treated as transparent evidence and identities treated as given
edges.evidence_note: Criticism targets treating experience as self-explanatory. It does not establish that experience disappears from historical explanation. The 1991 primary passages, pp. 776–778 and 796–797, now support the named critique. Scott explicitly retains experience as an object of explanation; the 1986 source alone did not establish this later essay’s precise argument.
edges.map_label: Scott: historicize experience and social categories

edges.relationship: informs analysis of constructed categories
edges.evidence_note: Scott’s treatment of categories is one route; Omi/Winant and Crenshaw retain distinct intellectual contexts. Scott’s pp. 1067–1068 connect contested representations with institutions and subjectivity; her approach is not simply a claim that language determines everything.

edges.relationship: Said’s discourse analysis and Spivak’s deconstruction provide different textual routes into colonial critique
edges.evidence_note: Said’s discourse analysis and Spivak’s deconstruction name different routes within a broad umbrella. The newly checked primary passages support their respective uses; no single linguistic programme is asserted.
edges.map_label: Said and Spivak: distinct textual methods

edges.relationship: Ginzburg’s intensive cases challenge automatic transfer between general categories and particular situations
edges.evidence_note: Intensive cases test the adequacy of aggregate categories and general accounts; they need not reject every generalization. His 1993 pp. 32–33 explain constructed categories and contextual inquiry; this critique coexists with a newly specified positive contribution to relational social history.

edges.relationship: shares attention to meaning and situated practice
edges.evidence_note: Meaning and local practice are shared questions; methodological overlap does not establish intellectual descent.

edges.relationship: Microhistorical inquiry questions whether aggregate categories capture relations made in practice
edges.evidence_note: The target is the sufficiency of aggregate categories, not the use of numbers as such. Ginzburg’s discussion of Levi and Cerutti supports the bounded category claim, without adjudicating all quantitative methods.

edges.relationship: Annales geography and multiple time scales as a source of ideas and a temporal affinity for environmental history, acknowledged by Worster (1990) and Cronon (1993); McNeill (2003) later reassessed the Annales treatment of environmental change while crediting their general approach as inspirational
