edges.relationship: Staples history as a disputed Canadian antecedent of environmental history: Cook's continuity claim (1990) and Forkey's rejection (1998)
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts first; they disagree. (1) Continuity: Ramsay Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) claims a long Canadian concern with environment: 'In a broad sense the writing of Canadian history has always been concerned with the environment' (p. 6). Against reading the older historians as nationalists only, he writes that nationalism 'was not a full-time interest for any of them. Certainly not Harold Innis for whom the fur trade, the cod fisheries and other staple products were the real stuff of history' (p. 6). He also marks a break: 'Innis, Lower and Creighton also struggled with the question of the impact of the North American environment on European women and men', but 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), and 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus' (p. 7). (2) Rejection: Neil Forkey (CHR 79:1, 1998) rejects the line: 'Although the environment was an ingredient in the work of Harold A. Innis, Donald Creighton, and Arthur R.M. Lower, their studies do not serve as prototypes for Canadian environmental history'; 'In their approach, the environment exists only as a scaffolding on which human history unfolds, and not as an actor in the process' (p. 70). 'The staples model masks the essential role of social relationships and the dynamic between humans and nature', and 'More appropriate antecedents' are found in the historical geographer Andrew H. Clark (p. 71; n. 6 cites The Fur Trade in Canada and The Cod Fisheries). Classification: 'influence' here records a proposed antecedent that Canadian environmental historians disputed, not an established transmission of method; no in-period text read shows environmental historians taking up staples method, and neither position is presented as the Canadian field's. Later readings (2003–2024), labelled as such and not the evidence this edge rests on: Graeme Wynn (2003 review, p. 96) agrees that Forkey is right 'to puncture' claims 'that the staples approach represents an indigenous form of proto-environmental history'; Wynn (2004, p. 33) writes that the staples works 'focused on human uses of the environment', with 'little concern in this work for the reciprocity and mutuality of relations between people and nature'. Tina Loo (2014, p. 622) reclaims the work: 'it could be argued that some of the most influential work on the country's past was a kind of global environmental history, even if its practitioners did not call it that', naming Innis and Lower. Daniel Macfarlane's entry in NiCHE's 'Crash Course in Canadian Environmental History' (2024) holds that Innis's legacy 'still shapes many key debates and approaches in contemporary Canadian environmental history' and that, through works such as Cronon's Nature's Metropolis, the staples and metropolitan-hinterland theses 'are perhaps Canada's biggest contribution to international environmental history'. The edge records a proposed antecedent the field disagreed over; it does not say that Innis wrote environmental history or founded the field. Innis's books are unread here.

edges.relationship: Provincializing Europe: Europe as the silent referent of historical knowledge, the historicism of 'first in Europe, then elsewhere', and European categories held to be both indispensable and inadequate (1992–2000)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History', Representations 37 (1992), pp. 1–26, read in full (the hosted copy's text layer runs words together; spacing restored in quotations): 'insofar as the academic discourse of history—that is, “history” as a discourse produced at the institutional site of the university—is concerned, “Europe” remains the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call “Indian,” “Chinese,” “Kenyan,” and so on'; '“Indian” history itself is in a position of subalternity'; 'Europe' and 'India' are 'treated here as hyperreal terms', figures of the imaginary 'subject to contestation' (p. 1). 'That Europe works as a silent referent in historical knowledge itself becomes obvious in a highly ordinary way': 'Third-world historians feel a need to refer to works in European history; historians of Europe do not feel any need to reciprocate' (p. 2). The everyday paradox is that 'we find these theories, in spite of their inherent ignorance of “us,” eminently useful in understanding our societies' (p. 3). 'Let us call this the project of provincializing “Europe”' (p. 20); it 'does not call for a simplistic, out-of-hand rejection of modernity, liberal values, universals, science, reason, grand narratives, totalizing explanations' (p. 20), and 'must realize within itself its own impossibility' (p. 22). Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction pp. 3–23 read in the publisher's excerpt: historicism 'made modernity or capitalism look ... as something that became global over time, by originating in one place (Europe) and then spreading outside it. This “first in Europe, then elsewhere” structure of global historical time was historicist' (p. 7); it 'came to non-European peoples in the nineteenth century as somebody's way of saying “not yet” to somebody else', and Mill's argument 'consigned Indians, Africans, and other “rude” nations to an imaginary waiting room of history' (p. 8). European thought 'is both indispensable and inadequate', and 'this simultaneous indispensability and inadequacy of social science thought is the task this book has set itself' (p. 6); 'provincializing Europe is not a project of rejecting or discarding European thought' (p. 16). The problem of capitalist modernity is 'a problem of translation, as well' as of transition (p. 17). Chapter 1 'reproduces, in an abridged form, a programmatic statement ... that I published in 1992 in the journal Representations' (p. 19). In-period reception and criticism: Arif Dirlik (Critical Inquiry 20, 1994; read) cites the 1992 essay (p. 334, n. 7) for postcolonial criticism's repudiation of the modes-of-production narrative, and objects that 'The denial of capitalism's foundational status also reveals a culturalism in the postcolonialist argument': 'Without capitalism as the foundation for European power and the motive force of its globalization, Eurocentrism would have been just another ethnocentrism' (p. 346). Dirlik's main target is Gyan Prakash; Chakrabarty appears only in his notes (nn. 7, 12). The wider in-period debate, not aimed at him by name: Rosalind O'Hanlon and David Washbrook, 'After Orientalism: Culture, Criticism, and Politics in the Third World', Comparative Studies in Society and History 34:1 (1992), pp. 141–167. The body is closed access; only the publisher's first-page extract and the article's notes (as listed on Cambridge Core) were read. The extract calls Said's blend of themes 'virtually a paradigm for a new generation of historians and anthropologists' in Indian colonial history, directions 'most recently and sharply endorsed in Gyan Prakash's discussion' (p. 141); a note objects that 'Prakash's notion of what constitutes Marxist history is problematic' (n. 13). None of the notes cites Chakrabarty. The 1.132 adversarial review, reading an OCR copy not consulted here, summarises their case as doubting that the post-foundational programme can sustain historical explanation and political agency, and as holding that Marxist and social historians had already historicised their categories. Prakash replied in the same issue (pp. 168–184). This is criticism of the wider programme, principally Prakash's; it is not evidence of a criticism of Chakrabarty. A contribution, not a founding: the book's epigraph takes 'provincialized' from Gadamer (p. 3), and the post entry already maps Said and Spivak; his argument 'follows directly from my involvement' in Subaltern Studies (p. 15). edge_096 (post → modern) and edge_124 (post → global) stay: they record the group's critiques, which already name him.

edges.relationship: Subaltern pasts and the limits of the historian's translation: a member's critique of the transition narrative within Subaltern Studies (1992–2000)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. 'Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts', Perspectives (AHA), November 1997, read in full (web text, no page numbers; the live page refused automated access, so the July 2024 Internet Archive capture of the same URL was read): 'Let me call these histories subordinated or “subaltern” pasts'; they are 'pasts that resist historicization'; he puts the distinction tentatively: 'it is arguable that what differentiates the Subaltern Studies project from the older tradition of “history from below” is the self-critical awareness of this problem in the writings of the historians associated with this group'. Reading Guha's 'Prose of Counter-Insurgency' on the Santal rebellion of 1855, he writes that 'the historian as historian, unlike the Santal, cannot invoke the supernatural in explaining/describing an event'; the Santal statement 'has to be anthropologized ... before it finds a place in the historian's narrative'; 'Begun in an oppositional mode, “minority histories” can end up being additional instances of “good history.”' 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (1992, read in full) turns the critique on the collective: the transition narrative 'can be located in our own work in the Subaltern Studies project. My book on working-class history struggles with the problem' (p. 4); the project's founding statement shows 'The tendency to read Indian history in terms of a lack, an absence, or an incompleteness' (p. 5). Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction (read): Guha's critique of the category 'prepolitical' 'fundamentally pluralizes the history of power in global modernity' (p. 14), and the book 'elaborates some of the theoretical concerns that have arisen out of my involvement in Subaltern Studies, but it is not an attempt to represent the life practices of the subaltern classes' (p. 20). In-period criticism from inside the collective: Sumit Sarkar, 'The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies' (1997; pp. 84–85, 87 and 97 checked against the page images) quotes Chakrabarty's account of a shift from the attempt 'to write “better” Marxist histories' to the problem of 'universalism/Eurocentrism' and argues 'that the trajectory that has been outlined with considerable precision and frankness by Chakrabarty has been debilitating in both academic and political terms' (pp. 84–85); he asks of Chakrabarty's reading of Bengali domestic ideals, 'Beauty, pleasure, the good life ... for whom, it is surely legitimate to ask' (p. 97). Sarkar quotes two different Chakrabarty texts, neither read here, so both are mediated through Sarkar: the trajectory passage comes from 'Marx after Marxism: Subaltern Histories and the Question of Difference', Polygraph 6/7 (1993) (Sarkar n. 5, page image checked); the domesticity passage comes from 'The Difference-Deferral of a Colonial Modernity: Public Debates on Domesticity in British Bengal', Subaltern Studies VIII (Delhi, 1994), pp. 83–85 (Sarkar p. 97, n. 39, page image checked). A contribution, not a founding: in 1997 he calls Ranajit Guha 'the founder of the group'. edge_115 (subaltern → post) and edge_392 (subaltern → truthdebate) stay; the 1997 essay's engagement with Telling the Truth About History remains on edge_392.

edges.relationship: Bengal jute-mill workers against universal class narratives: culture, hierarchy and the assumption of bourgeois equality in Marx's 'capital' (1989), taken up and contested by labour historians (1990–97)
edges.evidence_note: His own statement of the book's aim. Rethinking Working-Class History (1989), preface pp. xi–xv and introduction pp. 3–6, read in the publisher preview (imprint: copyright 1989; first paperback printing 2000; preface dated February 1988): 'In looking at this history in terms of Marx's categories, however, my objective is to develop a critical understanding of these categories themselves'; 'there is an assumption regarding “culture” built into Marx's category of “capital,” and much of what I have to say on Indian labor history, and labor history in general, follows from this reading of Marx' (p. xi); 'this book is an extended polemic against the reductionism' of political-economic analysis of culture, the 'common sense' of Marxist labour history in India; 'Culture, one might say, is the “unthought” of Indian Marxism' (p. xii). 'Perhaps we have long overestimated capitalism's need or capacity to homogenize the cultural conditions necessary for its own reproduction' (p. xiii). He keeps a commitment to equality: 'The struggle to be a “citizen” must be part of the struggle to be a “comrade”' (p. xiv). The figure of the worker in Marx 'was that of a person who belonged to a society where the bourgeois notion of equality was ingrained in culture' (p. 3), and 'there is no “working class” or “working-class consciousness” that ... “is either transcendental in relation to the field of events or runs in its empty sameness throughout the course of history”' (p. 6, quoting Foucault). He separates his argument from Thompson's: 'That my argument is not the same as Thompson's will be clear to any careful reader' (p. 5, n. 9). In-period reception by labour historians: Janaki Nair's review in International Labor and Working-Class History 37 (1990, pp. 96–99; not re-read here; the graph's verification note records that she recognises the theoretical contribution while questioning cultural determination, the treatment of traditions as survivals and the analysis of gender). Rajnarayan Chandavarkar, '“The Making of the Working Class”: E. P. Thompson and Indian History', History Workshop Journal 43 (1997; written for the 1994 History Workshop conference on Thompson; pp. 177–196 read): Thompson's 'inheritance' 'turned in Dipesh Chakrabarty's hands into a static, timeless, indeed Orientalist characterization of a “traditional” Indian, implicitly “Hindu” culture — in Bengal, a predominantly Muslim province' (p. 182); 'Bengali society, indeed Indian society, was now represented as England's proverbial Other' (p. 183); the view 'recently restated by Dipesh Chakrabarty, that rural migrants “imported a peasant culture into the industrial setting”' 'was not the product of an extensive investigation of the nature of labour migration' (pp. 184–185). Sarkar (1997, p. 87, page image checked) praises 'Dipesh Chakrabarty’s stimulating, if controversial, essays on Bengal labour history'; his n. 10 identifies them as the earlier Subaltern Studies essays 'Conditions for Knowledge of Working-Class Conditions: Employers, Government and the Jute-Workers of Calcutta, 1890–1940' (Subaltern Studies II, 1983) and 'Trade Unions in a Hierarchical Culture: The Jute Workers of Calcutta, 1920–50' (Subaltern Studies III, 1984), not the 1989 book. Nair (1990) and Chandavarkar (1997) are the in-period readings of the book itself. In 1992 he wrote that 'My book on working-class history struggles with the problem' of the transition narrative ('Artifice', p. 4). Context, not a genealogy: Eric Hobsbawm is among those he thanks for reading the manuscript (acknowledgments, p. xvii). edge_742 (subaltern → labourhistory) names him and Nair; see the proposed relabel. edge_358 (subaltern → social) stays.

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm's category 'prepolitical', as quoted in Provincializing Europe, criticised as an instance of the historicism Western Marxism cultivated: the critique Guha began (1983), extended by Chakrabarty (2000)
edges.evidence_note: His own text. Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction pp. 11–15 read in the publisher's excerpt: 'Hobsbawm's category “prepolitical” revealed the limits of how far historicist Marxist thought could go in responding to the challenge posed to European political thought by the entry of the peasant into the modern sphere of politics' (p. 11). Hobsbawm 'readily admitted that it was the “acquisition of political consciousness” by peasants that “made our century the most revolutionary in history”', yet 'missed the implications of this observation for the historicism that already underlay his own analysis' (p. 11). Chakrabarty quotes Hobsbawm calling peasants 'pre-political people who have not yet found, or only begun to find, a specific language in which to express themselves. [Capitalism] comes to them from outside, insidiously by the operation of economic forces which they do not understand', and writes that in 'Hobsbawm's historicist language, the social movements of the peasants of the twentieth century remained “archaic”' (p. 12). Hobsbawm's words are given here only as Chakrabarty quotes them (a quoted-in witness; the bracketed '[Capitalism]' is in Chakrabarty's text). 'The analytical impulse of Hobsbawm's study belongs to a variety of historicism that Western Marxism has cultivated since its inception', including the language of 'survivals' and 'remnants' and 'variations on the theme of “uneven development”' (p. 12). The work quoted: the 1.132 adversarial review, reading a transcription of the book's notes, reports that note 36 (p. 261) cites Hobsbawm, Primitive Rebels (Manchester, 1978 edition; first published 1959), pp. 2–3, and that note 35 concerns rational-choice theory, not Hobsbawm. Neither the notes nor Hobsbawm's pages were read for this revision: the publisher's excerpt omits the notes, the transcription and the open OCR copies of Primitive Rebels were blocked or truncated, and the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only. The identification is therefore the reviewer's, and Hobsbawm's own wording is unverified here. The review also reports, from an OCR witness, that Hobsbawm's p. 2 speaks of the participants' aspirations where Chakrabarty's quotation has 'express themselves', and that Hobsbawm treats the movements of these pre-political people as consequential, not marginal; his book studies a selection of 'archaic forms of social movement' (its subtitle). The edge therefore records Chakrabarty's critique of the category as he presents it, not a verified reading of Hobsbawm's argument. He credits the critique to Guha: Subaltern Studies registered 'a deep sense of unease with the very idea of the “political”' in English-language Marxist historiography, 'Nowhere ... more visible than in Ranajit Guha's criticism of the British historian Eric Hobsbawm's category “prepolitical” in his 1983 book Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency' (p. 11). He keeps Marx: 'Marx is critical for the enterprise' (p. 18), and in 1992 Marx 'remains ... a relevant and fundamental critic of both capitalism and liberalism' ('Artifice', p. 4). The same argument appears in Public Culture (2000, p. 670): read historically, Marx's 'not yet' 'refers us back to the idea of history as a waiting room ... the period to which the Third World is often consigned'. No in-period reply by Hobsbawm was looked for or read.

edges.relationship: Climate change and the collapse of the distinction between natural and human history: humans as geological agents, species history and the history of capital (2009)
edges.evidence_note: Dated 2009, after the atlas's 1920–2000 frame: drafted after the user's decision of 2026-10-14 to end the 2000 break. No claim here concerns his work before 2000. 'The Climate of History: Four Theses', Critical Inquiry 35, no. 2 (Winter 2009), pp. 197–222, read in full. The first thesis: 'Anthropogenic Explanations of Climate Change Spell the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History' (p. 201). His readings in 'globalization, Marxist analysis of capital, subaltern studies, and postcolonial criticism ... had not really prepared me for making sense of this planetary conjuncture' (p. 199). On environmental history: 'the rise of environmental history in the late twentieth century made the breach wider', but 'environmental history, where it was not straightforwardly cultural, social, or economic history, looked upon human beings as biological agents', quoting Crosby's preface to The Columbian Exchange (p. 205); 'Scholars writing on the current climate-change crisis are indeed saying something significantly different from what environmental historians have said so far ... Humans now wield a geological force' (p. 206); the distinction between human and natural histories, 'much of which had been preserved even in environmental histories that saw the two entities in interaction—has begun to collapse' (p. 207). 'The mansion of modern freedoms stands on an ever-expanding base of fossil-fuel use' (p. 208). 'A critique that is only a critique of capital is not sufficient' (p. 212), yet 'the story of capital ... cannot be denied by recourse to the idea of species' (p. 219); the task is 'to mix together the immiscible chronologies of capital and species history' (p. 220). He ends with a 'negative universal history' (p. 222). Reception after 2009, labelled by date: Robert Emmett and Thomas Lekan, eds., Whose Anthropocene? Revisiting Dipesh Chakrabarty's 'Four Theses' (RCC Perspectives 2016/2, from a February 2015 workshop; read in part): the essay 'has become a primary text for understanding the problematic nature of the Anthropocene as a cultural category' (p. 7) and challenges 'ecological histories that situate humans as biological agents' (p. 8). The environmental historian Timothy J. LeCain (2016) writes, tentatively, that the theses 'may prove more radical than even he intended, or perhaps desires' (p. 15). Criticism: in his 2016 response Chakrabarty concedes to Carol Boggs that 'one can no longer separate the biological agency of humans from their geological agency in the way in which I appeared to do' (p. 104), and reports that 'Andreas Malm and Alf Hornborg took me to task' over 'There are no lifeboats for the rich', quoting Kathleen McAfee: 'Contra Chakrabarty, the rich may face the same storms and they do have lifeboats' (p. 108). Malm and Hornborg (2014) are known here only through his response; their article is unread. A contribution that disputes the field's prior framing of human agency, not a founding claim for climate history.

edges.relationship: Craft culture and class conflict: skilled workers' culture as a resource in working-class formation, from 'Most Uncommon Common Men' (1976) to A Culture in Conflict (1979), carried on with Kealey in Dreaming of What Might Be (1982; known here only through later readings); contested by Bercuson (1981)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statement. 'Most Uncommon Common Men: Craft and Culture in Historical Perspective', Labour/Le Travailleur 1 (1976), pp. 5–31, read in full in the journal's PDF. Artisan radicalism 'was part and parcel of a larger context, a matrix of institutions, ideologies and traditions which, taken together, define the contours of a singular culture' (p. 7); 'in viewing culture as a resource and society as the arena in which that resource is utilized, we are necessarily led to a refinement of our conception of the "levels" at which culture operates' (p. 8); 'It has become a standard axiom of an emerging social history of the working class that the artisan, not the debased proletarian, fathered the labour movement. As a class for itself, the working class was born, not in the factory, but in the workshop' (p. 14), where Thompson, the Webbs, Musson and Pelling are cited as agreeing on the skilled mechanic's influence. In-period reception, from a critic: David Bercuson, 'Through the Looking Glass of Culture', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), pp. 95–112, pp. 95–97 re-read in the journal's PDF. He quotes A Culture in Conflict (his n. 10: pp. xii–xiv) for a method of 'sharp detail of limited chronology or restricted region to illustrate the human dimensions of the past', in which 'theory is meant to inform historical inquiry and, in turn, to be informed by historical research', and (n. 11: p. xiii) for 'a tradition of empirical Marxism' (p. 96); 'Palmer calls the skilled the cutting edge of the working class. They could just as easily be labelled the rearguard'; 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes"' (p. 97). Bercuson's methodological objection (pp. 107–108, read in the journal's PDF): 'Historians must prove that Canadian workers, men and women, skilled and unskilled, were bound by a common culture that was primarily the product of their class experience before they can use culture to explain anything'; workers 'seem to have responded as much from consciousness of job, place, church, ethnic group, and other factors as from a culture of class'; he asks whether 'class was a more important means of self-identification than gender' (p. 107), and writes that 'Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else' (p. 108). Kealey's companion defence in the same issue defends class analysis and culture (wcreq_kealey_1981; not re-read in 1.134). A Culture in Conflict (1979), Dreaming of What Might Be (1982) and Working-Class Experience (1983; 1992) were not read here; they are cited at title level and through Bercuson. The edge's in-period evidence covers 1976–81; the 1982 Knights of Labor book is mentioned in the relationship text but rests only on McCoy's later quotation, so the label's dates stop at 1979. Later readings, labelled as such: Nicholas Rogers (2021) reads A Culture in Conflict as following Thompson in finding resistance among skilled artisans and in quoting Thompson's working-class culture as a 'way of struggle' rather than a 'way of life' (citing pp. xii, xiv); Ted McCoy (2021) quotes Kealey and Palmer's chapter on the Knights: 'A subordinate class must reach toward an alternative hegemony if it ever hopes to dominate the ethos of society' (Dreaming, p. 277, as quoted). A contribution, not a founding: Freeman (2002) names Palmer with Kealey and Sangster in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail, and the 1976 essay calls its thesis an axiom of an emerging field. edge_890 (ep_thompson → cdn_working_class) and edge_886 (marx → cdn_working_class) stay: they record the Thompsonian and Marxist resources and the 1981 debate; this edge records Palmer's own contribution.

edges.relationship: Answers Scott's case for reconceiving labour history through language and gender, which he read as reducing class and its material relations to discourse (International Labor and Working-Class History forum, 1987); Scott replied that class struggle is produced in discourse, which she defined to include institutions and social practices. Descent into Discourse (1990) was his subsequent book-length intervention
edges.evidence_note: Scott's position in her own words. 'On Language, Gender, and Working-Class History', International Labor and Working-Class History 31 (Spring 1987), pp. 1–13; only p. 1 was read (publisher's preview image): gender 'has not been considered seriously for what it could provide in the way of a major reconceptualization of (labor) history'; theories of language 'offer a way of thinking about how people construct meaning, about how difference (and therefore sexual difference) operates in the construction of meaning'; labour historians' recent articles on 'language' 'reduce this important concept to the study of "words"' (p. 1). Palmer's response in the same issue, 'Response to Joan Scott', pp. 14–23; only p. 14 (preview image) and the notes listed by the publisher were read. It opens on the Halifax strikes of August 1842, with Palmer imagining himself at the scene, 'Conscious of "the need to avoid economic determinism" and aware of the extent to which "our needs are made of words"', thirsting 'for a dialogue with the participants that will both reveal all and deepen the discourse' (p. 14); n. 2 says the quoted phrases come from Stedman Jones's introduction to Languages of Class and from Ignatieff, 'texts that I take to be related to one another'. Scott's 'A Reply to Criticism', ILWCH 32 (Fall 1987), pp. 39–45, read in full, reports and quotes his response: Palmer and Christine Stansell 'share a fundamental disagreement with my emphasis on "language," arguing instead that material reality, social experiences, real or concrete events are the stuff of social history' (p. 39); she quotes his 'No discourse today! The class struggle has intervened' and answers: 'The opposition discourse versus class struggle is one I cannot accept, for class struggle is produced in discourse'; 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 40). She defines the term at once: 'By discourse I do not mean utterances, or "words" ... but whole ways of thinking, of understanding how the world operates and what one's place is in it. And not only ways of thinking, but ways of organizing lives, institutions, societies, ways of implementing and justifying inequalities, but also of refusing them'; to say that 'the working class family was created within working-class discourse' 'is not to say that "words" alone brought families into being' (p. 40). The reduction-to-discourse objection is therefore Palmer's interpretation of her argument, which she rejected. She says 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me, and little of it has to do with either women or gender' (p. 41), that he implies she has deviated from Marx's dialectical and historical materialism, to which she answers that 'there is more to Marx, greater complexity in his materialism, than Palmer's crude invocation of it' (p. 43), and that 'There is no choice, as Bryan Palmer insists there is, between a focus on class or gender; each is necessarily incomplete without the other' (p. 45). These are Scott's characterisations of his text. The forum had four voices, not two camps. Christine Stansell ('A Response to Joan Scott', pp. 24–29; only p. 24 read, publisher's preview image) called Scott's essay 'a welcome and important attempt to import some of the sophisticated concerns of current literary criticism into labor history' and sided 'with Joan Scott in believing that historians' willful lack of interest in poststructuralist debate is our loss—or, more properly, our missed opportunity' (p. 24). Anson Rabinbach ('Rationalism and Utopia as Languages of Nature: A Note', pp. 30–36; only p. 30 read) restated with approval her case that Stedman Jones's language 'is as instrumentalized in the notion of politics as economic interest is in the notion of class' (p. 30). Scott grouped Palmer with Stansell on 'language' and wrote that Rabinbach 'endorses and expands on my analysis' (p. 39); she answered Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject' (p. 42) and Rabinbach's case for rationalism and universalism (p. 44) separately. The rest of Stansell's and Rabinbach's essays was not read. Later readings, labelled as such: Ted McCoy (2021) quotes the response: 'To say that language matters is not to say it is all that matters' (p. 16, emphasis original) and 'Class is indeed a difficult development to grasp precisely because in both its subjective and objective guises it reproduces the social order at the same time as it challenges it. Language and gender figure in this decisively' (p. 22); he reads Palmer as granting that attention to the gendered features of language is 'indisputable'. Descent into Discourse (1990; unread here) carried the dispute into its chapter on gender: Nicholas Rogers (2021) and Chad Pearson (2021) quote it on Scott's appraisal of women in The Making of the English Working Class: in Pearson's quotation it 'thus tilts too problematically toward the determining power of discourse' (p. 85), while Rogers paraphrases it as tilting 'too problematically towards' it, and as quoting Scott's 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 180), the sentence read above in her 1987 reply. The arrow records Palmer's critique and Scott's rejoinder; it does not judge the dispute. Scott's own critique of Thompson's gendered account of class remains on edge_314 (gender → ep_thompson).

edges.relationship: Descent into Discourse: the linguistic turn in social history criticised as a 'reification of language', with class held to originate in relations of production rather than in discourse; Stedman Jones's languages of class a principal target (1987–90)
edges.evidence_note: The book (Temple University Press, 1990) was not read: the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only and its search-inside service returned HTTP 403. Its wording is taken from an in-period review that quotes it with page numbers: Alex Callinicos, Labour/Le Travail 29 (1992), pp. 311–313, read in full in the journal's PDF. Callinicos quotes Palmer: 'Much writing that appears under the designer label of poststructuralism/post modernism is, quite bluntly, crap' (199); Callinicos describes Palmer's standpoint, in his own words, as 'not that of a defensive empiricism but of a critical, anti-Stalinist Marxism', and quotes the book: 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected' (xiii); yet discourse theory 'contains insights and guides capable of opening new doors of understanding to historians committed to a materialism that recognizes the need for a rigorous reading of documents and texts/contexts' (189). The book is 'a critical survey of "the reification of language"' from the Russian Formalists through Foucault and Derrida that 'traces the vulgarization of their ideas by historians working in the fields of politics, gender, and class' (p. 312). Against 'the reduction by Gareth Stedman Jones et al. of class as a discursive construct', Palmer writes that 'class relations are, in origin, economic relations rooted in the capitalist process of accumulation, whereby one social stratum expropriates surplus from another' (138) (p. 312). Callinicos's in-period objections: Palmer is 'too willing to fall in line with the dominant way in which poststructuralism has been received in the English-speaking world' and misreads Foucault's Archaeology (p. 312); his claim that 'class as an objective economic reality is not present before the arrival of industrial capitalism' (139) sits oddly with Ste Croix; 'Perhaps, like Edward Thompson before him, Palmer has reacted to the dissolution of agency into structure by underestimating the objective determinants of subjective action' (p. 313). He calls the results 'admirable' and his disagreements 'relatively minor' (p. 312). The target was already set in 1987: Palmer's ILWCH response (p. 14 and n. 2, read) borrows phrases from Stedman Jones's Languages of Class for the first-person scene that opens it, and Scott's reply says 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me' (ILWCH 32, p. 41). Later readings, labelled as such: Rogers (2021) quotes Palmer in 1993 granting that 'Poststructurally inclined historians rightly stress the need for closer attention to language and representation' ('The Poverty of Theory Revisited', Left History 1:1, 1993, p. 94, as quoted; unread here); Finkel (2021) calls the book Palmer's 'anger with the discursive turn'. Scope: a critique of the linguistic turn's treatment of class, not of attention to language as such. edge_105 (language → social) and edge_200 (historyworkshop–language) stay.

edges.relationship: Liberal order criticised as an elastic, seemingly trans-historical category that sidesteps capitalism's changing historical structures, in a review of McKay's Reasoning Otherwise (2009)
edges.evidence_note: Dated 2009. 'Radical Reasoning', a feature review essay on Ian McKay, Reasoning Otherwise (2008), The Underhill Review (Carleton University), Fall 2009, read in full (web text; locators below are pages of the print PDF, https://www3.carleton.ca/underhillreview/09/fall/reviews/print/Palmer.pdf). He reads McKay's liberal order as a project 'in which liberty, equality, and private property are sanctified as the foundations of a civil society that valorizes individualism', and says past leftists 'never spoke of an enemy that they named "liberal order."' 'As an elastic category, liberal order can contain almost anything associated with what has traditionally been understood about modern developing societies'. 'The danger in deploying liberal order in this way, as a seemingly trans-historical analytic framework, is that it actually sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism's changing historical structures'; 'it may well be impossible to discern anything distinctly Canadian about the notion of liberal order'; 'The most serious problem with the liberal order perspective, then, is that it allows mainstream historians to avoid confronting just how critically important it is to name the frontline enemy: capitalism as systematic exploitation and endlessly proliferating oppression.' He adds that McKay's 'elastic understanding of Gramsci's hegemony conflates what Gramsci differentiated as a "separation of powers"'. The elasticity and capitalism argument is at pp. 3–4 and the Gramsci criticism at pp. 4–5. Qualifications kept: 'McKay is not necessarily captive of such tendencies himself' (p. 4), and the book 'stands as an undeniable achievement' (p. 31). This is Palmer's interpretation of the framework. McKay's own position, recorded under lof_mckay_2009 and known here through Fecteau's quotation, distinguishes the two analytically while treating them as historically close: 'Liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated. Yet, after the 1840s, they also could not be easily separated' (p. 385, as quoted by Fecteau, 2009). That chapter appeared in the same year and is not a reply to Palmer; no direct rejoinder was found. Scope: the essay reviews Reasoning Otherwise and quotes Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005, p. 84); it does not discuss the 2000 prospectus directly. McKay's reply, if any, was not checked. The critique-audit of 2026-10-14 proposed a group edge cdn_working_class → liberal_order_framework on this text; with the person entry, the person edge carries it and the group edge is not proposed. edge_845 (karl–liberal_order_framework, comparison) stays.

edges.relationship: Thompson's history of class and culture as a model for Palmer's labour history and the subject of his studies of Thompson (1976–94), with disagreements Palmer stated, including on base and superstructure
edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence. Palmer's 1976 essay (read) cites Thompson's Making for the skilled mechanic's leading role (p. 14 and notes). Bercuson (1981, p. 97, re-read): 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes."' Kealey (1981, p. 82; existing note, not re-read) cites Palmer's forthcoming book as the place where Thompson's work is analysed at length. Palmer's 1987 ILWCH response (notes as listed by the publisher) leans on Thompson: n. 8 cites The Making (pp. 529–40) for how historians have interrogated the language of sources, n. 10 says 'This unity of the political and the economic is fundamental to Thompson's Making', and n. 14 cites The Poverty of Theory (pp. 235–36). 'Homage to Edward Thompson', Labour/Le Travail 32 (1993) and 33 (1994), read at Part I pp. 67–68 and Part II pp. 16–18: Palmer sets out Thompson's socialist humanism against 'the mechanical idealism of Stalinism's appropriation of the base/superstructure metaphor' (Part I, p. 68) and quotes Thompson calling The Making 'a polemic against abbreviated economistic notations of Marxism' (Part II, p. 17; Thompson's interviews, cited in n. 9, not read). Palmer's two books on Thompson, The Making of E. P. Thompson: Marxism, Humanism, and History (1981) and E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions (1994), are cited at title and imprint level only (Open Library). Stated disagreement, in period: Callinicos (1992, p. 313) notes that Descent into Discourse 'takes Thompson and Raymond Williams to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure' (pp. 209–11 of the book, unread here). Later readings, labelled as such: Nicholas Rogers (2021) quotes Palmer's 1993 interview in Left History: 'it was relooking at The Making that convinced me to do labour history' (Left History 1:2, 1993, pp. 111–12, as quoted; the journal's PDF was behind a bot wall); Rogers calls The Making 'an exemplary model' for Palmer's dissertation, finds Palmer 'sympathetic and defensive of Thompson's position', but notes that 'Palmer does not necessarily agree with Thompson's reading of Marx' and 'is not a wholehearted advocate of Thompson's socialist humanism', since he holds to a revolutionary vanguard. Influence, not discipleship: the arrow records Thompson's work as Palmer's model and subject; it does not claim that Palmer adopted Thompson's positions whole.

edges.relationship: From within Marxism, rejects the 'economic automatism' of Stalinist base-and-superstructure Marxism and the treatment of class as 'a thing', holding to the 'dialectical interaction between social consciousness ... and social being' and faulting Marx's own 'clumsy static model' (1957–78)
edges.evidence_note: Thompson's own in-period statements. (1) 'Socialist Humanism: An Epistle to the Philistines', The New Reasoner 1 (Summer 1957), pp. 105–143, read in full in the Marxists Internet Archive transcription (no page numbers). Of Stalinist theory: 'How much easier if the people had no minds, if the "superstructure" was cut out and society was all "base"'; 'This economic automatism certainly is not Marxism.' 'In all their historical analysis Marx and Engels always kept in view this dialectical interaction between social consciousness (both active and passive) and social being. But in trying to explain their ideas they expressed them as a make-belief "model", the "basis" of social relations (in production) and the "superstructure" ... In fact no such basis and superstructure ever existed; it is a metaphor to help us to understand what does exist – men, who act, experience, think and act again. It turns out that it is a bad and dangerous model, since Stalin used it not as an image of men changing in society but as a mechanical model, operating semi-automatically and independently of conscious human agency.' 'An idea is not a reflex of a gasometer'; 'No "basis" ever invented a steam engine, or sat on the National Coal Board.' He does not exempt Marx: 'because Marx reduced his concept of process to a clumsy static model, Stalinism evolved this mystique'; features of Stalinism 'can be traced to ambiguities in the thought of Marx and, even more, to mechanistic fallacies in Lenin's writings'. Stalinism's three features are 'anti-intellectualism, moral nihilism, and the denial of the creative agency of human labour'. The revolt against Stalinism 'will, if successful, confirm the revolutionary confidence of the founders of the socialist movement'. (2) Preface to The Making of the English Working Class (1963), university-hosted transcription read in full (transcription pp. 1–2; printed pagination not collated): class is 'something which in fact happens (and can be shown to have happened) in human relationships'; 'There is today an ever-present temptation to suppose that class is a thing. This was not Marx's meaning, in his own historical writing, yet the error vitiates much latter-day "Marxist" writing', in which the class-consciousness that '"it" ought to have' is deduced and 'a cultural superstructure' lets recognition dawn 'in inefficient ways'; 'If we remember that class is a relationship and not a thing, we can not think in this way.' The same passage finds 'a similar error ... on the other side of the ideological divide', in the static sociology of Smelser and Dahrendorf, so the preface's target is reification in both camps. The preface's 'I am seeking to rescue the poor stockinger ...' is aimed at Fabian, economic-historian and 'Pilgrim's Progress' orthodoxies, not at Marxism, and is not used here. (3) 'The Poverty of Theory' (1978), section x, re-read in the Marxists Internet Archive transcription: 'Stalinism afforded a caricature of Marxism, which offered ... an identical reification of process, in which a "superstructure" was reduced to confirming or legitimating a base' (the identity is with Smelser's sociology), and no analogies 'derived from mechanical or organic mechanism' can 'encompass the logic of indeterminate historical process', since no analogy from another area can have 'any more than a limited, illustrative, metaphoric value (and often, as with basis and superstructure, a static and damaging one)'; in section vii he calls himself 'deeply indebted for certain concepts to Marx's own practice'. In-period readings: Palmer's 'Homage to Edward Thompson' (1993, Part I, p. 68) describes Thompson's socialist humanism as directed against 'the mechanical idealism of Stalinism's appropriation of the base/superstructure metaphor', and (1994, Part II, p. 17) quotes Thompson calling The Making 'a polemic against abbreviated economistic notations of Marxism' (from interviews, not read). The critique was itself contested inside Marxism: Callinicos (1992, p. 313) reports that Palmer's Descent into Discourse took Thompson and Raymond Williams 'to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure'. Later reading, labelled as such: Rogers (2021) sees in Thompson a 'rejection of economic determinism and the base–superstructure model of explanation favoured by many Marxists', preferring 'the co-determination of social being and social consciousness, mediated by experience'. Scope: a critique of economistic and Stalinist uses of historical materialism, and of Marx's own static model, made from within Marxism; it is not a rejection of historical materialism. The Althusser critique stays on edge_310 (ep_thompson → althusser) and edge_027 (marx → althusser); his contribution to Marxist social history stays on edge_309 (ep_thompson → marx).

verification.note: Expanded check: all 19 public scan images of the Land and Life reprint, printed 315–350, read through image inspection and local OCR, including notes. Opening four scan pages (printed 315–321) visually compared with the unfinished transcription; substantive opening claims confirmed, without claiming a perfect diplomatic transcription. sources.title: Aldo Leopold, A Sand County Almanac (1949); Aldo Leopold Foundation, author and book overview.
sources.citation: Aldo Leopold, A Sand County Almanac (1949); Aldo Leopold Foundation, author and book overview.

verification.note: Foundation overview checked for original 1949 Oxford University Press publication and the book’s natural observation and ethical concerns. The book was not read in full. Cronon’s separately cited afterword supplies the specific retrospective acknowledgment of landscape training modeled on Leopold’s course. Addendum 2026-10-13: Text of 'The Land Ethic' and 'Good Oak' read for the 1.131 person entry in two unpaginated transcriptions: an accessible-media text of the 1966 enlarged Oxford edition on the Internet Archive (item sand-county-almanac-with-essays-on-conservation-from-round-river-by-aldo-leopold; contents give 'Good Oak' p. 6 and 'The Land Ethic' p. 237 of that edition), and a transcription of 'The Land Ethic' headed 1949 (faculty.lsu.edu/kharms/files/leopold_1949.pdf). The two agree on the passages quoted. 'The land ethic simply enlarges the boundaries of the community to include soils, waters, plants, and animals, or collectively: the land.' 'In short, a land ethic changes the role of Homo sapiens from conqueror of the land-community to plain member and citizen of it.' 'That man is, in fact, only a member of a biotic team is shown by an ecological interpretation of history. Many historical events, hitherto explained solely in terms of human enterprise, were actually biotic interactions between people and land. The characteristics of the land determined the facts quite as potently as the characteristics of the men who lived on it.' The Kentucky cane-lands, 'when subjected to the particular mixture of forces represented by the cow, plow, fire, and axe of the pioneer, became bluegrass'; 'we do not even know where the bluegrass came from'; 'In short, the plant succession steered the course of history'; 'Is history taught in this spirit? It will be, once the concept of land as a community really penetrates our intellectual life.' 'Good Oak': 'Fragrant little chips of history spewed from the saw cut'; 'The three tools are requisite to good oak, and to good history.' 1949 pages, from others' citations only: history passage p. 205 (Worster 1990, n. 1; Wynn 2001, n. 55); bluegrass origin p. 206 (Worster 1990, n. 3); community boundaries p. 204 (Wynn 2001, n. 54); 'Good Oak' pp. 6–18 (Cronon 1993, n. 32; Wynn 2001, n. 48). The Almanac's 1933 forerunner, 'The Conservation Ethic' (Journal of Forestry 31:6, 634–643, doi:10.1093/jof/31.6.634), was not read.

Addendum 2026-10-13: Cambridge University Press sample PDFs of the second edition (assets.cambridge.org, ISBN 9780521546188: front matter, 18 pp.; excerpt, 10 pp.; image-only, OCR'd) read: imprint ('First published 1986; Canto edition first published 1993; Second edition first published 2004'), contents pp. xi–xii, 2004 preface pp. xv–xx, acknowledgments pp. xxi–xxii, prologue pp. 1–7 and the opening of chapter 2, pp. 8–10. Page numbers are the 2004 edition's; the 1986 edition (Open Library OL2713233M: xiv, 368 p., [16] p. of plates, ISBN 0521320097) has the same length as the 2004 body plus index, but its pagination was not seen. Quoted: 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation'; 'Europeans, in contrast, seem to have leapfrogged around the globe'; 'what I shall call the Neo-Europes, lands thousands of kilometers from Europe and from each other' (p. 2); 'factors perhaps best described as biogeographical' (p. 5); 'European flora and fauna, including human beings, can thrive in these regions if the competition is not too fierce'; 'what in heaven's name is the reason that the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion? Perhaps the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component' (p. 7). Contents: 'The Norse and the Crusaders' (41), 'The Fortunate Isles' (70), 'Winds' (104), 'Weeds' (145), 'Animals' (171), 'Ills' (195), 'New Zealand' (217), 'Explanations' (269), 'Conclusion' (294). Acknowledgments: 'William McNeill, who read the whole thing in first draft' (p. xxii); parts first appeared in Environmental Review and The Texas Quarterly. The 2004 preface (later) calls Pomeranz's The Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario' (p. xvii, n.) and says 'I am proud to have contributed to it' (p. xx). Chapters 2–12 are unread.

verification.note: Expanded from repository opening to complete available article OCR and notes, 107–116. Worster explicitly rejects monocausal ecological history (108), critically receives Malin, distinguishes entrepreneurial values from rival farming cultures (113), and allows varying intensity across regions (note17). His interpretation of 1977 imagery and predictions about later dust storms are historical arguments, not independently audited scientific findings. verification.note: Complete four-page transcription read, including acknowledgments: class as a historical relationship, conditioned experience and culturally formed consciousness, criticism of reification and static social roles, failed causes, English scope and Dorothy’s ideas/notebooks. Smelser and Dahrendorf are named targets; Hill, Briggs and Saville read drafts. Transcription has errors and is not collated with the printed edition. This is the primary preface, not a full-book reading or validation of its historical claims. Addendum 2026-10-14: Re-read in full for the 1.134 extra edge (ep_thompson → karl). Transcription pp. 1–2: 'There is today an ever-present temptation to suppose that class is a thing. This was not Marx's meaning, in his own historical writing, yet the error vitiates much latter-day "Marxist" writing'; the class-consciousness '"it" ought to have'; 'a cultural superstructure, through which this recognition dawns in inefficient ways'; 'a similar error is committed daily on the other side of the ideological divide' (Smelser, Dahrendorf); 'If we remember that class is a relationship and not a thing, we can not think in this way.' Transcription p. 3: the 'enormous condescension of posterity' passage answers Fabian, empirical economic-history and 'Pilgrim's Progress' orthodoxies. Rogers (2021, n. 1) places the class-consciousness passage at pp. 9–10 of the 1968 Penguin edition; printed pages were not checked.

sources.citation: Ian McKay, "A Note on 'Region' in Writing the History of Atlantic Canada," Acadiensis 29, no. 2 (Spring 2000): 89–101.

verification.note: Pages 89–90 read: a 1997 workshop programme dominated by gender, ethnicity and community rather than "regional underdevelopment, class conflict and the position of the Atlantic Provinces within Confederation"; this pluralism continues "the social-history revolution of the 1960s and 1970s" but "places a question mark over the very concept of an 'Atlantic Canada'". Checked against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (citation line on p. 89). Addendum 2026-10-13: the whole essay (pp. 89–101) read in the UNB PDF. Note 1 (p. 89): 'a lightly-edited version of the introductory talk I prepared for the Atlantic Canada Workshop which met in Halifax in August 1997'. Pages 90–91 state the liberal-order programme: 'a strategy of reconnaissance'; 'That project, very briefly, was the project of liberal order, a coherent attempt to install a liberal public philosophy and practice of "peace, order and good government" in northern North America'; 'Canada was thus a process, not a self-evident thing, and the key to this process was liberalization'. Where region fits that approach: 'Quite centrally' (p. 95). The essay sets aside natural and essentialist definitions (pp. 95–96), asks heartland–hinterland and dependency models to 'undergo the rigorous analysis of concepts' (pp. 96–99) and resists a nationalizing historiography (p. 99). It proposes exploring 'the remarkable extent to which Atlantic Canadians built the Canadian liberal project' (p. 99) and the region's 'communitarian critique of the liberal order' (p. 100). Page 89 names 'the Gramscian assumptions that have shaped my outlook'.

sources.citation: James W. St. G. Walker, "Allegories and Orientations in African-Canadian Historiography: The Spirit of Africville," Dalhousie Review 77, no. 2 (1997): 155–178.

verification.note: Full text read. Walker identifies five "orientations" (not schools) in African-Canadian historiography, distinguished by the role assigned to Black people: Black Clients (focus on white justice and philanthropy), Black Victims, Black Achievers, Black Community (which coincided with the social history movement) and, in the 1990s, Black Survivors. Africville serves as allegory for the African-Canadian experience. Note: the request cited this as CHR 1999; the checked record is Dalhousie Review 1997. Re-read 2026-10-12 for this draft: Clients (Landon, Riddell; Stouffer 1992), Victims (Silverman 1985; "American scholars pointed the finger at the racist reality lurking behind the North Star mythology"), Achievers, Community (Black Power, Black pride, social history; Winks said The Black Loyalists ended the "victims" school), Survivors (Brand 1991). About 80 articles, 50 books and 40 graduate theses in two decades; black women receiving increasing attention. The further-reading list was used to corroborate several records. Checked against: DalSpace (Dalhousie) repository record and full-text PDF.

verification.note: Abstract read: an analysis of “the concept of working-class culture as applied by some practitioners of the new labour history in Canada”; questions “the validity of using such a general framework” — the evidence at times supports working-class culture as an important determinant and at other times does not; argues that to insist history be studied “from the bottom up” is “as predeterministic as the notion that it should be studied ‘from the top down.’” Published in the issue’s Critiques section; Kealey replies in the same issue (wcreq_kealey_1981). Checked against: Labour/Le Travail article page with abstract, https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/2658 (read 2026-10-12); Crossref DOI record (JSTOR); answers/verification.json Q29. Addendum 2026-10-13: Full text read (Érudit PDF, id.erudit.org/iderudit/llt7cri02, pp. 95–112). p. 97: Canadian practitioners of the new labour history “follow the thinking of E.P. Thompson in Britain, Herbert Gutman in the United States, and others in applying the culturalist approach to Canadian experience”; “Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as ‘complementary processes’” (citing A Culture in Conflict, p. xii, which was not itself checked). p. 98: in Canada new labour historians “stand in the middle but so far tend to lean to the British experience. They study working-class culture for the explanation and definition they believe it offers in the Thompson sense”. p. 108: “Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else.” A critic’s characterization, not a self-description. Addendum 2026-10-14: Pp. 95–97 and 107–108 re-read for the 1.134 person entry in the PDF on the journal's site (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/2658). p. 96: the new labour history's method 'as Palmer describes it' ('sharp detail of limited chronology or restricted region to illustrate the human dimensions of the past'; 'theory is meant to inform historical inquiry and, in turn, to be informed by historical research'; n. 10: A Culture in Conflict, xii–xiv) and 'what Palmer labels "a tradition of empirical Marxism"' (n. 11: xiii). p. 97: 'Palmer calls the skilled the cutting edge of the working class. They could just as easily be labelled the rearguard'; 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes"' (n. 13: xii). pp. 107–108: 'Historians must prove that Canadian workers, men and women, skilled and unskilled, were bound by a common culture that was primarily the product of their class experience before they can use culture to explain anything'; workers 'seem to have responded as much from consciousness of job, place, church, ethnic group, and other factors as from a culture of class'; whether 'class was a more important means of self-identification than gender' (p. 107); 'Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else' (p. 108).

Read: Part I opening, p. 10: Thompson's histories “occupy a special and influential place”, alongside “a nagging denigration of his accomplishments”; a footnote lists Greg Kealey's obituary in the St. John's Evening Telegram (5 September 1993). Keyword search of both parts found biography and political history, not an account of Thompson's reception in Canadian labour history (except Queen's University seminars in 1988 and a Kingston theatre visit). Addendum 2026-10-14: Both parts downloaded from the journal's site (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/4897 and /4917) for the 1.134 drafts, searched in full and read at Part I pp. 67–68 and Part II pp. 16–18. Thompson, 48–51. The book is 'ambitieux, intelligent, informé, bien argumenté' but 'ne convainc pas tout à fait'; Huang-Yun, where the Yellow River and Grand Canal cross, covers roughly western Shandong (p. 242). sources.title: David S. Jones, “Virgin Soils Revisited,” William and Mary Quarterly, 3rd ser., 60, no. 4 (October 2003): 703–742.
sources.citation: David S. Jones, “Virgin Soils Revisited,” William and Mary Quarterly, 3rd ser., 60, no. 4 (2003): 703–742. doi:10.2307/3491697.

verification.note: Later reading. JSTOR copy read as posted in an MITx course on edX (courses.edx.org asset 'VirginSoilWMQ'), pp. 703–711 and 718–720 closely, the rest searched for 'Crosby'. Crossref 10.2307/3491697: WMQ 60(4), October 2003, from p. 703. Jones quotes Crosby's 1976 definition (pp. 703–704). 'Even as Crosby's model of virgin soil epidemics remains a central theme of the historiography of the Americas, it has been misunderstood and misrepresented. Crosby actually downplayed the "genetic weakness hypothesis" and instead emphasized the many environmental factors that might have contributed to American Indian susceptibility to Old World diseases, including lack of childhood exposure, malnutrition, and the social chaos generated by European colonization' (p. 704). Historians 'have often reduced the complexity of Crosby's model to vague claims that American Indians had "no immunity"' (p. 704). Writers who 'attribute depopulation to irresistible genetic and microbial forces ... risk being interpreted as supporting racial theories of historical development' (p. 705). Crosby 'later described how thousands of years of disease exposure in Eurasia had created an Old World "superman"' (p. 707; the paragraph's n. 12 cites Ecological Imperialism, p. 34). 'McNeill, Crosby, and other historians utilized virgin soil theory' to restore causation (p. 711). Crosby's opening assertion of immunological defencelessness 'and the Darwinian tone of his other work jarred with the article's concluding emphasis on environmental causes of Indian susceptibility'; 'Crosby's work has been cited as both proof of immunological weakness and as evidence against it' (p. 719).

sources.scope_note: Later reading (2003), labelled as such: the main critique of the virgin-soil model.

verification.note: Review read in full in the free Cambridge Core PDF (Crossref: Medical History 31(3), July 1987, 373–374; reviewer Robert Miller, Institute of Archaeology, London). Crosby documents the impact of 'what he calls the "portmanteau biota" of Old World crops, livestock, weeds, people, and pathogens' (p. 373); indigenous societies 'initially able to resist European military technology on nearly equal terms succumbed to hunger and disease', with malnutrition magnifying disease (p. 373); 'Crosby is in general conservative when it comes to estimating mortality from disease in post-contact history and is careful to take account of other social and biological factors that favoured the emergence of neo-Europes'; 'this is not just a study of disease, but a vividly written account of ecological transition, and Crosby is careful not to overestimate the significance of any single component' (p. 374). Accept the revised digital/web selection: two research-field entries, seventeen selected works, twenty-seven historical claims, thirty-one author credits, two version links, twenty contextual strands and twenty-six shared people. Practitioner contributions and critical scholarship coexist; no new teaching arrows. Exact 2000 baseline remains 1.121; no field-completeness claim.

Figure gaps: fifteen figures the review record ties to fields the atlas never named, approved by the user. Foucault joins New cultural history as the first of Hunt’s 1989 models, with a contribution edge and a strand; Prakash, Hall and Gilroy join postcolonial history; Rorty the linguistic turn; Lukács (precursor) and Kracauer the Frankfurt School; Davis and Broszat microhistory; Harvey, Benjamin and de Certeau urban history, with a strand; Davidoff (with coauthor Catherine Hall) and Fox-Genovese women’s history; Warburg (precursor) memory studies. No new people or full person nodes; no post-2000 imports.

Student beta: two bounded roster contributions from the figure audit. Said’s documented 1988 foreword joins Subaltern Studies; Cooper’s 1997 collaboration with Stoler joins the postcolonial-history context with one internal approach. Bibliographic and publisher-description limits remain explicit. No new entries, people, teaching arrows, or post-2000 claims.

Indigenous-history deep dive: 21 source-linked roster people, 15 distinct approaches, 27 scoped sources and nine additional person entries with approach-specific contribution links. Earlier manuscript/print and interwar practices, Canadian scholarship and Hawaiian historical inquiry become explicit. Preserve collective narrators, coauthors, original/reprint dates, source-reading limits and independent roots. No new influence arrows, external identity matches, venue mappings or post-2000 field extension.

Complex foundations of academic Indigenous history: community–university Stó:lō practice, labour and institutional histories, middle-ground interpretation, colonial geography and adjacent settler-colonial scholarship. Leddy’s 2010 methodological reflection adds one selected later intervention with distinct scholar, mentor and family-knowledge roles. Twelve new local participants and existing Cole Harris add thirteen roster rows; seven approaches and two undirected comparisons. No individual promotions or new influence arrows; exact-2000 baseline preserved.

Historiography in Canada: sixteen Canadian group entries (the national tradition, intellectual and cultural, religion and reform, the liberal order framework, moral regulation, working-class, women and gender, childhood and family, immigration and race, Black Canadian history, Indigenous–newcomer relations, Quebec historiography, military, political, the "Who Killed Canadian History?" debate, regional, the 1960s) and settler colonialism, drafted from verified sources and weighted by what 2009–2026 Canadian History PhDs cite. New people, sources and comparison, contribution and critique edges; no person entries, no extension interventions; exact-2000 baseline preserved.

Person-entry links for historiography in Canada: E. P. Thompson → Canadian working-class history and Joan Wallach Scott → Canadian women’s and gender history, each evidenced by pre-2000 Canadian texts read at the cited passages; Patrick Wolfe promoted to a person entry with contributions to settler colonialism and anthropology (1999 book: introduction pp. 1–2 read, the rest at contents level). The Marxist edge to working-class history no longer carries Thompson’s name. Catherine Hall’s edge is deferred: no checked pre-2000 passage.

Kenneth Pomeranz promoted to a person entry, with contributions to world / global history (reciprocal comparison), economic history (regional divergence) and environmental history (ecological constraint), on The Great Divergence (2000; introduction read) and The Making of a Hinterland (1993; contents and a full review). edge_063 no longer carries his name.

Environment family: person entries for William Cronon, Donald Worster, Alfred W. Crosby, Carolyn Merchant and Richard White (the 1990 JAH round table minus Pyne) and precursor entries for Aldo Leopold and Rachel Carson; Innis linked to environmental history as a disputed Canadian antecedent (Cook's continuity claim, Forkey's rejection); edge_111 revised from an undirected comparison to an Annales influence acknowledged by Worster and Cronon, reassessed later by McNeill; environment roster rows for Hays, Nash, Pyne, Le Roy Ladurie, Innis and Richard White; edge_720 and edge_336 no longer carry person names.

Dipesh Chakrabarty promoted to a person entry, with contributions to postcolonial history (provincializing Europe, 1992–2000), Subaltern Studies (subaltern pasts and historical translation) and labour history (Bengal jute workers and Marx's categories, 1989, contested by Nair and Chandavarkar), a critique of Hobsbawm's 'prepolitical', as quoted in Provincializing Europe, as historicist (2000), and a contribution to environmental history dated 2009 in its label and text ('The Climate of History'; no post-2000 flag is carried, dating conventions are left to revision 1.133). edge_742 no longer carries his name.

Open frame: the 1920–2000 cutoff ends. Prose coverage limits become coverage.reviewed_through (2000 for every group, pending field-by-field review); open spans; the exact-2000 view (1.121) moves to scope.archive; title "The Historiography Atlas".

Bryan D. Palmer promoted to a person entry, with a contribution to Canadian working-class history (craft culture and class conflict, 1976–82), critiques of Joan Scott (the 1987 International Labor and Working-Class History exchange, carried into Descent into Discourse, 1990), of the linguistic turn (Descent into Discourse, 1987–90) and of the liberal order framework (2009, dated in its label and text), and E. P. Thompson's influence on him (1976–94). One extra edge: Thompson's critique, from within Marxism, of economistic base-and-superstructure Marxism (ep_thompson → karl, 1957–78), to open the proposed 'question of class' pathway. No existing edge is revised.

edges.relationship: Founded in 1967 as an institutional home for the emerging social-history programme Peter Stearns sought to establish within the discipline.
edges.evidence_note: Censer’s publisher abstract explicitly connects the founding with Stearns’s effort to establish the field’s disciplinary position. This does not date the origin of all social history or assert that the journal founded the entire field.

edges.relationship: Founded in 1976 by History Workshop activists to advance collaborative, democratic historical work through a journal of socialist historians.
edges.evidence_note: The movement’s institutional account links the 1976 journal to its democratic-history purpose and 1975 manifesto. Feminist commitments developed further; the later subtitle is not projected unchanged onto 1976.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1929 to develop economic and social history across the divisions separating historians and researchers of contemporary societies.
edges.evidence_note: Bloch and Febvre’s first editorial states the interdisciplinary problem motivating the new periodical. The target is the atlas entry that includes this founding project, not a claim that every later Annales approach already existed. This record names the 1929 title rather than assigning its founding date to an unverified modern-title run.

edges.relationship: Hosted Stone’s 1979 Revival of Narrative essay and Hobsbawm’s 1980 comments, providing a concrete entry into the narrative-versus-structural-explanation controversy.
edges.evidence_note: Two publisher records identify the opening essay and named follow-up in adjacent issues. The existing revival entry supplies the qualified debate context. The journal hosted the disagreement; it did not endorse one side, and this exchange did not terminate quantitative history.

edges.relationship: Founded in 1952 through a coalition involving British Marxist historians to advance historical research for readers across periods, regions and specialisms.
edges.evidence_note: The link locates a journal-building initiative within Marxist social history while retaining its generalist purpose and participation beyond Marxism. It does not identify the journal as exclusively Marxist, date the birth of social history to 1952, or replace its separate narrative-debate edge.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1959 following the joint planning of SHOT and its journal, with a programme of bringing disciplines together in the history of technology.
edges.evidence_note: Participant recollections connect the 1958 institutional decision to the first-issue programme. The edge records institutional consolidation and interdisciplinary intent; older histories of technology are not erased and subsequent practice is not inferred from the manifesto.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1975 with a programme connecting historical inquiry and social-scientific analysis through thematic issues, research reports and discussion.
edges.evidence_note: Uses the already reviewed four-author founding foreword. Historical social science is broader than Sonderweg; neither all later journal contents nor every contributor is assigned to a single doctrine. The announced editorial mechanisms are not an audit of implementation.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1916 under Carter G. Woodson and ASNLH to preserve, publish and expand knowledge of Black historical experience and contributions.
edges.evidence_note: Contemporary reception reproduced in volume 1 describes the recovery and documentation programme. This institutional milestone falls within the atlas’s earlier roots; Black historical thought predates the journal. The 1916 original title remains distinct from the 2002 Journal of African American History title.

edges.relationship: Established as a project in 1912 to institutionalize history of science through Sarton’s programme of historical synthesis, set out in the first volume published in 1913.
edges.evidence_note: Preserves the existing 1912 foundation date and explicitly distinguishes 1913 first publication. The initial Sartonian synthesis is one programme within history of science; it does not characterize the entire field or the journal’s later pluralism.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1976 as part of the organizing effort that established an institutional community for environmental history in the United States and produced ASEH in 1977.
edges.evidence_note: The journal and society were planned together to organize an emerging field. This institutional formation is distinct from the later 1990 renaming, 1996 merger and the separate Environment and History launched in 1995. It does not make US institutionalization the origin of all environmental historical thought.

edges.relationship: A sustained interdisciplinary venue for women’s history.
edges.evidence_note: Norberg reviews historical writing across the journal’s first decades, including suffrage research; Smith-Rosenberg’s 1975 essay is an early anchor.
edges.selection_note: Selected for sustained historical contributions within feminist scholarship. This is a women’s-history link, not a claim that every article is historical or that the journal founded the field.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. The endpoint limits this review, not the journal’s later importance.

edges.relationship: A continuing feminist forum publishing women’s history and historical special issues.
edges.evidence_note: Institutional history documents connections with historians; Norberg identifies an enduring historical publishing role.
edges.selection_note: Selected for a sustained historical strand in an interdisciplinary journal, rather than an exclusive disciplinary identity.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary. Open from revision 1.133: 2000 was the atlas boundary.

edges.relationship: A specialist venue for feminist gender history during the 1990s.
edges.evidence_note: Norberg’s retrospective identifies the journal as a dedicated feminist-history outlet from 1989; the earlier institutional-history source supports its launch context.
edges.selection_note: Selected for the gender-history part of the atlas entry. This does not establish equivalent coverage of every racial-formation approach in that broad entry.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary. Open from revision 1.133: 2000 was the atlas boundary.

edges.relationship: A specialist venue connecting women’s history with feminist and gender analysis.
edges.evidence_note: Meade and Rupp trace a continuing forum from its diverse first volume through later methodological debates.
edges.selection_note: Selected for dedicated historical publishing. The retrospective rejects a simple progression from an exclusively white, US-centred beginning; this selection retains that qualification.
