sources.title: Past & Present editorial team, Celebrating the 250th Issue (2021)
sources.note: Read the institutional extract of Hilton and Walsham’s anniversary introduction: founding generalist, international and accessible ambitions. Retrospective account, not the 1952 editorial or a full longitudinal assessment.

sources.title: Dave Renton, Marxist History, IHR Making History (2008)
sources.note: Read discussion of the 1952 foundation, British Marxist historians and coalition-building on the early board. Used for the broad institutional connection, not every biographical or political label in this retrospective.

sources.title: SHOT, Melvin Kranzberg: participant recollections from Technology and Culture (1996)
sources.note: Read Robert P. Multhauf’s account of the January 1958 decision to establish SHOT and its journal, and the Case Years section quoting the interdisciplinary purpose in Kranzberg’s first-issue At the Start. First issue 1959 agrees with the accepted library record. Retrospective testimony; its sweeping claim that one man invented the field is not adopted.

sources.title: World History Association announcement, AHA Perspectives (1 October 1989)
sources.note: Read contemporary announcement: new journal to encourage systematic world-historical research from a global perspective, publication beginning 1990, Jerry Bentley editor. WHA founded 1982; journal launch is not the origin of world history.

sources.title: Helmut Berding, Wolfgang J. Mommsen, Hans-Jürgen Puhle and Hans-Ulrich Wehler, “Vorwort der Herausgeber,” Geschichte und Gesellschaft 1 (1975), 5–7; reprinted in Die Bielefelder Sozialgeschichte (2010), 91–94.
sources.note: Reused the atlas’s existing gg_founders_preface check and bielefeld/journal_programme reading. Complete primary foreword read in reproduced 2010 reader OCR at https://doi.org/10.14361/9783839415214-017 . Author heading names all four contributors; original publication footnote distinguishes 1975 original pages 5–7 from reprint 91–94. Includes final cooperation appeal. Publisher chapter direct access failed; no original-image collation. Programme and intended discussion/thematic-issue mechanisms are documented, not an audit of their practical success or entire editorial history. Later reader introduction is not backdated.

sources.title: The Journal of Negro History 1 (1916), first-issue masthead and April reception notices, Gutenberg transcription
sources.note: Read January masthead identifying Woodson and ASNLH, and April How the Public Received the Journal of Negro History: reproduced reviews describe the new journal’s document-preservation and historical-recovery aims. These are contemporaneous reception notices reproduced by the journal, not a signed founding editorial. No original-page collation.

sources.title: Feminist Studies, institutional history
sources.note: History page read: organizing discussions from 1969, first publication in 1972, scholarly and political purposes, and early connections with the Berkshire Conference on the History of Women. Retrospective institutional account.

sources.title: Signs, A History of the Journal
sources.note: Institutional history read, including the reproduced 1975 editorial statement on new scholarship about women and its interdisciplinary aims. Not a separate full reading of the original first issue.

sources.title: Anne E. C. McCants, Editor’s Introduction to Volume 40, Issue 1, Social Science History (2016)
sources.note: Publisher text read: 1976 first volume and the founding SSHA constitution printed there, stating a programme of improving historical explanation through selective use of social-science theories and methods.

sources.title: Richard Trainor with Aris Grivokostopoulos, Whatever happened to social history?, Economic History Society centenary project (2026)
sources.note: Society’s historical research post read: first-issue economic-and-social subtitle and Ashley’s 1927 programme. The society’s 1926 establishment is separate from the journal’s 1927 publication start.

sources.title: Oral History Association Newsletter 7(2), June 1973, announcement of the new Oral History Review
sources.note: Read the launch notice: new annual Review combining papers from the 1972 Austin colloquium with contributed articles, distributed to members. This establishes a publication mechanism for the association’s field, not a claim about all later methodological positions.

sources.title: David Henige, On Method: An Apologia and a Plea, History in Africa 1 (1974), 1–7
sources.note: Publisher’s substantial opening extract read, not the entire seven-page article. The first-volume editor explicitly gives the new journal a methodological purpose: critical evaluation of sources and their use. DOI 10.1017/S0361541300005751.

sources.title: Antoinette Burton, Some origins of gender history as a field, Gender History: A Very Short Introduction (2024), chapter 1
sources.note: Publisher abstract read, not the chapter or the 1989 founding editorial. It explicitly identifies the 1989 launch and the journal’s purpose of examining gender’s historical experience, meaning and significance.

sources.title: Robert Rotberg interview with Ed Freedman, Fifty years of the Journal of Interdisciplinary History, MIT Press (2019)
sources.note: Publisher interview with the founding editor read: social-science and innovative historical methods, with a special place for quantification but a programme also encompassing art, climate and other approaches.

sources.title: Gerald Holton, George Sarton, His Isis, and the Aftermath, Isis 100(1) (2009), 79–88
sources.note: Read discussion of Sarton’s founding programme, dated November 1912 and published in volume 1 in 1913, together with the distinction between the initial synthesizing project and later pluralism. DOI 10.1086/597571.

sources.title: Sylvia L. Thrupp, Editorial, Comparative Studies in Society and History 1(1) (1958), 1–4
sources.note: Opening pages 1–3 read: comparative research across history, humanities and social sciences, communication between specialists, and attention to differences as well as recurring problems. DOI 10.1017/S0010417500000037.

sources.title: John Hutchinson, Nations and Nationalism: the first 25 years, Nations and Nationalism 25(1) (2019), 5–15
sources.note: Founding section of the accepted manuscript read, including the reproduced 1995 editorial aims: a research forum consolidating an interdisciplinary scholarly community. Separates ASEN’s earlier formation from the 1995 journal launch. DOI 10.1111/nana.12489.

sources.title: American Society for Environmental History, History of ASEH
sources.note: Institutional history read: joint journal/association organizing effort in 1976, journal launch in 1976 and society formation in 1977. Evidence of field-building, not merely a publisher remit. Earlier intellectual roots and traditions outside the US are not erased.

sources.title: JSTOR, Environmental History: title history
sources.note: User-supplied page and complete-title-history export checked. Family contains overlapping environmental and forest-history branches, not one succession chain. Listed modern-title coverage ends in 2020; page links current issues elsewhere. Coverage endpoints are not cessation dates.

sources.title: Oxford Academic, Environmental History Review: About the Journal
sources.note: Publisher record read: Environmental Review 1976–1989 continues as Environmental History Review 1990–1995, which merges with Forest & Conservation History in 1996 to form Environmental History. The archive’s 2006 endpoint is not cessation.

sources.title: Kathryn Norberg, History in Signs, in Signs at 40: Editorial Commentaries (2015)
sources.note: Norberg’s historical-corpus commentary and Hawkesworth’s early-article discussion read. Topic-model weights are not article counts or importance scores. Norberg’s incidental 1990 date for Journal of Women’s History is not adopted; its own retrospective gives 1989.

sources.title: Feminist Studies: institutional history
sources.note: History page read, including Berkshire Conference links and later editorial organization; paired with Norberg’s retrospective assessment of historical publishing.

sources.title: Teresa A. Meade and Leila J. Rupp, Journal of Women’s History at 25 (2014)
sources.note: Participant retrospective read: first volume in 1989, early international and theoretical work, and subsequent relationship between women’s and gender history. First-volume examples are not misdated to 1990.

sources.title: Comparative Studies in Society and History, Editorial Foreword: CSSH at Fifty (2008), 1–8
sources.note: Read pp. 1–2 on successive editors and the continuing comparative forum. The 2008 article summaries are not evidence of pre-2000 content; dated atlas articles supply earlier anchors.

sources.title: Immanuel Wallerstein, “The Rise and Future Demise of the World Capitalist System: Concepts for Comparative Analysis,” Comparative Studies in Society and History 16.4 (1974), 387–415.
sources.note: Reused atlas source wallerstein_rise_primary. Original check: Read printed 387–400 and 411–415 using OCR; 401–410 unread. Named Braudel, Polanyi, Luxemburg, Frank/Santos and Sweezy resources; direct Rostow and Dobb criticism. The division-of-labor unit permits external arenas. Coerced-labor, agricultural-capitalism and future-system claims are arguments, not consensus. Final page endorses archival and quantitative work. Quoted originals and detailed semiperiphery mechanisms in unread pages not independently checked.

sources.title: Joan W. Scott and Louise A. Tilly, “Women’s Work and the Family in Nineteenth-Century Europe,” Comparative Studies in Society and History 17, no. 1 (1975): 36–64.
sources.note: Reused atlas source scott_tilly_work. Original check: Publisher-hosted primary opening extract and original issue metadata read. Questions assumptions that domestic women were unproductive or that paid work and emancipation formed one linear sequence. Remainder of article and data unread; online 2009 date is not original publication.

sources.title: Sherry B. Ortner, “Theory in Anthropology since the Sixties,” Comparative Studies in Society and History 26.1 (1984), 126–166.
sources.note: Reused atlas source ortner_practice_primary. Original check: Scan transcription of primary 126–128 and beginning 129 read; remaining essay unread. Page 127 calls practice an orientation embracing several theories/methods and explicitly locates the author’s perspective. Publisher metadata at Cambridge confirms January 1984, not 2009 online date. Platform-generated summary ignored; cited genealogies are Ortner’s assessments.

sources.title: Hans Medick, “Missionaries in the Row Boat”? Ethnological Ways of Knowing as a Challenge to Social History, Comparative Studies in Society and History 29(1) (1987): 76–98.
sources.note: Reused atlas source medick_missionaries. Original check: Cambridge primary opening and notes checked at https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/comparative-studies-in-society-and-history/article/abs/missionaries-in-the-row-boat-ethnological-ways-of-knowing-as-a-challenge-to-social-history/3FC3FA5BAC8CA59E26CB341A4A24075D . Introductory note engages Bernard Cohn’s critique of ahistorical anthropology; note 10 documents the working group since 1978 and Medick/Sabean, Interest and Emotion (1984). This substantiates a particular exchange; full article and earlier German version unread.

sources.title: Anne E. C. McCants, Editor’s Introduction to Volume 40, Issue 1 (2016)
sources.note: Read retrospective account of forty years of SSHA’s journal, continuity of analytical commitments and expanding international scope. Includes both qualitative and quantitative methods.

sources.title: Richard Trainor with Aris Grivokostopoulos, Whatever Happened to Social History? (EHS, 2026)
sources.note: Read the society’s century review, based on sampled journal contents and institutional records. Samples cover founding decades, 1960s–1970s and 1987–2005. Current quantitative proportions are not projected backwards.

sources.title: Kathryn Nasstrom, Troy Reeves and Andrew Shaffer, OHA fiftieth-anniversary virtual issue: Editors’ Introduction (2016)
sources.note: Complete five-page retrospective introduction read. Fifteen selected articles span the journal; pre-2000 examples are distinguished from later selections. Editors explicitly acknowledge a US emphasis.

sources.title: Robert Rotberg and Ed Freedman, Fifty Years of the Journal of Interdisciplinary History (MIT Press, 2019)
sources.note: Full interview text read: retrospective examples of inventories, population reconstruction, slave-trade records, climate, arts and other methods. Editors’ assessment is attributed, not an independent ranking.

sources.title: Gerald Holton, George Sarton, His Isis, and the Aftermath (2009), 79–88
sources.note: Read longitudinal discussion of issues from 1913, 1924, 1934, 1944, 1954, 1984 and 1994, and the late-century assessment. The existing 1912 foundation / 1913 first-volume distinction is preserved.

sources.title: John Hutchinson, Nations and Nationalism: the first twenty-five years (2019), 5–15
sources.note: Accepted-manuscript founding and development sections read, including early contributions, the 1996 Miller symposium, ongoing lectures and institutional editorial continuity. Later statistics are not used to rank its 1990s importance.

sources.title: Brian Fay interview on History and Theory (Wesleyan, 2008)
sources.note: Interview read on the journal’s 1960 origin, editorial continuity from 1965, and recurring theory/philosophy theme issues. Self-description as the leading journal is not adopted as a measured ranking.

sources.title: New Left Review, A Brief History, 1960–2010
sources.note: Institutional retrospective sections on changing editorial phases read, including British-history theses, Marxist theory and later historical contributions. Predecessors and the 2000 new series are distinguished.

sources.title: Jack R. Censer, On a Mission: Peter Stearns and the Journal of Social History (2018), 444–456
sources.note: Publisher abstract read, not the full article. It explicitly describes sustained importance, changing methods and Stearns’s continuing defence of social history. Selection is limited to that longitudinal abstract claim.

sources.title: History Workshop, Our History
sources.note: Institutional history section read, distinguishing the movement, the 1976 journal and 2010 digital magazine; acknowledges increasing academic professionalization.

sources.title: Raphael Samuel, “Local History and Oral History,” History Workshop Journal 1(1) (1976): 191–208.
sources.note: Reused atlas source samuel_local_oral. Original check: OUP bibliographic record checked. Full article remains unread: the OUP page offers restricted PDF access and a university reprint download returned 404. Publication documents a specific early journal venue; the separate Davin/Taylor participant account supports the teaching mechanism. No detailed argument is attributed from the title alone.

sources.title: Doreen Massey, Places and Their Pasts, History Workshop Journal 39(1) (1995):182–192.
sources.note: Reused atlas source massey_places_pasts. Original check: Accessible primary OCR across the complete article and notes read; numerous missing words marked [Link] and spacing errors prevent claiming complete textual collation. Publisher confirms date, pages and Spatial History section. Supports contested place histories, explicit Gilroy use and criticism of Harvey 303, independently checked here. Her political examples are attributed interpretations; original Gilroy/Wright/Bhabha passages not newly collated. Adjacent Ruskin course advertisement is separate.

sources.title: Past & Present, Celebrating Issue 250: selected articles and editorial commentaries (2021)
sources.note: Read commentaries on Hobsbawm 1952, Finley 1962, Lewin 1979, Davis 1981 and Stewart 1995. Contemporary evaluations are attributed to the retrospective editors; later selections are excluded.

sources.title: Michel R. Doortmont, Making History in Africa: David Henige and the Quest for Method in African History (2011), 7–20
sources.note: Read pp. 7–9 and 14–20: review of 36 volumes, source criticism and archival reports. Retains 1974 volume dating while noting the author’s April 1975 appearance date; no canonical chronology is changed.

sources.title: SHOT, Melvin Kranzberg: participant memorials
sources.note: Read recollections of journal editing, manuscripts, institutional development and the 1981 editorial handover; retrospective participant evidence, not a complete article census.

sources.title: World History Bulletin 28.2 (2012), Jerry Bentley remembrance
sources.note: Search-indexed retrospective passage read: the journal’s central role from its 1990 launch through Bentley’s editorship. Direct PDF now returns 404 and archive endpoint unavailable. No claim to have read the complete tribute.

sources.title: American Society for Environmental History, History: Publications
sources.note: Read institutional account of successive society journals and editors. This supports institutional continuity; title boundaries use the separately accepted publisher/JSTOR review.

sources.title: David Bloor, “Anti-Latour,” Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 30.1 (1999), 81–112.
sources.note: Reused atlas source bloor_anti_latour_primary. Original check: Downloaded original journal PDF. Read introduction 81–82, section-three opening 87–88, agency discussion 91–92, central symmetry paragraph on 102 and conclusion 110–111; additional adjoining passages read without claiming complete intervening pages or full article. Bloor distinguishes beliefs about nature from nature, includes material causes, and rejects equal credibility as the meaning of symmetry. His assessments of Latour and historical examples remain attributed claims. Final rejoinder at 131–136 unread. Additional reading in1.65: complete90 and opening91, including the response to Latour’s Pasteur example. Bloor proposes asking about interpretive resources and contrasts Koch’s response; historical case claims remain his.

sources.title: Bruno Latour, “For David Bloor… and Beyond,” Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 30.1 (1999), 113–129.
sources.note: Reused atlas source latour_bloor_reply_primary. Original check: Original journal PDF from author archive: complete 113–120 and opening 121 read, not remainder. DOI 10.1016/S0039-3681(98)00039-9 matches PubMed; 00038-7 belongs to Bloor. Page 114 and note 2 provide explicit debt and mediation testimony. Earlier CiteSeer, Melissa and legacy-page fetches failed; original located through author catalogue page 15. Claims about opponents and French epistemology remain Latour’s interpretations, not independent verdicts; translation credits are not separately collated.

sources.title: Anthony D. Smith and Ernest Gellner, Warwick debate, 24 October 1995; published in Nations and Nationalism (1996).
sources.note: Reused atlas source warwick_nationalism. Original check: Primary Smith opening read on the LSE resource page; Gellner’s reply at https://www.lse.ac.uk/researchAndExpertise/units/gellner/Warwick2.html consulted for cultural continuity and modern mobility/literate culture. The linked introduction dates the event to 1995, distinct from publication. Smith credits Gellner’s teaching but disputes sufficiency of modernist explanation; neither position is a consensus. Gellner’s provocative primordialist label does not define Smith’s own qualified ethno-symbolic position.

sources.title: Ernest Gellner, reply to Anthony D. Smith in the Warwick debate (published 1996)
sources.note: LSE primary reply consulted, previously read for atlas source warwick_nationalism. Event took place in October 1995; journal publication in 1996 is the venue date.

sources.title: Osvaldo Raggio, Microstoria e microstorie (Treccani, 2013)
sources.note: Read historical account through the microhistory laboratories section, especially the collective issues of 1976–1987. Participant scholarship; later book-series activity is distinguished from journal publication.

sources.title: Oladipupo Olugbodi and Olufunke Adeboye, Decolonization and Functionality of Knowledge in JHSN, 1956–1980 (2025), 19–48
sources.note: Downloaded published PDF; read historical development pp. 25–29 and conclusion pp. 41–43, plus abstract. The authors’ evaluation of practical relevance is attributed. Post-1980 continuity is not inferred; the conclusion records revival in 2005.

sources.title: JSTOR: Journal of the Historical Society of Nigeria
sources.note: Publisher-supplied title, society, 1956 start and ISSN checked. Archive endpoint 2021 is coverage, not cessation.

sources.title: Grace E. Riehm et al., What Is Ethnohistory? A Sixty-Year Retrospective (2019), 146–162
sources.note: University-hosted scholarly abstract read, not the full article. It reports sampled ten-year intervals from 1954 to 2013, North American predominance and expanding regional/methodological scope. No unreported quantitative results adopted.

sources.title: American Society for Ethnohistory: institutional history
sources.note: Read society history: Indian Claims Act research, changing institutional identity and journal publication since 1954. Present membership counts are not historical importance measures.

sources.title: Roberto Ceamanos Llorens, La historia obrera y social contemporánea en Francia a través del estudio de Le Mouvement Social (1960–2000), ACHSC 33 (2006), 311–336
sources.note: Published PDF read: abstract/introduction and conclusions pp. 334–335. Reconstructs the move from organized labour to broader social history. Its developmental judgment about overcoming Marxism is the author’s, not a claim adopted by the atlas.

sources.title: Pero Gaglo Dagbovie, Building upon a Century-Long Tradition of Excellence (2019)
sources.note: Read editorial retrospective, especially founding, segregation-era role and successive editors through 2001. Post-2002 topic percentages and current circulation are excluded from the pre-2000 selection.

sources.title: Annales / Cambridge University Press: Chronology of the journal
sources.note: Publisher’s explicit chronology read: 1929–1938, 1939–1941, 1942–1944, 1945, 1946–1993 and 1994 onward. These are title phases, not six unrelated journal foundations.

sources.title: Persée: Annales collection and title periods
sources.note: Checked post-1938 title identifiers and ESC/HSS boundaries. ESC and HSS share ISSN 0395-2649. The erroneous summary row naming 1929–1937 Mélanges is not adopted; publisher chronology governs. Holdings gaps are not missing publication years.

sources.title: Christoph Conrad, Une tradition d’innovation: Les Annales dans le paysage transnational des revues d’histoire, 1990–2020, Annales 75(3–4), 635–648 (2020 issue, online 2021)
sources.note: Published repository PDF read pp. 635–642, including scope/method, 1988–1994 transition and thematic examples. Exploratory comparison, not a representative global census. Later issue examples are not backdated.

sources.title: Peter Burke: Annales in its wider historical setting
sources.note: Reused scoped atlas check: Selected passages checked on generations, Berr, Pirenne, Simiand, and precedents. Comparative parallels are not automatically lines of transmission.

sources.title: Annales editors, “Histoire et sciences sociales. Un tournant critique?” (1988), “Tentons l’expérience” (1989); Bernard Lepetit, “L’histoire et les modèles” (1988), collected in the journal’s editorial archive.
sources.note: Reused scoped atlas check: Primary 1988 critical-turn text, Annales 43/2:291–293, read, including explicit microhistory/scale discussion; selected opening and closing 1989 passages, 44/6:1317–1323, and selected Lepetit model passages, 43/1:3–4, read. Experiments, evidence, comparison and generalization are discussed without declaring one replacement paradigm. Remaining archive, including the 1996 Lepetit obituary, not reviewed. The later collection date does not extend mapped coverage.

sources.title: Sergio Sismondo, 2012 Changes, part II, Social Studies of Science 42(5), 635–637
sources.note: Search-indexed opening retrospective read from the Citeseer-hosted published PDF: editorial succession and established STS role by the late 1970s. Direct Sage access unavailable and Citeseer download now 404. Complete editorial not read.

sources.title: JSTOR: Social Studies of Science title history
sources.note: Title history checked: Science Studies 1971–1974; Social Studies of Science from 1975. 2022 is archive coverage, not cessation.

sources.title: Trevor J. Pinch and Wiebe E. Bijker, “The Social Construction of Facts and Artefacts,” Social Studies of Science 14 (1984): 399–441.
sources.note: Reused scoped atlas check: Scanned journal pp. 399 and 402 visually inspected: authors explicitly combine SSK and technology research. Abstract names interpretative flexibility, closure and relevant groups; not a full-paper review.

sources.title: Robert Nye, Regard sur vingt ans de travaux: le Journal of the History of Sexuality, Clio 31 (2010), 239–266
sources.note: Read indexed opening of the article PDF and indexed journal abstract in issue abstracts (clio/pdf/9566), also matching author bibliography. Direct OpenEdition blocked by bot check; Cairn returned 403. Full article unread.

sources.title: Bob Weyeneth and John Dichtl, “Update on the Journal,” NCPH, 1 May 2012.
sources.note: Institutional account read: UCSB launch in 1978 and continuing editorial home, university/society/publisher partnership. A participant account of institutional continuity; it is not a quantified content survey or evidence for global representativeness.

sources.title: Robert Kelley, “Public History: Its Origins, Nature, and Prospects,” The Public Historian 1(1) (1978), 16–28.
sources.note: Downloaded scan; read pp. 16–20, including externally posed questions, museums, government, preservation, consultancy and Kelley/Johnson’s 1975 training discussion. Later pages unread. His claims for policy benefits are advocacy, not independent evaluation; this is a US professional formulation, not the origin of all public historical practice.

sources.title: Social History of Medicine editors, “Chairs’ Choices Anniversary Virtual Issue” (2020).
sources.note: Read introduction and dated pre-2001 selections: journal began in 1988 after the Society’s Bulletin; articles span public health, clinical records and medical knowledge through 2000. Editors attribute choices to teaching, reception and personal experience. Later examples are not backdated; a commemorative selection is not a representative content census.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Urban History: 50th Anniversary Collection, selected pre-2001 extracts and abstracts.
sources.note: Read extracts of 1974 editorial, Reeder’s 1979 Dyos appreciation and Rodger’s 1992 retrospect; abstract of Lees (1994) and Lilley (2000). Publisher dates distinguish issue years from 2009 digitization. Full articles unread. Supports institutional continuity and varied approaches, not a uniform school or global census.

sources.title: Cambridge: Urban History past titles
sources.note: Publisher lists Urban History Yearbook volumes 1 (1974)–18 (1991); Rodger’s volume 19 (1992) extract confirms the succeeding journal. Digitization dates are not publication origins.
